The city was sacked by the Mongols in 1258; the books of the House of Wisdom were thrown into the Tigris until the river is said to have run black with ink for days. The Mongol destruction ended the Islamic Golden Age.

question: From 1556 to 1605 the Mughal emperor of India was Akbar the Great, who united much of the subcontinent and pursued an unusual religious policy for the era — allowing freedom of religion, abolishing taxes on non-Muslims, and inviting scholars of all faiths to his court for debate. What did Akbar call this principle?
answer: Sulh-i-kul — 'universal peace'
choices: Sulh-i-kul — 'universal peace'
Bismillah — 'in the name of God'
Sharia — 'the path'
Hijab — 'the cover'
context: Akbar was illiterate but had books read to him constantly. He invited Hindu, Jain, Zoroastrian, Christian (Jesuit), and Sikh scholars to debate religion in his throne room. He even tried to create a syncretic 'Din-i-Ilahi' (Divine Faith) combining elements of all major religions — though it never spread beyond his court. His great-grandson Aurangzeb (r. 1658-1707) reversed Akbar's tolerant policies, imposing strict Islamic law and persecuting Hindus and Sikhs, weakening the empire long-term.

question: Between 1325 and 1354 a young Moroccan scholar set out for the pilgrimage to Mecca and ended up traveling about 75,000 miles across Africa, Asia, and parts of Europe — almost three times farther than Marco Polo. He visited 44 modern countries. Who was this traveler?
answer: Ibn Battuta
choices: Ibn Battuta
Zheng He
Marco Polo
Vasco da Gama
context: Ibn Battuta visited Mecca seven times and served as a judge in the Maldives and as an ambassador for the Sultan of Delhi. He went as far as China and as far south in Africa as Tanzania. He dictated his memoirs (called the Rihla, or 'Journey') to a court scribe back in Morocco. Few people anywhere traveled as widely as Battuta until the 19th century. The crater Ibn Battuta on the Moon is named for him; so is a major shopping mall in Dubai.

question: Around 533 BC a 29-year-old Indian prince named Siddhartha Gautama, sheltered all his life inside a royal palace, went outside for the first time and saw four sights that changed him forever — an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering holy man. He renounced his royal life to seek spiritual enlightenment. The man Siddhartha became is known by what title?
answer: The Buddha
choices: The Buddha
The Mahatma
The Avatar
The Bodhisattva
context: Siddhartha spent six years as an extreme ascetic, nearly starving to death, before deciding that the 'Middle Way' between luxury and starvation was the path to enlightenment. He reached enlightenment under the Bodhi Tree at age 35 (around 528 BC) and spent the next 45 years teaching across northern India. He died around 483 BC, possibly from food poisoning. Buddhism became one of the world's major religions, especially across East and Southeast Asia.

question: From about 1100 to 1450 AD a city of stone walls, towers, and buildings — without mortar, just precisely fitted blocks — flourished in southern Africa. At its peak it may have had 18,000 residents. European explorers in the 1800s refused to believe Africans had built it. What is the site called?
answer: Great Zimbabwe
choices: Great Zimbabwe
Timbuktu (Mali)
Aksum (Ethiopia)
Lalibela (Ethiopia)
context: Great Zimbabwe ('the great stone houses') was the capital of a powerful trading state that controlled the gold and ivory trade between the African interior and the Swahili coast. Its central enclosure has walls 36 feet high. The site was abandoned around 1450, probably from environmental degradation. The modern nation of Zimbabwe took its name from the site. The Great Zimbabwe Bird, an elegant soapstone sculpture found there, appears on the modern Zimbabwean flag.

question: On February 12 1912 a six-year-old boy was forced to abdicate as emperor of China, ending 2,000 years of imperial rule. He had been put on the throne at age 2 and would have a strange life — briefly restored as a Japanese puppet emperor in Manchuria in the 1930s, then captured by the Soviets, then 're-educated' as an ordinary citizen by communist China. What was his name?
answer: Pu Yi (Aisin Gioro)
choices: Pu Yi (Aisin Gioro)
Sun Yat-sen
Mao Zedong
Chiang Kai-shek
context: Pu Yi was the last emperor of the Manchu Qing Dynasty and the last emperor of China. After the Chinese revolution of 1911, he was allowed to live in the Forbidden City as a private person until 1924. The Japanese installed him as 'Emperor of Manchukuo' in 1932 (a puppet state). After the war he was held by the Soviets, then handed to communist China in 1950 for re-education. He died in 1967 as an ordinary worker. His life inspired Bertolucci's 1987 film 'The Last Emperor.'

question: In 1701 a Japanese lord was provoked into drawing his sword inside the shogun's palace and was forced to commit ritual suicide. His 47 loyal samurai, now masterless, secretly planned for two years, then attacked and killed the man they blamed for their lord's death. They turned themselves in and were ordered to commit ritual suicide together. What were these masterless samurai called?
answer: Ronin — 'wave men, drifters'
choices: Ronin — 'wave men, drifters'
Daimyo — 'great names'
Geisha — 'art persons'
Shogun — 'general'
context: The 47 Ronin (Akō rōshi) story is one of the most famous in Japanese history. The men's tombs at Sengaku-ji temple in Tokyo are still visited daily by Japanese paying respect. The story has been retold endlessly in Kabuki, film, and modern manga. The story exemplifies bushido — total loyalty to one's lord, even unto death, even years after the lord's death. The 47 ronin's master had been Lord Asano; the man they killed was Lord Kira.

question: The Inca Empire of the 1400s built a road network of about 25,000 miles across the Andes Mountains — stone-paved, with rope-suspension bridges over canyons, runners carrying messages 150 miles a day. Remarkably, the Incas built all this without three specific things common in other empires. Which list correctly names what the Incas did NOT have?
answer: No wheel, no iron, no written language
choices: No wheel, no iron, no written language
No bronze, no horses, no cities
No agriculture, no army, no currency
No fishing, no boats, no astronomy
context: The Incas used llamas as pack animals but never invented wheeled vehicles (wheels would have been useless in the rugged Andes anyway). They recorded census and tribute information on quipus — sets of knotted cords. Their stone-masonry walls were so precisely cut that a knife blade cannot fit between stones, and they have stood through major earthquakes. The empire was destroyed when Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro captured and executed Emperor Atahualpa in 1533 with only about 168 men.

question: On March 12 1930 a slight, bespectacled Indian lawyer started walking from his home toward the Arabian Sea coast, gathering followers as he went. After 240 miles he reached the sea and picked up a handful of salt — illegal under British colonial law (which gave the British a monopoly on salt). His act sparked mass civil disobedience across India. Who was he?
answer: Mohandas Gandhi
choices: Mohandas Gandhi
Jawaharlal Nehru
Subhas Chandra Bose
Vallabhbhai Patel
context: Gandhi's 'satyagraha' (truth-force or non-violent resistance) was the model for Martin Luther King Jr.'s civil rights movement decades later. The Salt March made Gandhi a worldwide symbol of peaceful resistance. India won independence from Britain in August 1947 — but at the cost of partition between Hindu India and Muslim Pakistan, with about a million people killed in the violence and 15 million displaced. Gandhi was assassinated in January 1948 by a Hindu extremist who blamed him for being too tolerant toward Muslims.

question: Long before and after the Atlantic slave trade, an internal slave trade ran across the African continent — Africans selling other Africans to coastal kingdoms, who sold them to Arab and Swahili traders. One famous late-19th-century slave-trader operated out of the island of Zanzibar with caravans reaching into central Africa. The Royal Navy West Africa Squadron eventually suppressed the trade. What was this slave-trader's name?
answer: Tippu Tip
choices: Tippu Tip
Mansa Musa
Shaka Zulu
Cetshwayo
context: Tippu Tip (real name Hamad bin Muhammad al-Murjabi) ran a slaving and ivory empire across what is now eastern Congo until the 1890s. He worked with the explorer Henry Morton Stanley and later with Belgian colonial agents. The Royal Navy West Africa Squadron, formed 1808 after Britain banned the slave trade, intercepted slave ships and freed an estimated 150,000 Africans between 1808 and the 1860s. David Livingstone's published accounts of the brutality he saw in East Africa helped end the trade.

question: In November 1532 the Spanish conquistador Francisco Pizarro, with about 168 men, captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa. Atahualpa offered a stunning ransom — to fill a large room once with gold and twice with silver. What happened?
answer: Pizarro took the gold then executed Atahualpa anyway
choices: Pizarro took the gold then executed Atahualpa anyway
Pizarro accepted and released Atahualpa as promised
The Inca freed themselves in a surprise night attack
The two leaders signed a treaty splitting the empire
context: Pizarro took eight months to collect the ransom (about $1.5 billion in modern prices) and then had Atahualpa baptized and garrotted on July 26 1533. The Spanish then captured the Inca capital Cuzco. Pizarro was himself assassinated by Spanish rivals in 1541. The 1532 capture is one of the most studied 'tipping points' in history — how 168 Spaniards with horses, steel, and disease conquered an empire of perhaps 10 million.

question: In 60-61 AD a queen of the Iceni tribe in Roman-occupied Britain led a massive revolt against Roman rule after Roman officials had her flogged and her daughters assaulted. Her army burned three Roman cities — Camulodunum (Colchester), Verulamium (St. Albans), and Londinium (London) — and killed about 70,000-80,000 people. Who was this warrior queen?
answer: Boudicca of the Iceni
choices: Boudicca of the Iceni
Hatshepsut of Egypt
Zenobia of Palmyra
Cleopatra of Egypt
context: Boudicca's army was finally defeated by Roman governor Gaius Suetonius Paulinus, despite being vastly outnumbered. Boudicca either took poison or died of illness shortly afterward. Her story was forgotten until rediscovered by Renaissance writers. A large bronze statue of Boudicca driving a war-chariot stands by Westminster Bridge in London today, a few hundred yards from the Parliament that now governs the nation she fought to free.

question: In March 1974 Chinese farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an stumbled on broken clay heads. Archaeologists eventually uncovered about 8,000 life-size painted clay warriors, horses, and chariots — guarding the tomb of China's first emperor Qin Shi Huang. What are the figures called?
answer: The Terracotta Army
choices: The Terracotta Army
The Clay Battalion
The Imperial Guard of Bronze
The Soldiers of the Han
context: The Terracotta Army was buried about 210 BC to guard the first Chinese emperor in the afterlife. Each soldier has unique facial features, hair, and armor — possibly modeled on real members of the imperial guard. The figures were originally brightly painted but the paint has faded after exposure to air. The main tomb of Qin Shi Huang himself has not yet been opened — ancient records describe rivers of mercury inside, and modern soil tests show mercury levels around the tomb are 100x normal. The site is now a UNESCO World Heritage location.

question: When the Roman army sacked Syracuse in 212 BC, the 75-year-old mathematician Archimedes was at his work table drawing geometry problems in sand. A Roman soldier entered. According to ancient sources, Archimedes spoke one short sentence to the soldier before being run through with a sword. What did Archimedes say?
answer: 'Don't disturb my circles'
choices: 'Don't disturb my circles'
'Strike, but hear me first'
'I am a citizen of Syracuse'
'Spare an old man his last theorem'
context: Roman general Marcellus had ordered Archimedes not be harmed — he wanted the famous engineer alive. The story is told by Plutarch, Livy, and Valerius Maximus. Archimedes had spent the previous two years designing the war machines that defended Syracuse against the Roman siege — cranes that lifted ships out of the water, catapults, possibly a heat ray of polished bronze mirrors. He was buried with a cylinder-and-sphere figure on his tomb — his proudest geometric proof.

question: On July 20 1969 American astronaut Neil Armstrong climbed down the ladder of the lunar module Eagle and stepped onto the surface of the Moon. About 650 million people watched on television. What words did Armstrong say as his boot touched the surface?
answer: 'One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'
choices: 'One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'
'The Eagle has landed safely on the Sea of Tranquility'
'God speed to the future of humanity'
'For all peoples of the Earth, we have arrived'
context: Armstrong always insisted he had said 'one small step for A man' but that the 'a' was lost in radio static. Buzz Aldrin followed Armstrong down 19 minutes later. The U.S. flag and Armstrong's bootprints are still up there — no wind or rain to disturb them. The Apollo 11 lunar module's command module Columbia hangs today in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

question: On April 13 1970 an oxygen tank on the Apollo 13 spacecraft exploded 200,000 miles from Earth on its way to the Moon. The three astronauts had to use the lunar lander as a lifeboat and return home with limited power, oxygen, and water. As the crew reported the problem to mission control, astronaut Jack Swigert spoke one famous five-word sentence. What did Swigert say?
answer: 'Houston, we've had a problem'
choices: 'Houston, we've had a problem'
'Houston, we are losing power'
'Houston, the oxygen tank is gone'
'Houston, please send help home'
context: The famous phrase is usually quoted as 'Houston, we have a problem' — but Swigert and then commander Jim Lovell both said 'Houston, we've HAD a problem' in past tense. The three astronauts (Lovell, Swigert, Fred Haise) made it home alive after four tense days — possibly the greatest space rescue in history. The story was dramatized in the 1995 Tom Hanks film 'Apollo 13.' All three astronauts were Navy or Air Force test pilots accustomed to handling emergencies.

question: In 1905 a 26-year-old patent clerk in Bern, Switzerland published four scientific papers in a single year that revolutionized physics — explaining Brownian motion, the photoelectric effect (the basis for the Nobel Prize he later won), the special theory of relativity, and the equivalence of mass and energy (E = mc²). What was the clerk's name?
answer: Albert Einstein
choices: Albert Einstein
Werner Heisenberg
Niels Bohr
Max Planck
context: Einstein's 1905 'miracle year' (annus mirabilis) is considered the most productive single year in the history of physics by any one person. He could not get a university position after graduating, so he took the Swiss patent office job and did his physics on the side. The fourth paper introduced E = mc² — the famous formula meaning a small amount of mass converts to a vast amount of energy. Einstein moved to Berlin in 1914 and then to Princeton in 1933 as Hitler took power. He won the 1921 Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect work, not for relativity.

question: Polish-French physicist Marie Curie discovered the radioactive elements polonium (named for her homeland Poland) and radium. She worked for years with samples of pitchblende ore and had no idea what the radiation was doing to her body. Her laboratory notebooks from the early 1900s are so dangerous they are kept in lead-lined boxes today. About how long until they are safe to handle without protection?
answer: About 1,500 more years
choices: About 1,500 more years
About 80 more years
About 15 more years
About 500,000 more years
context: Radium-226 has a half-life of 1,600 years; the notebooks will remain radioactive for many centuries. Visitors to the French national archive who want to read them must wear protective clothing and sign a liability waiver. Marie Curie died in 1934 of leukemia caused by her radiation exposure. She remains the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911). Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie also won the Nobel in Chemistry (1935), making them history's only mother-daughter Nobel pair.

question: In September 1928 the Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming returned to his cluttered London lab after a vacation and noticed that one of his bacterial culture dishes had been contaminated by a stray mold. Around the mold, the bacteria had died. Fleming named the substance the mold produced. What did he call it?
answer: Penicillin
choices: Penicillin
Streptomycin
Sulfa drug
Tetracycline
context: Penicillin became the first widely-used antibiotic and may have saved more lives than any other medicine ever discovered. Fleming did not develop it into a usable drug himself; that was done by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford in 1940-41. Mass production for the Allied armies began in 1943, in time to save countless WWII wounded from infected wounds. Fleming, Florey, and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Fleming reportedly said: 'When I woke up just after dawn on September 28 1928, I certainly didn't plan to revolutionize all medicine by discovering the world's first antibiotic.'

question: On May 24 1844 American inventor Samuel Morse demonstrated his electric telegraph by sending a coded message over an experimental 38-mile telegraph line from Washington, D.C. to Baltimore. What four-word biblical message did Morse choose?
answer: 'What hath God wrought'
choices: 'What hath God wrought'
'Glory to the Father'
'Behold the new age'
'Speed to the people'
context: The phrase is from the Bible — Numbers 23:23 — meaning 'See what God has done.' Morse had been working on the telegraph for over a decade. He also developed the dot-and-dash code that still bears his name — Morse code — for sending letters by short and long electrical pulses. Within 15 years a transatlantic telegraph cable was laid from Ireland to Newfoundland (1858) that briefly let London and New York exchange messages in minutes rather than weeks.

question: In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner noticed that local milkmaids who had caught a mild disease called cowpox seemed immune to deadly smallpox. He tested his idea by injecting an 8-year-old boy with cowpox material, then exposing him to smallpox. The boy did not get sick. What word in medicine comes from the Latin for 'cow'?
answer: Vaccine — from 'vacca' (cow)
choices: Vaccine — from 'vacca' (cow)
Inoculation — from 'oculus' (eye)
Immunity — from 'immunis' (exempt)
Smallpox — from English small + pox
context: Smallpox had killed an estimated 300-500 million people in the 20th century alone before being eradicated. Jenner's vaccine was the first vaccine in history. A global vaccination campaign led by the WHO eradicated smallpox by 1980 — the only human disease ever wiped out. Stocks of the smallpox virus exist today only in two labs — one in Russia, one at the U.S. CDC. Polio is the next disease likely to be eradicated.

question: On November 24 1859 the English naturalist Charles Darwin published a book proposing that all species had evolved from common ancestors through a process he called natural selection. The first 1,250-copy printing met a striking fate the very same day. What happened?
answer: The entire first printing sold out that day
choices: The entire first printing sold out that day
The Church of England banned the book
Darwin's wife Emma asked the publisher to delay
Queen Victoria personally bought the first copy
context: Darwin had been working on the theory for over 20 years; he was finally pushed to publish by a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace, who had independently come up with a similar theory. Wallace's contribution is sometimes underrated. The first edition's full title was 'On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection.' Darwin died in 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey near Isaac Newton.

question: On October 21 1879 the American inventor Thomas Edison demonstrated a long-lasting electric light bulb in his New Jersey laboratory. The bulb burned for 13.5 hours — proving the concept practical. Edison had tested thousands of materials trying to find a long-lasting filament. What did the first successful filament turn out to be?
answer: Carbonized cotton thread
choices: Carbonized cotton thread
Iron-nickel alloy wire
Copper wire coated in glass
Tungsten metal in a vacuum
context: Edison later switched to carbonized bamboo, which lasted over 1,200 hours. He famously said: 'I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work.' Edison's Menlo Park lab also developed the phonograph, the motion picture camera, and the first practical electric power-distribution system. He held 1,093 U.S. patents. Modern incandescent bulbs use tungsten filaments, switched from carbon in 1906 by William Coolidge. LED bulbs are now replacing incandescents worldwide.

question: On December 2 1942, under the football stadium at the University of Chicago, the Italian physicist Enrico Fermi achieved the world's first sustained nuclear chain reaction. A coded phone message was sent to report success. What did the cryptic message say?
answer: 'The Italian navigator has just landed in the New World'
choices: 'The Italian navigator has just landed in the New World'
'The Roman engineer has crossed the bridge to safety'
'The professor has lit the lamp inside the cellar'
'The eagle has flown the nest into the morning sun'
context: Fermi's experiment proved a controlled nuclear chain reaction was possible — the essential step for both atomic weapons and nuclear power plants. The Chicago Pile-1 reactor produced only about half a watt of power but it ran. The whole experiment had no shielding; everyone in the room got a dose of radiation. Fermi had escaped fascist Italy in 1938 because his wife Laura was Jewish.

question: After Apollo 11's historic Moon landing in July 1969, the three astronauts toured the world as heroes. The mission commander, however, was famously reluctant to be a celebrity. He rarely gave interviews, refused most paid speaking engagements, and lived a quiet life as a college professor and businessman. Who was this first man on the Moon?
answer: Neil Armstrong
choices: Neil Armstrong
Buzz Aldrin
Michael Collins
John Glenn
context: Armstrong (1930-2012) was an Ohio native who flew 78 combat missions as a Navy pilot in Korea, then became a NASA test pilot before joining the astronaut corps. He taught engineering at the University of Cincinnati for nine years. He served on the commissions investigating Apollo 13 and the 1986 Challenger disaster. Armstrong died in August 2012 at age 82 from complications of heart surgery. He was buried at sea by the U.S. Navy.

question: On February 28 1953 two scientists at Cambridge University announced in the pub at lunchtime that they had solved the structure of DNA, the molecule of heredity. The structure was a twisted ladder of two intertwined strands. What is the shape called?
answer: The double helix
choices: The double helix
The triple helix
The protein spiral
The molecular pyramid
context: James Watson (American, age 24) and Francis Crick (British, age 36) built models from sheet metal and wire to match X-ray crystallography images of DNA — most importantly an image called Photo 51 taken by Rosalind Franklin's lab at King's College London. Franklin's contribution was not adequately credited at the time; she died of ovarian cancer in 1958 at age 37 without knowing how important her work had been. Watson, Crick, and Maurice Wilkins shared the 1962 Nobel Prize. Nobel rules forbid posthumous awards, so Franklin was excluded.

question: In 1989 a British computer scientist working at the European nuclear research center CERN in Switzerland wrote a proposal for a way to link documents across the world using the internet. He called his invention by a famous three-word name. What is it?
answer: The World Wide Web
choices: The World Wide Web
The Universal Net
The Global Library
The Internet Hub
context: Tim Berners-Lee created the Web essentially as a tool to help scientists at CERN share research papers more easily. He chose to give away his invention free, not patent it. The first website went online on August 6 1991. The first web browser was called WorldWideWeb (later renamed Nexus). The Mosaic browser (1993) brought the Web to ordinary users. Berners-Lee was knighted in 2004. His invention transformed the world in 30 years more than the printing press transformed it in 300.

question: On November 30 2022 a San Francisco company called OpenAI publicly released a chatbot powered by a large language model. It became the fastest-adopted technology in history, reaching 100 million users in two months. What was the chatbot called?
answer: ChatGPT
choices: ChatGPT
BardAI
DeepMind
AlphaGo
context: ChatGPT's release marked a turning point in artificial intelligence. The 'GPT' stands for 'Generative Pre-trained Transformer.' Earlier technologies took years to reach 100 million users — Facebook took 4.5 years, Instagram took 2.5 years. ChatGPT reached 100 million in two months. The 2020s have seen rapid advances in AI capabilities. Anthropic (founded by ex-OpenAI staff) released its competing Claude in 2023. AI has begun to transform research, programming, education, and writing.

question: On January 9 2007, at a Macworld convention in San Francisco, Apple CEO Steve Jobs walked onstage and announced 'three revolutionary products' that he then revealed were a single device — a phone, a music player, and an internet communicator combined. What was the device called?
answer: The iPhone
choices: The iPhone
The iPad
The Apple Watch
The iPod Touch
context: The iPhone launched in June 2007 at $499. It transformed phone design overnight — physical keyboards on phones almost disappeared. It also created the App Store ecosystem (2008), changing software economics. Jobs (1955-2011) had founded Apple in 1976 with Steve Wozniak in his parents' garage, been forced out of Apple in 1985, founded Pixar, returned to Apple in 1997, and saved it from bankruptcy. He died of pancreatic cancer in October 2011 at age 56. His Stanford commencement address (2005) about facing death is one of the most-watched speeches on YouTube.

question: After the space shuttle Challenger exploded on January 28 1986, the U.S. government appointed an investigation commission. One of the commissioners was a Nobel Prize-winning physicist. During a televised hearing he demonstrated the failure cause by dropping a small rubber ring into a glass of ice water. Who was the physicist?
answer: Richard Feynman
choices: Richard Feynman
Murray Gell-Mann
Carl Sagan
Stephen Hawking
context: Feynman (1918-1988) showed that the rubber O-ring lost its flexibility when chilled — exactly what had happened to the booster seals on the freezing morning of the launch. The simple demonstration cut through bureaucratic obfuscation. Feynman had worked on the Manhattan Project as a young man, won the 1965 Nobel Prize for his work on quantum electrodynamics, and was famous for his physics lectures at Caltech. He was dying of cancer during the Challenger investigation; he died in 1988.

question: On November 23 1654 the French mathematician Blaise Pascal had a two-hour direct encounter with God. He scribbled a record on parchment headed by the single word 'Feu' — 'Fire.' For the remaining eight years of his life he carried that parchment with him everywhere by sewing it into a specific item. Where did Pascal sew it?
answer: Into the lining of his coat
choices: Into the lining of his coat
Into the cover of his Bible
Into a leather amulet around his neck
Into the soles of his walking boots
context: The parchment is called the Mémorial. It was discovered by a servant after Pascal's death in 1662, sewn into his clothing — he had transferred it from coat to coat over the years. The note begins: 'The year of grace 1654 / Monday, 23 November... FIRE / God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars.' Pascal had already invented mechanical calculation and the modern theory of probability.

question: Between 1609 and 1619 the German astronomer Johannes Kepler discovered three laws describing how planets move around the Sun. The first law overturned 2,000 years of astronomical tradition. According to Kepler's first law, what shape are planetary orbits?
answer: Ellipses (oval shapes), not perfect circles
choices: Ellipses (oval shapes), not perfect circles
Perfect circles centered on the Sun
Spirals slowly closing inward toward the Sun
Figure-eights that loop around two stars
context: Greek astronomers from Plato onward had insisted the heavens must be perfect circles. Kepler's discovery that orbits are slightly elliptical — based on Tycho Brahe's careful Mars observations — overturned that ancient assumption. Kepler was deeply religious; he saw God as a divine mathematician and the laws of nature as God's design. His mother Katharina was tried as a witch in 1620-21 and Kepler spent over a year defending her in court. He died in poverty in 1630 at age 58.

question: Around 1530 the Polish-Prussian astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus completed a book arguing the Earth was not the center of the universe — instead the Earth and planets all moved around the Sun. He delayed publication for years. When did Copernicus actually see his finished book?
answer: On his deathbed, the day he died in 1543
choices: On his deathbed, the day he died in 1543
Twenty years before his death, in 1523
He never saw the finished printed book
On his 60th birthday in 1533
context: Copernicus suffered a stroke in late 1542. The first copy of his book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres reached him on May 24 1543 — the day he died. The book sparked the Scientific Revolution, though it would take Galileo's telescope (1609-10) and Kepler's laws to firmly establish the heliocentric model. The Catholic Church did not formally condemn Copernicus's book until 1616, after Galileo had publicly championed the idea.

question: After Howard Carter opened King Tutankhamun's tomb in November 1922, his patron Lord Carnarvon died five months later in Cairo of an infection that began with a mosquito bite. Newspapers seized on the story of an ancient curse. Was Carnarvon's death from a curse on the tomb?
answer: No — it was an infected mosquito bite
choices: No — it was an infected mosquito bite
Yes — the tomb's air contained ancient toxins
Yes — the gold of the tomb was deeply radioactive
Yes — a slow virus from the mummy infected him
context: Most members of Carter's expedition lived long lives. Howard Carter himself lived another 17 years and died in 1939. The 'curse of the pharaohs' became a tabloid sensation but had no real basis. Modern epidemiologists have found that mortality rates among the team who entered the tomb were no different from a control group of similar background. The tomb contained over 5,000 objects, including the famous solid-gold death mask. King Tut had died around 1323 BC at about age 19.

question: In 1799 French soldiers during Napoleon's Egyptian campaign uncovered a large stone slab inscribed with the same text in three different scripts — Egyptian hieroglyphs, demotic Egyptian, and Greek. Because scholars could read the Greek, the stone gave them the key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs for the first time in 1,400 years. What is this slab called?
answer: The Rosetta Stone
choices: The Rosetta Stone
The Behistun Inscription
The Code of Hammurabi
The Phaistos Disc
context: The stone was named after the Egyptian port town near where it was found. After the British defeated Napoleon in Egypt, the Rosetta Stone went to London under the Treaty of Alexandria; it has been at the British Museum since 1802. French scholar Jean-François Champollion finally deciphered the hieroglyphs in 1822, after years of work. Hieroglyphs had been a dead language no one could read for 14 centuries before Champollion's breakthrough. The Rosetta Stone is the British Museum's most-visited object.

question: In 1705 the English astronomer Edmond Halley realized that several historical comet sightings were actually the same comet returning on a regular schedule. He predicted it would return in 1758. The comet did return — 16 years after Halley's death. About how often does Halley's Comet return?
answer: About every 76 years
choices: About every 76 years
About every 12 years
About every 400 years
About every 25 years
context: Halley's Comet is the only short-period comet bright enough to be seen with the naked eye from Earth. Its last appearance was 1986; its next appearance will be 2061. Halley was a friend of Isaac Newton and paid out of his own pocket to print Newton's Principia (1687) when the Royal Society ran out of money. Halley also served as Britain's Astronomer Royal. He correctly predicted his comet's return, becoming the first person to identify a periodic comet.

question: On May 20-21 1927 a 25-year-old American pilot took off from Long Island in a tiny single-engine plane and flew alone across the Atlantic Ocean nonstop to Paris in 33 hours. He won a $25,000 prize and became the most famous person in the world overnight. What was his plane named?
answer: The Spirit of St. Louis
choices: The Spirit of St. Louis
The Eagle of America
The Lone Aviator
The Atlantic Conqueror
context: Charles Lindbergh was greeted in Paris by a crowd of about 150,000 people. He had stayed awake for 55 hours straight including preparation time. The plane was funded by business backers from St. Louis, Missouri. Lindbergh's later fame turned tragic — his infant son was kidnapped and murdered in 1932 in 'the crime of the century.' The Spirit of St. Louis now hangs in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

question: On February 14 1990, at the suggestion of astronomer Carl Sagan, NASA turned the Voyager 1 spacecraft (then 3.7 billion miles from Earth, beyond Pluto's orbit) around to take one last photograph of its home planet. Earth appeared as a tiny dot — less than a single pixel — surrounded by sunbeams scattered through the camera's lens. What is the photograph called?
answer: The Pale Blue Dot
choices: The Pale Blue Dot
The Lonely Earth
The Distant World
The Last Image
context: Sagan's words about the image became one of the most famous passages in modern astronomy: 'Look again at that dot. That's here. That's home. That's us. On it everyone you love, everyone you know... every saint and sinner in the history of our species lived there — on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.' Voyager 1 launched in 1977 and is still operating in interstellar space today, the farthest human-made object from Earth.

question: In December 1995 astronomers pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at a tiny seemingly empty patch of sky no larger than a grain of sand held at arm's length, and let it stare for ten days. The resulting picture showed thousands of galaxies in a previously 'empty' spot. What was this picture called?
answer: The Hubble Deep Field
choices: The Hubble Deep Field
The First Light Image
The Galactic Census
The Empty Sky Stare
context: The Hubble Deep Field showed about 3,000 galaxies in a sky patch covering one 24-millionth of the whole sky. Extrapolated to the entire sky, there are at least 100 billion galaxies in the observable universe — and we now know the number is probably 1-2 trillion. The Hubble Space Telescope launched in 1990; the famous astronaut servicing missions (1993-2009) repaired and upgraded it five times. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) launched in December 2021 and is now Hubble's successor.

question: On the cold morning of January 28 1986 the space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after liftoff from Florida, killing all seven astronauts aboard. The crew included an ordinary citizen — a Concord, New Hampshire high school social studies teacher who was to teach a lesson from space. What was the teacher's name?
answer: Christa McAuliffe
choices: Christa McAuliffe
Sally Ride
Judith Resnik
Barbara Morgan
context: McAuliffe was chosen from 11,000 applicants for the Teacher in Space Project. Millions of American schoolchildren were watching the launch live in their classrooms. The shuttle program was grounded for almost three years afterward. NASA's Challenger Center for Space Science Education was founded by the astronauts' families and runs space-themed STEM programs for children. McAuliffe's backup, Barbara Morgan, eventually flew to space herself in 2007.

question: During WWII a British team of mathematicians and codebreakers at a country estate north of London worked to crack the secret codes used by Nazi Germany's military command. A brilliant young mathematician named Alan Turing led the team that broke a particular electromechanical cipher machine. What was the German machine called?
answer: Enigma
choices: Enigma
Lorenz
Geheimschreiber
Sigaba
context: Bletchley Park's codebreakers shortened WWII by perhaps two years and saved millions of lives. The Polish Cipher Bureau had originally broken into Enigma in the 1930s and shared their work with British and French intelligence in 1939. Turing's team built code-breaking machines called 'bombes' that ran possible keys at high speed. Turing (1912-1954) was also a founder of modern computer science. After the war he was prosecuted for homosexuality in 1952 (then illegal in Britain), chemically castrated, and died in 1954 of cyanide poisoning at age 41 — most likely suicide.

question: In the 1840s an English aristocrat wrote what is now considered the first computer program — an algorithm for calculating Bernoulli numbers — for a mechanical calculating engine designed by her friend Charles Babbage. The engine was never actually built in her lifetime. Her father was a famous Romantic poet. Who was she?
answer: Ada Lovelace, daughter of Lord Byron
choices: Ada Lovelace, daughter of Lord Byron
Mary Shelley, daughter of Mary Wollstonecraft
Charlotte Brontë, daughter of Patrick Brontë
Florence Nightingale, daughter of William Nightingale
context: Ada Lovelace (1815-1852) had been raised by her mother to study mathematics specifically to keep her away from the wild artistic temperament of her father, Lord Byron, whom she never knew (he died when she was eight). She translated and annotated an Italian paper about Babbage's Analytical Engine, adding her own program. The U.S. Department of Defense named its programming language Ada (1980) in her honor. She died of cancer at age 36.

question: Hypatia of Alexandria was a famous female mathematician and Neoplatonist philosopher, teaching at the Mouseion of Alexandria around 400 AD. In March 415 AD, during a political feud between the city's Christian Patriarch Cyril and the prefect Orestes (whose adviser she was), a mob ambushed her chariot, dragged her into a church, and killed her. What did the mob reportedly use as weapons?
answer: Sharpened oyster shells or roof tiles
choices: Sharpened oyster shells or roof tiles
Long ceremonial daggers from the temple of Serapis
Their bare hands and stones from the road
Hot iron tongs taken from a nearby blacksmith's forge
context: The historian Socrates Scholasticus (a Christian writing within decades of the event) records the oyster-shell or roof-tile detail. Hypatia's murder is often used as a symbol of the end of antique scholarship — though the Library of Alexandria had been declining for centuries by then. Her killing was not ordered by Cyril (who was eventually made a saint), but the political climate he had fostered is generally held responsible. She was probably around 50-60 years old. Edward Gibbon's 'Decline and Fall' (1776) helped make her a major figure in Enlightenment anticlerical writing.

question: In the 1570s the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe received from his king an entire island in the Sound between Denmark and Sweden, with funding to build a great observatory. Tycho's instruments (still using only the naked eye — there were no telescopes yet) measured the positions of stars and planets with unprecedented accuracy. What was Tycho's observatory called?
answer: Uraniborg — 'castle of Urania (the heavens)'
choices: Uraniborg — 'castle of Urania (the heavens)'
Stellarum — 'place of the stars'
Cosmicum — 'cosmic house'
Caelum — 'the heavens'
context: Tycho's island Hven (now Ven) was given to him by King Frederick II of Denmark. Tycho got such generous funding because nobles believed astronomy could predict the future — Tycho had successfully predicted an eclipse and a comet. After Frederick's death the new king was less generous; Tycho left in 1597 and became Imperial Mathematician to Rudolph II in Prague, where he died in 1601. His Mars observations passed to his young assistant Kepler, who used them to discover the laws of planetary motion.

question: Joan of Arc was a teenage French farm girl who told everyone that angels had spoken to her, instructing her to drive the English out of France and crown her king. Most adults dismissed her. At 17 she finally got the chance to meet the uncrowned French king. Who was he?
answer: Charles VII (the Dauphin)
choices: Charles VII (the Dauphin)
Louis XI (the Spider King)
François I (the Renaissance King)
Henry V (king of England)
context: Charles VII (1403-1461) had not yet been crowned. He was called only 'the Dauphin' (heir to the French throne) because the English controlled Reims, where French kings were traditionally crowned. After Joan's military victories at Orleans, Charles was anointed king at Reims Cathedral on July 17 1429, with Joan beside him. Joan was burned at the stake by the English in 1431; Charles never tried to ransom her. He was widely accused of cowardly inaction in her case.

question: Around midnight on December 29 1566, the 20-year-old Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe fought a sword duel in pitch darkness with his cousin Manderup Parsberg, over a disagreement about a mathematical formula. The duel left Tycho with a lifelong disfigurement. What part of his face did Tycho lose?
answer: The bridge of his nose
choices: The bridge of his nose
His right eye
His left cheekbone
His upper lip
context: Tycho wore a metal prosthesis for the rest of his life — exhumations of his grave in 1901 and 2010 confirmed the everyday prosthesis was brass (green tint left on the skull bone). He reportedly had a fancier gold-and-silver one for formal occasions. The duel was not lethal but the wound bled heavily for hours. Tycho went on to be the greatest naked-eye astronomer in history; his observations of Mars enabled Kepler's three laws of planetary motion.

question: In 1687 Isaac Newton published the most important book in the history of physics, presenting three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation. The book showed that the same physics governs falling apples on Earth and orbiting planets in the heavens. What is this book called by its short Latin title?
answer: Principia (the Principia Mathematica)
choices: Principia (the Principia Mathematica)
Opticks (Newton's later work)
De Motu (an earlier draft)
Arithmetica Universalis (Newton's algebra book)
context: The full Latin title is Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica ('Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy'). Newton wrote the Principia in 18 months when he was about 44. Edmund Halley personally paid out of pocket to print the book when the Royal Society ran out of money. Newton served as Master of the Royal Mint in his later years and ruthlessly hunted down counterfeiters — he sent several to the gallows. He was knighted by Queen Anne in 1705 and buried in Westminster Abbey in 1727.

question: In October 1829 the British engineer George Stephenson entered his improved steam locomotive in the Rainhill Trials — a competition to find the best engine for the new Liverpool and Manchester Railway. His engine won by reaching the unheard-of speed of 30 miles per hour. What did Stephenson name his winning locomotive?
answer: The Rocket
choices: The Rocket
The Comet
The Lightning
The Iron Horse
context: The Rocket weighed about 4 tons. Other competing engines either broke down or could not match the Rocket's speed. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in September 1830 as the world's first intercity passenger railway. At the opening ceremony, William Huskisson, a Member of Parliament, was struck and killed by the Rocket — the first widely reported railway fatality. Within 50 years railways had transformed daily life across Europe and North America.

question: On April 14-15 1912 the largest passenger ship ever built — said by some to be 'unsinkable' — hit an iceberg in the North Atlantic on its first voyage from Southampton to New York. The ship sank in 2 hours 40 minutes; about 1,500 people died, mostly because there were not enough lifeboats. What was the ship's name?
answer: RMS Titanic
choices: RMS Titanic
RMS Lusitania
RMS Queen Mary
RMS Britannic
context: The Titanic had lifeboats for only about half its passengers and crew. The disaster led to lasting changes in maritime safety law — lifeboats for everyone, mandatory radio watches, and the International Ice Patrol. The wreck was found in 1985 by a team led by Robert Ballard, lying in two pieces 12,500 feet deep on the ocean floor. James Cameron's 1997 film Titanic became one of the highest-grossing movies of all time and won 11 Oscars.

question: In December 1911 a Norwegian explorer became the first person to reach the geographic South Pole. He beat a British expedition by 33 days; the British team led by Robert Falcon Scott reached the pole only to find a Norwegian flag and then died on the return journey. Who was the Norwegian?
answer: Roald Amundsen
choices: Roald Amundsen
Fridtjof Nansen
Ernest Shackleton
Ranulph Fiennes
context: Amundsen used sled dogs (and ate some of them along the way for food); Scott used ponies, which died, and then man-hauled his sledges. Amundsen reached the pole on December 14 1911; Scott reached it on January 17 1912. Scott's entire five-man team died on the return — frozen in a tent only 11 miles from a supply depot. Amundsen later became the first person to reach both poles when he flew over the North Pole in an airship in 1926. He died in 1928 in a plane crash searching for a missing Italian expedition.

question: On May 29 1953 two climbers became the first to reach the summit of the world's tallest mountain — 29,032 feet above sea level. One was a New Zealand beekeeper named Edmund Hillary; the other was a Nepalese Sherpa mountaineer. Who was Hillary's climbing partner?
answer: Tenzing Norgay
choices: Tenzing Norgay
Reinhold Messner
Ang Tharkay
Apa Sherpa
context: Hillary and Tenzing spent only about 15 minutes on the summit before descending. News of their success reached London on June 2 — coronation day of Queen Elizabeth II — and was treated as a coronation gift. The two never said publicly who had stepped on the summit first; they had agreed they reached it 'together as a team.' Tenzing died in 1986; Hillary died in 2008 at age 88. Mount Everest has been climbed thousands of times since 1953; over 300 people have died on it.

question: On July 2 1937 a famous American female pilot, attempting to fly around the world along the equator, disappeared over the Pacific Ocean somewhere between Papua New Guinea and Howland Island. The largest naval search in history at that time found no trace. Who was the pilot?
answer: Amelia Earhart
choices: Amelia Earhart
Bessie Coleman
Harriet Quimby
Jacqueline Cochran
context: Earhart (1897-1937) was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean (1932), making her the most famous female pilot in the world. She and her navigator Fred Noonan were never found. Theories about her fate include running out of fuel, capture by the Japanese, or surviving as castaways on a remote island. Bone fragments found on Nikumaroro atoll in 1940 may have been hers, but the bones were lost before DNA testing existed. Her disappearance remains one of aviation's great mysteries.

question: Before becoming the first man to climb Mount Everest in 1953, Edmund Hillary worked at his family's business in New Zealand. What was Hillary's occupation before he became famous as a mountaineer?
answer: Beekeeper
choices: Beekeeper
Schoolteacher
Sheep farmer
Fisherman
context: Hillary worked in his family's apiary in Auckland from his teens. He served as a Royal New Zealand Air Force navigator during WWII and got serious about climbing after the war. After his Everest summit, he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II. He devoted much of the rest of his life to charitable work in Nepal — building schools, hospitals, and airstrips for Sherpa communities. The Hillary Step on Everest (a famous rock obstacle near the summit) is named for him. He died in 2008 at age 88 and is featured on New Zealand's $5 bill.

question: In the 1680s-1730s an Italian violin-maker in the small town of Cremona produced about 1,100 stringed instruments. About 650 survive today and are considered the finest violins ever made; one can sell for $15-20 million. Who was this master craftsman?
answer: Antonio Stradivari (Stradivarius)
choices: Antonio Stradivari (Stradivarius)
Giuseppe Guarneri (del Gesù)
Andrea Amati
Niccolò Paganini
context: Stradivari (1644-1737) lived to age 93 and continued making violins past age 90. His secret has never been duplicated despite centuries of effort — modern researchers have proposed varnish chemistry, wood density from the Little Ice Age, treatment with salts, and many other explanations. Cremona's small group of violin-making families (Stradivari, Guarneri, Amati) produced the greatest instruments in the world during a single Golden Age. The town's name is now synonymous with the highest standard of stringed instruments.

question: In 1951 a Black tobacco-farming American woman from Virginia named Henrietta Lacks was treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. Without her knowledge or consent, doctors took tissue samples; her cells turned out to be the first human cells that would reproduce indefinitely in a laboratory dish. They are still used worldwide in medical research today. What are these cells called?
answer: HeLa cells
choices: HeLa cells
Stem cells
Mother cells
Lacks cells
context: HeLa cells (named for the first two letters of Henrietta Lacks's first and last names) have been used in over 70,000 medical studies, including the polio vaccine and AIDS research. Her family was not informed for over 20 years and never received any compensation, despite billions of dollars made from products derived from her cells. Lacks died of cancer in 1951 at age 31. Rebecca Skloot's 2010 book 'The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks' brought her story to wide attention.

question: John Wesley founded the Methodist movement, riding on horseback across England, Wales, and the American colonies for 50 years. He preached up to 40,000 sermons in his lifetime — sometimes to crowds of 20,000 in the open air. About how many total miles did Wesley travel on horseback?
answer: About 250,000 miles — roughly 10 times around the Earth
choices: About 250,000 miles — roughly 10 times around the Earth
About 25,000 miles — once around the Earth
About 800,000 miles — three times to the Moon
About 50,000 miles — twice across America
context: Wesley's Aldersgate experience on May 24 1738 launched his career as an evangelical preacher. He averaged about 5,000 miles per year on horseback for 50 years. His followers were called 'Methodists' for their disciplined methodical approach to Christian practice. The Methodist movement eventually became one of the largest Protestant denominations in the world, especially strong in the United States.

question: Around 1498-99 a young Italian sculptor carved a marble statue of the Virgin Mary holding the body of the crucified Christ for a French cardinal's tomb in Rome. The young artist later carved his signature into the strap across Mary's chest after he overheard others crediting the work to a different sculptor. About how old was Michelangelo when he carved the Pietà?
answer: About 24 years old
choices: About 24 years old
About 40 years old
About 60 years old
About 16 years old
context: Michelangelo was furious that visitors had credited another sculptor; he sneaked into the chapel at night and carved 'MICHAELA[N]GELVS BONAROTVS FLORENT[INVS] FACIEBA[T]' ('Michelangelo Buonarroti of Florence made this') into the strap. The Pietà has been displayed in St. Peter's Basilica in Rome since the 16th century. In 1972 a deranged Hungarian-Australian geologist attacked it with a hammer, breaking off the Virgin's arm and parts of her face; it was carefully restored. The statue now stands behind bulletproof glass.

question: Summer 1666: plague closed Cambridge and the 23-year-old Isaac Newton went home to his mother's farm at Woolsthorpe. In a single 'year of wonders' he invented calculus, the laws of motion, and the law of universal gravitation. According to legend, Newton was sitting in the garden when one specific event made him think about gravity. What was the event?
answer: An apple fell from a tree
choices: An apple fell from a tree
A bird flew into a window
A bucket fell down a well
A leaf drifted slowly to the ground
context: Newton himself told the apple story to several visitors including the antiquarian William Stukeley. A descendant of the tree still grows at Woolsthorpe Manor today. The apple did NOT hit Newton on the head — that detail was added by later embellishments. Newton was 23 and had only just earned his Cambridge degree. He waited 20 years before publishing the Principia (1687). The Royal Society of London elected him president in 1703, a post he held until his death in 1727.

question: On May 30 1431, after being captured by the Burgundians, sold to the English, and condemned for heresy at age 19, Joan of Arc was burned alive at the stake in the market square of Rouen. Her last word, eyewitnesses said, was the name of Jesus. The English then did something specific to her remains to deny the French any relic to venerate. What did the English do?
answer: Threw her ashes into the Seine
choices: Threw her ashes into the Seine
Sealed them in a lead box and shipped them to England
Buried them in unmarked ground at midnight outside the city
Crushed her bones to powder and scattered them at sea
context: Joan was 19. The execution was deliberately public, intended to discredit Charles VII — the king she had helped crown at Reims in 1429. A retrial in 1456 — after the English had been driven from France — found her innocent and called her a martyr. Joan was canonized as a saint by the Catholic Church in 1920. She is one of the nine secondary patron saints of France today.

question: In June 1215 the English barons forced an unpopular king to ride out to a meadow on the River Thames near Windsor and seal a great charter restricting his royal power. The charter said even the king must obey the law. What was the king's name?
answer: King John
choices: King John
Richard the Lionheart
Henry II
Edward the Confessor
context: King John (1166-1216) had lost most of England's possessions in France and raised taxes to try to win them back. The barons revolted. Magna Carta ('Great Charter') had 63 clauses, mostly about feudal taxes, but clause 39 — no free man imprisoned except by lawful judgment of his peers — became the foundation of English liberty and later inspired the U.S. Constitution. John tried to break the charter immediately; he died the next year of dysentery while fleeing his enemies. Four original 1215 copies survive.

question: On April 6 1896 the first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens, Greece — the first international athletic competition since the ancient Olympics had been banned by the Roman emperor Theodosius in 393 AD. About 280 athletes from 14 nations competed. Who founded the modern Olympic movement?
answer: Pierre de Coubertin
choices: Pierre de Coubertin
Theodore Roosevelt
Avery Brundage
Juan Antonio Samaranch
context: The French educator Pierre de Coubertin (1863-1937) believed athletic competition built international understanding and personal character. His Olympic motto 'Citius, Altius, Fortius' ('Faster, Higher, Stronger') is still in use today (a fourth word 'Communiter' — 'Together' — was added in 2021). The 1896 Athens Games included track and field, swimming, gymnastics, cycling, fencing, and wrestling. The marathon race (26.2 miles, the legendary distance from Marathon to Athens) was introduced at the 1896 Games. The Greek runner Spyridon Louis won it to massive national celebration.

question: On Christmas Eve 1968 the three astronauts of Apollo 8 — the first humans to orbit the Moon — gave a live television broadcast back to Earth. They took turns reading aloud from a famous ancient text. What did the Apollo 8 crew read?
answer: The opening verses of Genesis from the Bible
choices: The opening verses of Genesis from the Bible
The Gettysburg Address by Abraham Lincoln
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
The opening of Homer's Odyssey in Greek
context: Astronauts Frank Borman, Jim Lovell, and Bill Anders took turns reading Genesis 1:1-10 ('In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth...'). The broadcast was the most-watched television event in history at that time. It came at the end of a violent, divisive year (1968 had seen the Vietnam Tet Offensive, the assassinations of MLK and RFK, urban riots, and chaos at the Democratic Convention). The crew also took the famous 'Earthrise' photograph showing Earth rising over the lunar horizon — perhaps the most influential photograph of the 20th century.

question: After the Chernobyl nuclear plant exploded on April 26 1986, the Soviet Union called up about 600,000 people — mostly Red Army reservists, miners, and construction workers — to contain the disaster. They were sent to clean radioactive debris, build the concrete sarcophagus, and decontaminate surrounding areas. What were these workers called?
answer: Liquidators
choices: Liquidators
Volunteers
Sacrifices
Heroes
context: Many liquidators worked in extreme conditions for only 30-90 seconds before reaching their lifetime safe radiation dose. Helicopter pilots dumped boron and sand on the burning reactor; some died of radiation within months. Coal miners dug a tunnel under the reactor to install a heat exchanger. Soldiers in canvas overalls cleared roofs of radioactive graphite. The Soviet authorities downplayed the dangers and refused to provide adequate dosimeters. Tens of thousands of liquidators have died early from radiation-linked diseases; many more suffered chronic illness.

question: On June 28 1914 in the Bosnian capital Sarajevo, a Serbian nationalist teenager named Gavrilo Princip shot the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne and his wife. Within five weeks Europe was at war — what became World War I. Who was the murdered heir?
answer: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
choices: Archduke Franz Ferdinand
Emperor Franz Joseph
King Alexander of Serbia
Tsar Nicholas II of Russia
context: Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were riding in an open car. Their driver took a wrong turn and reversed in front of the deli where Princip was standing after an earlier assassination attempt had failed. Princip fired twice. The assassination set off a chain of alliance commitments — Austria attacked Serbia; Russia mobilized for Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia and France; Britain entered when Germany invaded Belgium. The war killed about 17 million people over four years and destroyed four empires (German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman, Russian).

question: In 490 BC, after the Athenian hoplites defeated the Persian invasion at Marathon, a runner named Pheidippides was sent racing the roughly 26 miles to Athens with news of the victory. He delivered one Greek word and then collapsed dead from the run. What did Pheidippides say before he died?
answer: 'Nenikēkamen' — 'We have won'
choices: 'Nenikēkamen' — 'We have won'
'Eleutheria' — 'Freedom'
'Athēnai sōzontai' — 'Athens is saved'
'Persai pheugousin' — 'The Persians flee'
context: The Marathon legend comes mainly from Lucian, writing centuries later; Herodotus tells a different Pheidippides story (a run to Sparta). The modern marathon race distance of 26.2 miles was fixed at the 1908 London Olympics to start at Windsor Castle. The Athenian victory under Miltiades saved the young democracy from a Persian Empire that outnumbered them roughly two to one.

question: In 480 BC, King Leonidas of Sparta held the narrow pass of Thermopylae against the Persian army of Xerxes with about 300 Spartans and a few thousand allies. When Xerxes demanded the Greeks surrender their weapons, Leonidas sent back a two-word reply in Greek that became one of the most famous defiant phrases in history. What did Leonidas write?
answer: 'Molon labe' — 'Come and take them'
choices: 'Molon labe' — 'Come and take them'
'Ouk eikō' — 'I do not yield'
'Mēden agan' — 'Nothing in excess'
'Gnōthi seauton' — 'Know thyself'
context: Leonidas and his 300 Spartans died holding the pass after a local traitor named Ephialtes showed the Persians a goat path around the position. The Spartans bought enough time for the Greek fleet to win at Salamis weeks later. A modern monument at Thermopylae bears the inscription 'Molon labe' in Greek.

question: In 399 BC, the 70-year-old Athenian philosopher Socrates was condemned by an Athenian jury for 'corrupting the youth' and 'impiety toward the gods.' His friends arranged for him to escape into exile easily. Socrates refused. Instead he drank the cup of poison the city handed him. What poison did Athens use for executions?
answer: Hemlock
choices: Hemlock
Belladonna
Wolfsbane
Henbane
context: Plato's dialogue Phaedo describes Socrates' final hours, walking around until his legs grew heavy, then lying down as the cold paralysis worked upward. His last words were reportedly: 'Crito, we owe a rooster to Asclepius. Pay it and do not neglect it.' Asclepius was the god of healing — Socrates was treating his death as a cure.

question: Around 343 BC, the philosopher Aristotle was hired by King Philip II of Macedon to tutor his teenage son for three years at a place called Mieza. The boy went on to conquer the largest empire the world had ever seen by age 30. Which student did Aristotle tutor?
answer: Alexander the Great
choices: Alexander the Great
Ptolemy I Soter
Seleucus I Nicator
Antigonus the One-Eyed
context: Aristotle was about 41, Alexander about 13, when the tutoring began. Alexander carried a copy of Homer's Iliad annotated by Aristotle on his Persian campaigns and slept with it under his pillow. The two later quarreled over Alexander's treatment of Aristotle's grand-nephew Callisthenes, whom Alexander executed.

question: The sculptor Phidias supervised the building of the Parthenon on the Athenian Acropolis between 447 and 432 BC under Pericles. Inside the temple he placed his crowning masterpiece: a 40-foot statue of Athena. The statue was made of two extraordinarily expensive materials over a wooden frame. What materials covered it?
answer: Ivory for the skin and gold for the robes
choices: Ivory for the skin and gold for the robes
Marble inlaid with silver and lapis lazuli
Polished bronze with semi-precious stone eyes
Painted cedar wood with garments of beaten copper
context: Phidias also made the even larger Zeus at Olympia, which was one of the Seven Wonders. The Athena Parthenos was lost in antiquity; full-size replicas exist (the Nashville Parthenon has one). Phidias was later accused of embezzling gold from the project and possibly of impiety for putting his own face on Athena's shield; he died in disgrace or was driven into exile.

question: The king of Syracuse asked Archimedes around 250 BC to determine whether a goldsmith had cheated him by mixing silver into his crown without melting it down. Archimedes solved it in a bathtub by realizing displaced water revealed volume. He was reportedly so excited he ran naked through the streets shouting one Greek word. What did Archimedes shout?
answer: 'Eureka!' — 'I have found it!'
choices: 'Eureka!' — 'I have found it!'
'Aletheia!' — 'Truth!'
'Sophia!' — 'Wisdom!'
'Theoria!' — 'Insight!'
context: The story comes from Vitruvius, writing two centuries later. The principle of buoyancy — that a body displaces its own volume of water — let Archimedes compare the crown's density to pure gold without harming it. Archimedes was killed in 212 BC at the sack of Syracuse, still working geometry problems in the sand when a Roman soldier ran him through.

question: In January 49 BC, the Roman general Julius Caesar stood at the bank of a small river in northern Italy with his legion behind him. Roman law forbade any general from crossing it under arms; doing so meant civil war. Caesar crossed, and as he did, he reportedly spoke a now-famous Latin phrase. What did Caesar say?
answer: 'Alea iacta est' — 'The die is cast'
choices: 'Alea iacta est' — 'The die is cast'
'Veni vidi vici' — 'I came, I saw, I conquered'
'Roma victrix' — 'Rome the victorious'
'Senatus deletur' — 'The Senate is destroyed'
context: The river was the Rubicon, which marked the border between Caesar's province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy proper. Crossing under arms was treason. Suetonius records the line; Plutarch gives it in Greek as a quotation from the playwright Menander. Caesar's civil war ended four years later with him as dictator. He was assassinated on the Ides of March (March 15) 44 BC.

question: In 458 BC, Rome was facing destruction when the Senate summoned a farmer named Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus and made him dictator with absolute power. He saved the city in sixteen days, then voluntarily resigned and went back to his small farm. What did Cincinnatus go back to?
answer: Plowing his four-acre field by hand
choices: Plowing his four-acre field by hand
Teaching his sons to read Latin
Hunting wild boar in the hills outside Rome
Selling olive oil at the Roman forum
context: Cincinnatus became the Roman model of civic virtue — power exercised for duty and surrendered without hesitation. George Washington was nicknamed 'the American Cincinnatus' for resigning his commission after the Revolutionary War in 1783. The Society of the Cincinnati, founded by Revolutionary officers, takes its name from him. The city of Cincinnati, Ohio is named for the society.

question: The Roman emperor Augustus reigned from 27 BC to 14 AD and transformed the city through massive building projects — temples, forums, baths, and the Ara Pacis. On his deathbed he reportedly summed up his achievement with a single boast about the city. What did Augustus claim he had done to Rome?
answer: 'I found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble'
choices: 'I found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of marble'
'I found Rome a republic and left it an empire'
'I found Rome at war and left it at peace'
'I found Rome a town and left it the world'
context: The line is preserved by Suetonius. Augustus's building program included the Forum of Augustus, the Theatre of Marcellus, and the renovation of dozens of temples. The Ara Pacis (Altar of Peace), dedicated 9 BC, still stands in Rome and shows Augustus and his family in procession. Augustus reigned 41 years — the longest of any Roman emperor.

question: On October 28, 312 AD, before the battle of the Milvian Bridge outside Rome, the emperor Constantine reportedly saw a vision in the sky that converted him to Christianity. He won the battle and changed the religious history of the West. What did Constantine reportedly see?
answer: A cross of light above the sun with the words 'In this sign, conquer'
choices: A cross of light above the sun with the words 'In this sign, conquer'
An angel holding a sword of fire above the Tiber river
A dove descending onto his battle standard at dawn
Three crowns floating over the Roman senate house
context: The story is preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea, who said Constantine told it to him personally. Constantine had his soldiers paint the Chi-Rho monogram (the first two letters of 'Christ' in Greek) on their shields. He defeated his rival Maxentius, who drowned in the Tiber. The Edict of Milan in 313 legalized Christianity throughout the empire.

question: The Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius (161-180 AD) wrote a private notebook of philosophical reflections in Greek during his decade of military campaigns on the German frontier. He never intended it for publication. It survived by accident and became one of the most-read books of antiquity. What is the work called?
answer: Meditations
choices: Meditations
Confessions
Discourses
Reflections
context: Marcus titled his work 'To Himself' (Ta eis heauton); 'Meditations' is the conventional English title. He was the last of the so-called Five Good Emperors. Edward Gibbon called his reign the period 'in which the human race was most happy and prosperous.' The work is one of the foundational texts of Stoic philosophy alongside Epictetus and Seneca.

question: Around 530 AD, an Italian monk named Benedict founded a monastery at Monte Cassino south of Rome and wrote a short rule for monastic life — moderate, practical, ordered around prayer and work. His rule became the foundation of nearly all Western monasticism for the next 1,500 years. What Latin phrase summarized its core principle?
answer: 'Ora et labora' — 'Pray and work'
choices: 'Ora et labora' — 'Pray and work'
'Sola fide' — 'By faith alone'
'Soli Deo gloria' — 'Glory to God alone'
'Pax et bonum' — 'Peace and goodness'
context: Benedictine monasteries preserved classical learning through the chaos of the early medieval period — monks copied manuscripts in scriptoria, kept agricultural and medical knowledge alive, and ran the only hospitals and schools in many regions. Monte Cassino was destroyed by the Lombards, the Saracens, an 1349 earthquake, and Allied bombing in 1944 — and rebuilt each time.

question: On Christmas Day in the year 800, in St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, Pope Leo III placed a crown on the head of the Frankish king Charles, declaring him the first new Roman emperor in the West in over 300 years. The act founded what became the Holy Roman Empire. By what name is this king known to history?
answer: Charlemagne — Charles the Great
choices: Charlemagne — Charles the Great
Clovis I — first Frankish king
Pepin the Short — Charlemagne's father
Otto I — later Saxon emperor
context: Charlemagne reportedly told his biographer Einhard that he would never have entered St. Peter's that day had he known the pope planned to crown him — the act outraged the existing Roman emperor in Constantinople. Charlemagne's empire covered most of Western and Central Europe. After his death in 814 his empire was divided among his grandsons in 843; the eastern part became Germany, the western part France.

question: On May 30, 1431, a 19-year-old French peasant girl was burned at the stake in the marketplace of Rouen by English-aligned authorities after a political trial for heresy. Two years earlier she had led the French army to lift the siege of Orleans and had crowned the dauphin king at Reims. Who was she?
answer: Joan of Arc
choices: Joan of Arc
Marie of Anjou
Isabeau of Bavaria
Christine de Pizan
context: Joan claimed to hear the voices of Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret giving her instructions from God. Her trial transcript survives and shows a remarkably composed young woman cross-examining theologians. Twenty-five years after her death, a retrial declared her innocent. She was canonized as a saint by Pope Benedict XV in 1920 — nearly 500 years later.

question: Around 1450 in the German city of Mainz, the goldsmith Johannes Gutenberg invented movable metal type and used it to print roughly 180 copies of an enormous Latin Bible. About 49 copies survive today, kept in some of the world's great libraries. By what name is Gutenberg's Bible commonly known?
answer: The 42-line Bible — for the lines of text per page
choices: The 42-line Bible — for the lines of text per page
The Mainz Psalter — for the city of its printing
The Codex Aureus — for its gold-leaf decoration
The Latin Vulgate — for its translation source
context: Gutenberg's invention combined movable type, oil-based ink, the wooden press (adapted from wine presses), and a metallurgical alloy for the type. The 42-line Bible took about three years to print starting around 1452. Within 50 years roughly 200 European cities had printing presses; over 20 million books had been printed by 1500 — more than all the manuscripts copied by hand in the previous thousand years.

question: Filippo Brunelleschi built the dome of Florence's cathedral between 1420 and 1436 without scaffolding from below — the opening was too vast to span. His four million bricks locked each course in place as the dome rose, using a specific masonry pattern he had studied in ancient Roman ruins. What brick pattern did Brunelleschi use?
answer: Herringbone — bricks set at angles that lock the courses together
choices: Herringbone — bricks set at angles that lock the courses together
Stretcher bond — long bricks laid end to end in single rows
Stack bond — bricks laid directly atop one another in vertical columns
Flemish bond — alternating long and short bricks in each row
context: The dome is 143 feet (44 meters) in diameter and remains the largest masonry dome in the world — no later builder has matched the span without steel or modern concrete. Brunelleschi refused to disclose his method before winning the commission, instead demonstrating his genius by balancing an egg upright on a marble slab. The cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, had stood with no dome for 130 years before Brunelleschi solved it.

question: When Donatello unveiled his bronze David in Florence around 1440, viewers were shocked — not by the subject (David with Goliath's head was a familiar Christian image) but by something the sculpture WAS that had not been done for 1,000 years. What was unprecedented about Donatello's David?
answer: It was the first freestanding nude statue made since Roman antiquity
choices: It was the first freestanding nude statue made since Roman antiquity
It was the first life-sized statue cast in bronze rather than carved in marble
It was the first sculpture displayed outdoors rather than inside a church
It was the first statue signed by the artist on the base for all to see
context: Commissioned by the Medici, probably for the courtyard of the Palazzo Medici. The bronze stands about 5'2" / 158 cm. Donatello had earlier carved a marble David in 1408, but it was clothed. The bronze nude opened a millennium-long absence — Christian art had largely avoided the form since the fall of Rome. Michelangelo's marble David, finished 1504, was a deliberate response to it.

question: Pope Julius II forced the Sistine Chapel ceiling commission on Michelangelo in 1508 over his protests — Michelangelo insisted he was a sculptor, not a painter. He painted 5,000 square feet of fresco alone on a scaffold he designed himself, including the famous Creation of Adam. Roughly how long did the ceiling take Michelangelo to complete?
answer: About four years — finished October 1512
choices: About four years — finished October 1512
About one year — finished December 1509
About fifteen years — finished spring 1523
About twenty-five years — finished autumn 1533
context: Michelangelo's own sonnet to Giovanni da Pistoia describes the physical cost: his beard turned up to heaven, his nape fixed on his spine, his face soaked in paint drops. He returned 22 years later to paint The Last Judgment on the altar wall. The ceiling holds nine scenes from Genesis including the Creation of Adam, in which the fingers of God and man are separated by about an inch — one of the most reproduced images in Western art.

question: On August 3, 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west from Palos in Spain with three small ships, financed by Queen Isabella of Castile and King Ferdinand of Aragon. Ten weeks later he sighted land in the Bahamas. He believed until his death that he had reached the East Indies by sailing west. What were Columbus's three ships called?
answer: Santa María, Pinta, Niña
choices: Santa María, Pinta, Niña
Trinidad, Concepción, Victoria
Mayflower, Speedwell, Sparrow
Bonaventure, Esperanza, Triunfo
context: The Santa María was the largest (about 85 feet) and was wrecked on a reef off Hispaniola Christmas night 1492 — Columbus used its timbers to build the first European settlement in the New World, named La Navidad. The Niña was a nickname; her formal name was Santa Clara. Columbus made four voyages between 1492 and 1504, reaching the Caribbean, Central America, and the northern coast of South America, but never the North American mainland.

question: On October 31, 1517, an Augustinian monk and theology professor in the small German town of Wittenberg posted 95 theses in Latin on the door of the castle church, attacking the sale of indulgences (paid certificates for forgiveness of sins). The act became the spark of the Protestant Reformation. Who posted the theses?
answer: Martin Luther
choices: Martin Luther
John Calvin
Huldrych Zwingli
Philip Melanchthon
context: The church door at Wittenberg functioned as the university bulletin board, so Luther's posting was an academic invitation to debate, not initially a public protest. Within weeks the theses had been translated into German and printed across Europe by the new Gutenberg presses. Luther was excommunicated in 1521. At the Diet of Worms he reportedly said: 'Here I stand. I can do no other. God help me. Amen.'

question: In September 1519, Ferdinand Magellan led five Spanish ships westward to find a route to the Spice Islands by sailing around South America. Three years later, one ship limped back to Spain — but Magellan was not on it. He had been killed in 1521 in the Philippines. What was the historic significance of that one returning ship?
answer: It completed the first circumnavigation of the globe
choices: It completed the first circumnavigation of the globe
It carried the first map of the Pacific Ocean
It returned with the first potatoes brought to Europe
It was the only ship to discover the South Pole
context: The ship was the Victoria, captained by Juan Sebastián Elcano after Magellan's death. Of the roughly 270 men who sailed in 1519, only 18 returned in September 1522 — about 7% survival. Magellan was killed in the Battle of Mactan by warriors loyal to a local chieftain named Lapu-Lapu, who is honored as a Filipino national hero. The voyage proved the Americas were a separate continent (not the eastern edge of Asia) and showed how vast the Pacific actually was.

question: In 1519 the Spanish conqueror Hernán Cortés landed near modern Veracruz, Mexico with about 600 men, and faced the Aztec Empire of millions ruled by Montezuma II at the city of Tenochtitlán. To prevent any of his men from deserting and sailing home, Cortés ordered a drastic act before marching inland. What did Cortés do to his ships?
answer: Scuttled or burned them so retreat was impossible
