choices: Scuttled or burned them so retreat was impossible
Sent them back to Cuba with the wounded and old
Buried them under sand on the beach for hidden return
Sold them to local fishermen for supplies and silver
context: Cortés scuttled the ships by drilling holes; some accounts say burning, but the contemporary records suggest sinking. His tiny force then marched 200 miles inland through Tlaxcalan territory, recruited tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan allies who hated the Aztecs, and entered Tenochtitlán on November 8, 1519. Tenochtitlán fell on August 13, 1521 after a brutal siege.

question: In June 1633, the 69-year-old Italian astronomer Galileo Galilei knelt before the Roman Inquisition and formally recanted his teaching that the Earth orbits the Sun. According to a legend that emerged a century later, as he rose from his knees he muttered four words under his breath about the Earth. What is Galileo reputed to have said?
answer: 'Eppur si muove' — 'And yet it moves'
choices: 'Eppur si muove' — 'And yet it moves'
'Veritas vincit' — 'Truth conquers'
'Lux fugiet' — 'The light flees'
'Caelum tacet' — 'The heavens are silent'
context: Galileo spent the rest of his life under house arrest at his villa near Florence. He went blind by 1638 but continued to dictate work to his students — including Two New Sciences (1638), which laid the foundation for modern physics. The Vatican formally rehabilitated Galileo in 1992, 359 years after the trial. The 'Eppur si muove' line first appears in print in 1757.

question: The German astronomer Johannes Kepler (1571-1630), using the precise observations of his teacher Tycho Brahe, discovered that the planets do not move in perfect circles around the Sun. He showed they trace a different geometric shape, with the Sun off-center. What shape did Kepler prove the planetary orbits to be?
answer: Ellipses — with the Sun at one focus
choices: Ellipses — with the Sun at one focus
Spirals — with the Sun at the center
Parabolas — with the Sun at the vertex
Hyperbolas — with the Sun at the focus
context: Kepler's three laws of planetary motion (published 1609 and 1619) made Newton's gravitational synthesis possible 60 years later. Kepler's mother was tried as a witch in 1620-21; Kepler spent six years defending her and got her acquitted. His own life was hard — he buried two wives and several children, and worked partly under the eccentric Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II.

question: On All Saints' Day, November 1, 1755, an enormous earthquake destroyed Lisbon, Portugal, killing roughly 50,000 people while many were at Mass. The disaster shook European thinkers' confidence in the optimist philosophy that 'all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds.' One French philosopher used the earthquake to attack that philosophy in a famous 1759 satirical novel. Who wrote it?
answer: Voltaire — in his novel Candide
choices: Voltaire — in his novel Candide
Denis Diderot — in his Encyclopédie
Jean-Jacques Rousseau — in his Emile
Baron d'Holbach — in his System of Nature
context: Voltaire's target was Gottfried Leibniz's optimism, popularized by Alexander Pope's Essay on Man ('whatever is, is right'). Candide travels the world watching disasters and concludes that we should simply 'cultivate our garden.' The book was banned almost everywhere on publication and sold tens of thousands of copies. Voltaire's earlier Poem on the Lisbon Disaster (1756) was his first direct attack on theological optimism.

question: The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier (1743-1794) overthrew the older 'phlogiston' theory of burning by proving that combustion is a chemical reaction between fuel and a specific gas in the air. He identified the gas and gave it the name we still use. What did Lavoisier name the gas that supports burning?
answer: Oxygen — from Greek meaning 'acid-former'
choices: Oxygen — from Greek meaning 'acid-former'
Hydrogen — from Greek meaning 'water-former'
Nitrogen — from Latin meaning 'lifeless air'
Carbon — from Latin meaning 'charcoal'
context: Lavoisier also established the conservation of mass: matter is neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions. He was a tax collector for the French monarchy as well as a scientist. The Reign of Terror sent him to the guillotine on May 8, 1794. The judge reportedly said 'the Republic has no need of savants.' The mathematician Lagrange said the next day: 'It took an instant to cut off that head, and 100 years may not produce another like it.'

question: On July 14, 1789, a Paris mob stormed an old royal fortress and prison on the east side of the city. Only seven prisoners were inside, but the political symbolism set off the French Revolution. The fortress was demolished in the months that followed. What was the building called?
answer: The Bastille
choices: The Bastille
The Conciergerie
The Tuileries
The Hôtel des Invalides
context: July 14 is still France's national holiday — Bastille Day. The mob seized the fortress for its gunpowder, not the prisoners. The Bastille's stones were carted away as souvenirs; one set of stones was carved into a model of the fortress and sent on tour through France. Within months France had abolished feudalism, issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man, and nationalized Church lands.

question: On November 24, 1859, the English naturalist Charles Darwin published a book proposing that all species evolved over vast time by a process he called 'descent with modification through natural selection.' The first printing sold out on the day of publication. What is the book's title?
answer: On the Origin of Species
choices: On the Origin of Species
The Voyage of the Beagle
The Descent of Man
The Expression of the Emotions
context: Darwin had developed his theory by 1842 but delayed publishing for 17 years, partly fearing religious backlash. He was finally pushed to publish when Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay in 1858 outlining the same theory independently. The two men's papers were jointly presented to the Linnean Society in London in July 1858. Darwin is buried in Westminster Abbey next to Isaac Newton.

question: In May 1881, the French chemist Louis Pasteur staged a public demonstration of his new anthrax vaccine at a farm in Pouilly-le-Fort. He vaccinated 25 sheep, left 25 unvaccinated, then infected all 50 with anthrax. The results, displayed two weeks later, made Pasteur famous worldwide. What happened to the sheep?
answer: All 25 vaccinated lived; all 25 unvaccinated died
choices: All 25 vaccinated lived; all 25 unvaccinated died
Vaccinated and unvaccinated all survived but the vaccinated grew faster
About half the vaccinated died; nearly all unvaccinated died as well
All 50 died, but the vaccinated took longer to succumb than the unvaccinated
context: Pasteur followed the demonstration in 1885 by giving the first human rabies vaccine to nine-year-old Joseph Meister, who had been bitten 14 times by a rabid dog. The boy lived; Pasteur became a national hero. Meister grew up to become caretaker of the Pasteur Institute. In 1940, when German troops ordered him to open Pasteur's crypt, he reportedly committed suicide rather than disturb the tomb.

question: Johann Sebastian Bach's St. Matthew Passion premiered in Leipzig in 1727. After Bach's death in 1750, his music fell out of fashion. The work was largely forgotten for 102 years until a 20-year-old prodigy revived it in Berlin in 1829, launching the modern Bach revival. Who staged the revival?
answer: Felix Mendelssohn — using a manuscript copy his grandmother had given him
choices: Felix Mendelssohn — using a manuscript copy his grandmother had given him
Robert Schumann — at the Leipzig Gewandhaus orchestra
Johannes Brahms — as part of his Hamburg youth concerts
Franz Liszt — during his Weimar conducting tenure
context: Bach was respected as an organist in his lifetime but unfashionable by the time of his death — Baroque counterpoint was being eclipsed by Classical style. His son Wilhelm Friedemann's widow famously sold off Bach manuscripts as scrap paper. Mendelssohn's grandmother, Bella Salomon, had bought a manuscript copy of the St. Matthew Passion and given it to her grandson for his 14th birthday.

question: On May 7, 1824, the deaf composer Ludwig van Beethoven conducted the premiere of his Ninth Symphony at Vienna's Kärntnertor Theater — the symphony that ends with the choral 'Ode to Joy.' At the end Beethoven could not hear the audience's response. What was done so he could see it?
answer: A contralto turned him around to face the audience cheering and waving handkerchiefs
choices: A contralto turned him around to face the audience cheering and waving handkerchiefs
The orchestra stood and bowed in his direction to signal applause was happening
Stagehands rolled a mirror onstage so he could see the audience behind him
The conductor beside him raised both hands toward the crowd in pantomime
context: Beethoven had begun losing his hearing around 1798 in his late twenties and was completely deaf by the Ninth's premiere. He had stopped public performance long before. The Ninth's last movement uses Schiller's 1785 poem 'An die Freude' (To Joy). The orchestra had been instructed to follow the official conductor Michael Umlauf, not Beethoven. The contralto soloist Karoline Unger is credited with turning him to see the ovation.

question: In late 1791 Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, aged 35, was working frantically in Vienna on a commissioned funeral mass — a work he came to believe he was writing for his own funeral. He died on December 5, 1791 with the Requiem unfinished. His student completed it after his death. Who finished Mozart's Requiem?
answer: Franz Xaver Süssmayr — Mozart's student and copyist
choices: Franz Xaver Süssmayr — Mozart's student and copyist
Antonio Salieri — Mozart's rival at the Viennese court
Joseph Haydn — Mozart's friend and mentor
Carl Czerny — Mozart's eventual successor as court composer
context: The Requiem had been commissioned anonymously by Count Franz von Walsegg, who wanted to pass it off as his own composition in memory of his late wife. Mozart's widow Constanze needed the second half of the commission fee, so she had Süssmayr complete the work secretly. Mozart's exact cause of death is debated — rheumatic fever, kidney failure, and several other diagnoses have been proposed. He was buried in a simple common grave in St. Marx Cemetery.

question: In the 1660s, in the small Dutch town of Delft, the painter Johannes Vermeer (1632-1675) produced about 35 surviving paintings — quiet domestic interiors with extraordinary handling of light. One of these is often called 'the Mona Lisa of the North,' showing a young woman in a blue and yellow turban looking back over her shoulder. What is the painting commonly called?
answer: Girl with a Pearl Earring
choices: Girl with a Pearl Earring
The Lacemaker at Her Window
Lady in Blue Reading a Letter
The Milkmaid at the Table
context: Vermeer worked slowly, produced few paintings, and died bankrupt at 43 from the financial stress of the Franco-Dutch War. His work was largely forgotten for two centuries; the 19th-century French critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger rediscovered him in the 1860s. The painting (c. 1665) hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague. The pearl in the painting may not actually be a pearl — some art historians suggest it is glass or tin, since real pearls of that size were extraordinarily rare.

question: In the same year that the American colonies declared independence, the Scottish moral philosopher Adam Smith published a five-book economic treatise that became the founding work of modern economics. The book argued that free markets, guided by what Smith called 'the invisible hand,' produce social benefit. What is the book's title?
answer: The Wealth of Nations
choices: The Wealth of Nations
The Theory of Moral Sentiments
Principles of Political Economy
An Essay on the Principle of Population
context: Smith's full title was An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, published March 9, 1776 in London. Smith had earlier written The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), in which he argued that human sympathy is the foundation of ethics. The two books are sometimes treated as in tension but Smith intended them as complementary — markets work because moral agents within them have sympathy and conscience.

question: The English philosopher John Locke (1632-1704) published in 1689 a book that grounded political authority in the consent of the governed and claimed certain rights belonged to every person by nature, not by gift of king or parliament. Thomas Jefferson would draw on Locke heavily 87 years later in the Declaration of Independence. What did Locke call these inalienable rights?
answer: Life, liberty, and property
choices: Life, liberty, and property
Faith, hope, and charity
Order, justice, and tradition
Reason, conscience, and worship
context: Locke's Two Treatises of Government were written largely during his exile in Holland in the 1680s, when he feared royal arrest. Jefferson adapted Locke's 'life, liberty, and property' as 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness' in the 1776 Declaration. Locke also wrote A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689), arguing the state had no business compelling religious belief — a foundational document for religious freedom in the Anglo-American tradition.

question: On June 18, 1815, the French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte fought his last battle against a combined British-Dutch-German army under the Duke of Wellington and a Prussian army under Marshal Blücher in present-day Belgium. The crushing defeat ended his 100-day return from exile. What is the battle called?
answer: Waterloo
choices: Waterloo
Austerlitz
Borodino
Leipzig
context: Wellington famously called Waterloo 'the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life.' Napoleon was exiled a second time, this time to the remote South Atlantic island of Saint Helena, where he died in 1821 at age 51. The Prussian arrival on Napoleon's right flank in the late afternoon turned the battle. The Prussian commander Blücher was 72 years old and had been thrown from his horse two days earlier at Ligny.

question: After Napoleon's defeat, the great powers of Europe met from 1814 to 1815 in a long diplomatic congress to redraw the map and balance power on the continent. The Austrian foreign minister Klemens von Metternich dominated the gathering, which set the European order for the next century. In which city did the congress meet?
answer: Vienna
choices: Vienna
Berlin
Paris
London
context: The Congress of Vienna restored several monarchies dethroned by Napoleon (the Bourbons in France, the Pope in Rome), created the German Confederation, expanded Prussia, gave Britain Malta and the Cape Colony, and gave the Russian czar most of Poland. Metternich's settlement preserved peace among the great powers (with brief exceptions) until World War I broke out in 1914 — almost exactly 100 years later.

question: In 1831 a 25-year-old French aristocrat traveled across the young United States for nine months on an official mission to study American prisons. Instead he wrote a two-volume book on the new American democracy and its character — one of the most insightful books ever written about America by a foreigner. Who wrote it?
answer: Alexis de Tocqueville
choices: Alexis de Tocqueville
Gustave de Beaumont
Marquis de Lafayette
François Guizot
context: Tocqueville traveled with his friend Gustave de Beaumont, ostensibly to study prison reform; both produced major books from the trip. Democracy in America appeared in two volumes (1835 and 1840). Tocqueville foresaw both the eventual dominance of America and Russia on the world stage, and the danger that democratic equality might produce a 'soft despotism' of pervasive bureaucratic management. He also predicted the American Civil War over slavery.

question: In 1769 the Scottish instrument-maker James Watt patented a critical improvement to the steam engine — a separate condenser chamber that kept the main cylinder hot while steam was cooled elsewhere. The change drastically increased efficiency and launched the practical industrial age. Watt's name is now the SI unit of what?
answer: Power — one watt equals one joule per second
choices: Power — one watt equals one joule per second
Heat — one watt equals one calorie of warming
Pressure — one watt equals one pound per square inch
Volume — one watt equals one cubic meter at standard temperature
context: Watt did not invent the steam engine — Thomas Newcomen had built workable atmospheric engines decades earlier — but Watt's separate condenser made the engine practical for factories, mines, and (eventually) locomotives and ships. Watt later partnered with Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton; their firm dominated the British steam-engine business for decades. Watt also coined the term 'horsepower' to help customers compare his engines to working horses.

question: On October 21, 1879, the American inventor Thomas Edison and his Menlo Park laboratory team in New Jersey successfully tested a long-burning electric lamp using a specific kind of filament inside a vacuum-sealed glass bulb. The breakthrough made domestic electric lighting commercially viable. What was Edison's filament made of?
answer: Carbonized cotton thread (later carbonized bamboo)
choices: Carbonized cotton thread (later carbonized bamboo)
Coiled platinum wire with a thin copper coating
Twisted nickel-iron alloy in a hydrogen atmosphere
Tungsten filament drawn into a fine wire (the modern type)
context: Edison's team tested thousands of materials before settling on carbonized cotton; later they switched to carbonized bamboo for longer life. The Pearl Street Station in Manhattan, opened September 1882, was the first commercial central power plant — supplying about 80 customers in downtown New York. The modern tungsten filament was developed later, around 1904-1910. Edison was eventually issued 1,093 U.S. patents.

question: On May 29, 1913, at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris, the Ballets Russes premiered a new Stravinsky ballet — angular, primitive, with dissonant rhythms and pagan ritual imagery. The audience response made musical history. What happened at the premiere?
answer: The audience rioted — fistfights broke out in the seats during the performance
choices: The audience rioted — fistfights broke out in the seats during the performance
The audience walked out in silence — leaving the dancers performing to an empty hall
The audience demanded twelve encores — keeping the dancers onstage until midnight
The audience set fire to the program books — the police cleared the theater
context: The riot at the Rite of Spring premiere is one of the most famous scandals in musical history. Witnesses described shouting matches between supporters and opponents, slapping, and dancers unable to hear the orchestra. The work was repeated quietly within a year as a concert piece without choreography and was a triumph. Stravinsky lived until 1971 — long enough to see The Rite of Spring become a standard orchestra piece and (via Disney's Fantasia, 1940) reach millions.

question: On April 26, 1937, German and Italian aircraft sent to support Franco's nationalist forces in the Spanish Civil War carpet-bombed a Basque town on a market day, killing hundreds of civilians. The Spanish painter Pablo Picasso, then living in Paris, responded with an enormous black-and-white mural-sized canvas. What is the painting called?
answer: Guernica — for the bombed Basque town
choices: Guernica — for the bombed Basque town
Las Meninas — for the Spanish royal court
The Three Musicians — for the trio depicted
Demoiselles d'Avignon — for the French city
context: Picasso painted Guernica in about five weeks for the Spanish Pavilion at the 1937 Paris International Exposition. The painting is roughly 25 feet wide and 11 feet tall. Picasso refused to let it return to Spain while Franco was alive; it lived at MoMA in New York until 1981, when it was finally moved to Madrid. The bombing was an early test of Luftwaffe terror-bombing tactics that Germany would use across Europe in WW2.

question: After being placed under imperial ban at the Diet of Worms in 1521, Martin Luther was hidden by Frederick the Wise at Wartburg Castle in Thuringia. In just eleven weeks of intensive work that autumn, Luther produced a translation that became one of the foundational documents of modern German literature. What did Luther translate?
answer: The New Testament — into German from the original Greek
choices: The New Testament — into German from the original Greek
The Latin Mass — into German liturgical settings
The 95 Theses — into a popular German pamphlet
Augustine's Confessions — into modern German
context: Luther worked from Erasmus's 1516 Greek New Testament rather than the standard Latin Vulgate, going back to older sources — a radical move at the time. His complete Bible (Old and New Testaments) appeared in 1534. Luther's German shaped the standard form of the language much as the King James Bible (1611) shaped English. The Wartburg manuscript desk where Luther worked is still shown to visitors.

question: The French Protestant reformer John Calvin (1509-1564) settled in the Swiss city of Geneva in 1536, where over the next 28 years he shaped its civic and religious life so thoroughly that the city became famous across Europe as a Protestant equivalent to Rome. What was Calvin's most influential systematic theological work, first published 1536 and expanded throughout his life?
answer: Institutes of the Christian Religion
choices: Institutes of the Christian Religion
Commentary on the Romans
Geneva Confession of Faith
On the Bondage of the Will
context: Calvin's Institutes went through four editions during his lifetime, growing from a small handbook in 1536 to a four-volume work by 1559. Geneva became a refuge for Protestants fleeing Catholic persecution across Europe — including John Knox, who would carry Calvinist Presbyterianism back to Scotland. Calvin's doctrines of predestination and election shaped Reformed Christianity from the Netherlands and Scotland to New England Puritanism.

question: On October 25, 1415 — Saint Crispin's Day — a small English army under the young King Henry V destroyed a much larger French force in a muddy field in northern France. The decisive weapon was a particular kind of bow that English yeomen had trained on since childhood. What was the weapon?
answer: The longbow
choices: The longbow
The crossbow
The composite bow
The catapult
context: The English longbow (about six feet long, draw weight 100+ pounds, yew wood) had a longer range and faster rate of fire than the crossbows of the French infantry. French knights bogged in deep mud were cut down. Estimates of the kill ratio are debated but were heavily lopsided in England's favor. Shakespeare made the day immortal in Henry V (c. 1599) with the 'St. Crispin's Day' speech: 'We few, we happy few, we band of brothers.'

question: On the snowy night of March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a Boston mob, killing five colonists in what became known as the Boston Massacre. When the soldiers were put on trial, a young Boston lawyer agreed to defend them — a wildly unpopular decision that he believed the rule of law required. He later became a U.S. president. Who defended the British soldiers?
answer: John Adams
choices: John Adams
Samuel Adams
Patrick Henry
John Hancock
context: Adams secured acquittal for six of the eight soldiers; two others were convicted of manslaughter and branded on the thumb. He later called his decision to defend the soldiers one of the best he ever made. The first to fall in the massacre was Crispus Attucks, a man of African and Native American descent — considered one of the first martyrs of the American Revolution. Adams's cousin Samuel Adams was meanwhile using the event as propaganda.

question: On the night of December 16, 1773, about 100 Sons of Liberty disguised as Mohawk Indians boarded three British ships in Boston Harbor and dumped 342 chests of tea into the water — roughly 92,000 pounds, worth about $1.7 million in modern terms. They were protesting which British policy?
answer: The Tea Act of 1773 — which kept a tax on tea sold in the colonies
choices: The Tea Act of 1773 — which kept a tax on tea sold in the colonies
The Stamp Act of 1765 — which taxed printed documents
The Quartering Act — which required colonists to house British soldiers
The Coercive Acts — which closed the port of Boston permanently
context: The Tea Act actually lowered the price of tea in the colonies but kept the small Townshend duty as a symbolic assertion of Parliament's authority to tax. King George III and his ministers responded with the Coercive Acts (the colonists called them the Intolerable Acts), which closed Boston Harbor until the tea was paid for. The crisis convinced the colonies to convene the First Continental Congress in September 1774.

question: In March 1775, with war approaching, a Virginia lawyer named Patrick Henry rose to speak at St. John's Church in Richmond, urging the Virginia Convention to arm the militia. His speech ended with an electrifying five-word phrase. What did Henry reportedly say?
answer: 'Give me liberty or give me death'
choices: 'Give me liberty or give me death'
'Stand and resist or die kneeling'
'Freedom now and freedom forever'
'For God and country we fight'
context: Henry's speech was reconstructed from memory by biographer William Wirt 40 years later; no contemporary transcript exists. Whether the exact words match what Henry said is debated. The Virginia Convention passed Henry's resolutions arming the militia. Henry would later become Governor of Virginia and was an Anti-Federalist who opposed ratification of the U.S. Constitution because it lacked a Bill of Rights.

question: On April 19, 1775, British regulars marched from Boston to seize colonial weapons stored at Concord, Massachusetts. They were met by armed Minutemen on the village green at Lexington at dawn. Somebody fired — nobody knows who — and the American Revolution began. Ralph Waldo Emerson later memorialized that first shot with a famous phrase. What did Emerson call it?
answer: 'The shot heard round the world'
choices: 'The shot heard round the world'
'The musket of liberty's birth'
'The dawn-fire of America'
'The first whisper of freedom'
context: Emerson's phrase comes from his 'Concord Hymn' (1837), written for the dedication of the Battle of Concord monument. Eight Minutemen died at Lexington. The British column moved on to Concord, where Americans turned them back at North Bridge. The retreat to Boston that day was a 20-mile running battle in which militia harassed the British column the entire way. British losses for the day: 273; American: 95.

question: In January 1776 a 39-page pamphlet appeared in the American colonies, arguing in clear popular language for an immediate declaration of independence and against the very institution of monarchy. It sold about 120,000 copies in the first three months and decisively shifted colonial opinion toward independence. Who wrote it?
answer: Thomas Paine
choices: Thomas Paine
Thomas Jefferson
Samuel Adams
John Dickinson
context: Paine had arrived in the colonies just 14 months earlier, an English corset-maker turned writer with letters of introduction from Benjamin Franklin. Common Sense argued that it was absurd for a large continent to be ruled by a small island, and that monarchy itself was both irrational and unchristian. Paine later wrote The American Crisis (December 1776) — opening with 'These are the times that try men's souls' — which Washington had read aloud to his troops before Trenton.

question: On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress in Philadelphia adopted a document drafted mainly by a 33-year-old Virginia delegate at his Market Street lodgings. It declared the 13 colonies free of Britain and proclaimed certain truths to be 'self-evident.' Who was the principal drafter?
answer: Thomas Jefferson
choices: Thomas Jefferson
John Adams
Benjamin Franklin
Roger Sherman
context: Jefferson worked on the draft for about two weeks. Adams and Franklin made small edits before the full Congress debated and revised it July 2-4. The most-quoted line — that all men are created equal and endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness — adapts John Locke. Adams predicted July 2 (the day independence was voted) would be celebrated forever; instead Americans chose July 4, the adoption date of the Declaration's text.

question: On Christmas night 1776, with his army nearly destroyed and enlistments expiring in a week, George Washington led 2,400 Continentals across the ice-choked Delaware River in a snowstorm to attack the Hessian garrison at Trenton at dawn. The complete dawn victory saved the Revolution. What three-word password did Washington use that night?
answer: 'Victory or Death'
choices: 'Victory or Death'
'Liberty or Slavery'
'God and Country'
'Live Free or Die'
context: The Continental Army took 900 Hessian prisoners for the loss of two Americans frozen on the march. Trenton (December 26 1776) plus Princeton (January 3 1777) are called the 'Ten Crucial Days.' The campaign restored enough hope that enlistments were renewed and the Continental Army survived. Washington wrote the password on each soldier's hat the night before the crossing.

question: On September 22, 1776, the British army hanged a 21-year-old Continental Army officer in New York City as a spy. As he stood on the scaffold he reportedly delivered a famous defiant final line. Who was he and what did he say?
answer: Nathan Hale — 'I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country'
choices: Nathan Hale — 'I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country'
Benedict Arnold — 'God spare the cause though I cannot live to see it'
Joseph Warren — 'A free people stand or fall together'
Henry Knox — 'My only sorrow is to leave my comrades behind'
context: Hale's quote, recorded by British Captain John Montresor at the scene, may have been adapted from Joseph Addison's 1713 play 'Cato' — 'What a pity it is that we can die but once to serve our country.' Hale was a Yale graduate and schoolteacher who had volunteered for intelligence work after Washington's defeat at Long Island. Benedict Arnold, a brilliant Continental general, defected to the British in 1780 — his name became synonymous with treason.

question: In October 1777 an American army under Horatio Gates and Benedict Arnold surrounded and captured an entire British army of about 6,000 troops under General John Burgoyne in upstate New York. The stunning American victory had one immediate diplomatic consequence that probably won the entire Revolution. What did the Battle of Saratoga accomplish?
answer: Convinced France to enter the war openly on the American side
choices: Convinced France to enter the war openly on the American side
Forced King George III to begin direct peace negotiations within six months
Triggered a slave uprising in the British West Indies that drained Royal Navy strength
Persuaded Spain to land an invasion army on the New England coast
context: Benjamin Franklin had spent over a year in Paris trying to convince Louis XVI that the Americans could win. Saratoga was the proof. The Franco-American alliance was signed February 6 1778; France brought money, ships, troops, and eventually (at Yorktown 1781) the naval blockade that trapped Cornwallis. Spain and the Dutch Republic also joined the war against Britain. The British ended up fighting three European powers and the Americans simultaneously. Saratoga also turned Burgoyne's career — he was widely blamed in London for the disaster and never commanded again.

question: From December 1777 through June 1778, Washington's Continental Army endured a brutal winter encampment at a place 20 miles northwest of British-occupied Philadelphia. About 2,000 of 12,000 soldiers died from disease, cold, and starvation. A Prussian volunteer arrived in February and transformed the army through professional drill training. Who was the drillmaster?
answer: Baron Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben
choices: Baron Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben
Marquis de Lafayette of France
Tadeusz Kościuszko of Poland
Comte de Rochambeau of France
context: Von Steuben spoke no English. He drilled the troops by shouting German and French commands while an aide translated. He wrote the Continental Army's first standardized drill manual ('the Blue Book') by candlelight. Lafayette also served at Valley Forge — a teenage French aristocrat who would become Washington's surrogate son. The army that marched out of Valley Forge in June 1778 was disciplined enough to fight the British to a standstill at Monmouth Court House.

question: On October 19, 1781, after a three-week siege by combined American and French forces, British General Charles Cornwallis surrendered his army of about 8,000 at a Virginia tobacco port. According to legend, the British band played a particular tune as the defeated army marched out. What was the tune?
answer: 'The World Turned Upside Down'
choices: 'The World Turned Upside Down'
'God Save the King'
'The British Grenadiers'
'Rule Britannia'
context: The tune story is traditional but disputed by some historians. What is certain: French Admiral de Grasse's fleet had defeated the British Royal Navy at the Battle of the Chesapeake in September, sealing Cornwallis's escape. Cornwallis claimed illness and did not appear at the surrender; his second-in-command General O'Hara offered Cornwallis's sword first to Rochambeau (who deferred to Washington), and Washington in turn deferred to his second-in-command Benjamin Lincoln, who had been humiliated at Charleston the year before.

question: In December 1783, after defeating Britain, George Washington did something that astonished King George III. He appeared before Congress at Annapolis, gave a brief speech, handed over his commission, and went home to Mount Vernon. King George said he would be 'the greatest man in the world.' What had Washington done?
answer: Voluntarily resigned his command and returned to private life as a farmer
choices: Voluntarily resigned his command and returned to private life as a farmer
Refused the crown when officers offered to make him king of America
Wrote a new constitution single-handedly and brought it to Congress
Burned his wartime correspondence so no battlefield records survived
context: The painting by John Trumbull (1824) hangs in the U.S. Capitol Rotunda. Washington's act was without precedent — Cromwell had become Lord Protector; Caesar had crossed the Rubicon. Washington went back to his plow like Cincinnatus. He would be called back to the presidency in 1789, then resign that office too after two terms.

question: From May through September 1787, 55 delegates from the 13 states met in secret in Philadelphia's State House to revise the failing Articles of Confederation. Instead they wrote an entirely new framework of government — the document under which America still operates. Who presided over the convention?
answer: George Washington
choices: George Washington
Benjamin Franklin
James Madison
Alexander Hamilton
context: Washington's presence was thought essential for the convention's legitimacy. He said almost nothing during the four months of debate but his stature commanded respect. James Madison, then 36, took the convention's most detailed notes; he is now considered the 'Father of the Constitution.' Benjamin Franklin, 81, was the oldest delegate and persuaded several delegates to sign even though they disagreed with parts of the document. The Constitution was ratified in 1788 and the new government began March 1789.

question: On the morning of July 11, 1804, sitting Vice President Aaron Burr fatally wounded the former Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, across the Hudson from New York City. Hamilton died the next day. What had caused the duel?
answer: Insulting letters Hamilton had written about Burr in a New York election dispute
choices: Insulting letters Hamilton had written about Burr in a New York election dispute
Hamilton's affair with Burr's daughter that came to light that summer
A trade-policy disagreement that led to a public personal feud
Burr's open attempts to seize the western territories for an independent empire
context: Hamilton fired into the air (or shot wide); Burr fired directly at Hamilton and hit him in the abdomen. Hamilton died at 49, leaving his wife Eliza with seven children. The pair had used the same Wogdon dueling pistols three years earlier when Hamilton's eldest son Philip was killed in a duel at the same spot. Burr was indicted in New Jersey and New York but never tried. He went on to plot what may have been a separatist conspiracy in the western territories, was tried for treason in 1807 by Chief Justice John Marshall, and acquitted.

question: In April 1803, Napoleon Bonaparte sold the United States about 828,000 square miles of French territory in central North America for 15 million dollars — roughly three cents per acre. The transaction doubled the size of the country. Which U.S. president completed the purchase?
answer: Thomas Jefferson
choices: Thomas Jefferson
John Adams
James Madison
James Monroe
context: Jefferson's diplomats Robert Livingston and James Monroe had been authorized only to negotiate the purchase of New Orleans. They were astonished when Napoleon's foreign minister Talleyrand offered them the entire territory. Napoleon needed the cash for European wars and had given up on his American empire after the failed reconquest of Haiti. Jefferson was a strict constitutional constructionist who privately doubted he had the constitutional authority to make the purchase, but he made it anyway.

question: In May 1804, an expedition commissioned by Thomas Jefferson set out from St. Louis up the Missouri River to explore the new Louisiana Purchase territory and find a route to the Pacific. The two captains commanding the Corps of Discovery were aided crucially by a Shoshone woman who joined them with her infant son. Who was she?
answer: Sacagawea
choices: Sacagawea
Pocahontas
Lozen
Nancy Ward
context: Sacagawea was 16 or 17 when she joined the expedition with her French-Canadian trader husband Toussaint Charbonneau. She gave birth to her son Jean Baptiste in February 1805 at Fort Mandan. Her language skills, knowledge of edible plants, and presence as a woman with a baby (signaling the expedition was not a war party) were all essential. Lewis and Clark reached the Pacific Ocean in November 1805 and returned to St. Louis in September 1806.

question: In August 1814, during the War of 1812, British troops captured Washington, D.C. and burned the White House, the Capitol, and other public buildings — retaliation for an American raid on York (Toronto) in 1813. Before fleeing the White House, First Lady Dolley Madison saved a famous painting from the State Dining Room. What did Dolley Madison save?
answer: The full-length portrait of George Washington by Gilbert Stuart
choices: The full-length portrait of George Washington by Gilbert Stuart
The first official portrait of John Adams in oils
The hand-painted family Bible of Thomas Jefferson
The original Declaration of Independence and a few signed letters
context: The Gilbert Stuart 'Lansdowne' portrait of Washington (1796) hangs today in the East Room of the White House, restored after the burning. Dolley Madison had the frame broken so the canvas could be quickly rolled and removed. President James Madison was away with the army; Dolley fled across the Potomac with the painting. The British officers ate the dinner she had prepared before setting fire to the building. The White House was rebuilt and reoccupied in 1817.

question: On September 13-14, 1814, a Washington lawyer named Francis Scott Key was aboard a British warship in Baltimore Harbor negotiating a prisoner exchange when the Royal Navy began bombarding the American Fort McHenry. Key watched all night through smoke. The garrison flag was still flying at dawn. Key wrote a poem about the night. What is the poem now called?
answer: The Star-Spangled Banner
choices: The Star-Spangled Banner
Hail, Columbia
America the Beautiful
My Country 'Tis of Thee
context: Key's poem was set to the tune of 'To Anacreon in Heaven,' a British drinking song. It was adopted as the U.S. national anthem in 1931 — 117 years after Key wrote it. The huge garrison flag (30 by 42 feet, 15 stars and 15 stripes) had been sewn by Baltimore widow Mary Pickersgill the year before; it now hangs in the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Fort McHenry's defenders held off the British Navy and the city of Baltimore was saved.

question: In 1794, farmers in western Pennsylvania resisted a federal excise tax on distilled spirits — a key Hamilton revenue measure. The protest turned violent. President George Washington did something no later U.S. president has done: he personally led federal troops to suppress an armed rebellion. About how many troops did Washington lead west?
answer: About 13,000 — larger than most Continental armies of the Revolution
choices: About 13,000 — larger than most Continental armies of the Revolution
About 500 — a token force to make a symbolic point
About 2,500 — the federal regular army of the period
About 25,000 — most of the state militias of all 13 states
context: Washington rode at the head of the column wearing his old Continental Army uniform; he turned back at Bedford, Pennsylvania, leaving Alexander Hamilton in operational command. The 'rebels' largely dispersed before the army arrived. Two men were convicted of treason and Washington later pardoned them. The episode established federal authority to enforce its own tax laws and demonstrated that the new government would respond to armed resistance.

question: In September 1796, near the end of his second term, George Washington declined to run for a third and published a long open letter in a Philadelphia newspaper offering advice to the nation he was leaving in others' hands. The address became one of the most important political documents in American history. What did Washington warn against?
answer: Permanent foreign alliances and the spirit of political faction
choices: Permanent foreign alliances and the spirit of political faction
Slavery's expansion into new western territories beyond the Mississippi
Industrial development that would corrupt the nation's farming character
The election of any future president from the South rather than the North
context: Washington's Farewell Address (drafted in part by Alexander Hamilton) urged Americans to avoid 'entangling alliances' with European powers and warned that political parties would tear the country apart. The two-term tradition Washington established held until Franklin Roosevelt won four straight elections starting 1932; the 22nd Amendment formally limited future presidents to two terms in 1951. Washington died at Mount Vernon in December 1799 at age 67.

question: Two of the most prominent Founders — political rivals turned old-age friends — both died on the same day, in different states, an extraordinary coincidence that became a national legend. The day was Independence Day 1826. Who were they?
answer: Thomas Jefferson and John Adams — both on July 4, 1826
choices: Thomas Jefferson and John Adams — both on July 4, 1826
James Madison and James Monroe — both on July 4, 1826
John Adams and Alexander Hamilton — both on July 4, 1826
Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson — both on July 4, 1826
context: Adams, 90, in Massachusetts, and Jefferson, 83, in Virginia, died within five hours of each other on the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. Adams's reputed last words were 'Thomas Jefferson survives' — though Jefferson had actually died about five hours earlier. The two had spent decades exchanging letters in their old age, mending what had been a bitter political rivalry. James Monroe, the fifth president, would die five years later — also on July 4.

question: Between 1838 and 1839, under the Indian Removal Act signed by President Andrew Jackson, the U.S. Army forcibly marched the Cherokee Nation about 800 miles from their ancestral lands in Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Alabama to Indian Territory (modern Oklahoma). Roughly 4,000 of 16,000 Cherokees died on the journey. What did the Cherokees come to call it?
answer: The Trail of Tears
choices: The Trail of Tears
The Long Walk
The March of Sorrows
The Path of Bones
context: The Supreme Court in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) had ruled that Georgia had no authority over Cherokee lands. President Jackson reportedly responded: 'John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it.' Five tribes were forcibly removed in this period — Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole. The Cherokee removal was the largest and most deadly. The Cherokees in Oklahoma rebuilt their nation, including a written language created by Sequoyah in 1821.

question: From February 23 to March 6, 1836, about 200 Texan defenders held a fortified Spanish mission in San Antonio against the much larger Mexican army of Antonio López de Santa Anna. All the defenders died including frontier figures Jim Bowie and Davy Crockett. The defeat became a rallying cry for the Texan revolution six weeks later. What was the mission called?
answer: The Alamo
choices: The Alamo
The Goliad
The Presidio
The Mision Concepción
context: The Alamo siege bought time for Sam Houston to organize the Texan army. On April 21, 1836 at the Battle of San Jacinto, Houston's army surprised Santa Anna's camp during the afternoon siesta, won the battle in 18 minutes, and captured Santa Anna himself the next day — forcing him to sign the Treaty of Velasco recognizing Texan independence. The Texan battle cry that day was 'Remember the Alamo!' Texas remained an independent republic until annexation by the U.S. in 1845.

question: In 1845 the New York editor John O'Sullivan wrote it was 'the fulfillment of our manifest destiny to overspread the continent.' The phrase caught fire and became the slogan for American westward expansion through the 1840s and 1850s. What major territorial acquisitions immediately followed?
answer: Texas annexation 1845 and Mexican Cession 1848 — California to New Mexico
choices: Texas annexation 1845 and Mexican Cession 1848 — California to New Mexico
Louisiana Purchase 1803 and Florida acquisition 1819 — from France and Spain
Alaska 1867 and Hawaii 1898 — from Russia and the Hawaiian kingdom
Cuba 1898 and the Philippines 1898 — after the Spanish-American War
context: The Mexican-American War (1846-48) ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, in which Mexico ceded California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Colorado and Wyoming to the United States in exchange for $15 million. Combined with the Texas annexation and the Oregon Treaty with Britain (1846), the United States in three years acquired most of what is now the American West. The Gold Rush began in California in 1848, just days before the treaty was signed.

question: On July 19-20, 1848, about 300 people met at a Methodist chapel in Seneca Falls, New York for the first women's rights convention in the United States. The convention produced a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence, declaring that 'all men and women are created equal.' Who was the convention's principal organizer?
answer: Elizabeth Cady Stanton — with Lucretia Mott
choices: Elizabeth Cady Stanton — with Lucretia Mott
Susan B. Anthony — with Sojourner Truth
Harriet Beecher Stowe — with Sarah Grimké
Dorothea Dix — with Lucy Stone
context: Stanton drafted the Declaration of Sentiments, which listed grievances against laws and customs denying women legal rights, education, and the vote. Frederick Douglass attended and spoke in favor of women's suffrage; his support was crucial to passing the suffrage resolution. Susan B. Anthony, who would become Stanton's lifelong partner in suffrage organizing, was not at Seneca Falls. The 19th Amendment giving American women the right to vote was finally ratified in 1920 — 72 years later.

question: In October 1859, an abolitionist named John Brown and 21 followers seized the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia (now West Virginia), hoping to spark a general slave uprising. The raid failed within 36 hours. Brown was captured by U.S. Marines commanded by a future Confederate general and hanged in December. Who led the Marines that captured Brown?
answer: Robert E. Lee — then a U.S. Army colonel
choices: Robert E. Lee — then a U.S. Army colonel
Stonewall Jackson — then a VMI instructor
Jefferson Davis — then U.S. Secretary of War
P.G.T. Beauregard — then a U.S. engineer officer
context: Brown's raid did not spark a slave uprising but it terrified the South and galvanized Northern abolitionist sentiment. Brown's gallows speech included the line: 'I, John Brown, am now quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood.' Eighteen months later, the Civil War began. Robert E. Lee resigned his U.S. commission in April 1861 and accepted command of Virginia's forces, becoming the senior general of the Confederate Army.

question: On April 12, 1861, Confederate batteries in Charleston Harbor opened fire on the federal garrison at a fort in the harbor entrance, forcing its surrender after a 34-hour bombardment. The opening shots of the American Civil War were fired at which fort?
answer: Fort Sumter
choices: Fort Sumter
Fort Pickens
Fort Monroe
Fort Pulaski
context: The garrison commander, Major Robert Anderson, had been Beauregard's artillery instructor at West Point years earlier. No one was killed in the bombardment itself — one Union soldier died accidentally during the formal surrender salute. Within days Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers; four more states (Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Arkansas) seceded. By the war's end in 1865, roughly 750,000 Americans had died — more than in all other U.S. wars combined until Vietnam.

question: On March 21, 1861 — three weeks before Fort Sumter — Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens delivered a speech in Savannah explicitly stating the cause for which the Confederacy had been founded. It is now called the Cornerstone Speech. What did Stephens declare the Confederacy's foundation to be?
answer: The principle that slavery is the natural and moral condition of the African race
choices: The principle that slavery is the natural and moral condition of the African race
The defense of states' rights against federal economic interference
The protection of agricultural Southern culture against Northern industry
The preservation of the original 1787 Constitution against Northern revision
context: Stephens stated: 'Our new government is founded upon... the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man; that slavery — subordination to the superior race — is his natural and normal condition.' He explicitly contrasted this with Jefferson's view in the Declaration that 'all men are created equal,' which Stephens called a 'fundamentally wrong' premise. The cornerstone speech, alongside each seceding state's official declarations of causes (Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas, etc.), settles the historical question of the Confederacy's stated purpose.

question: On March 9, 1862, two ironclad warships fought a four-hour duel in Hampton Roads, Virginia — the world's first battle between iron-armored steam ships. Wooden navies became obsolete overnight. The Confederate ship was a converted hull formerly named USS Merrimack, rebuilt as CSS Virginia. What was the Union ironclad called?
answer: USS Monitor
choices: USS Monitor
USS Hartford
USS Cumberland
USS Galena
context: The Monitor was designed by Swedish-American engineer John Ericsson and built in just 118 days at Greenpoint, Brooklyn. The duel ended in a draw, but it confirmed iron's dominance over wood at sea. The Monitor sank in a storm off Cape Hatteras in December 1862 — 16 sailors died. The CSS Virginia was blown up by Confederates in May 1862 to prevent capture as Union forces took Norfolk. Both wrecks have been partially recovered.

question: On September 17, 1862, Robert E. Lee's army of about 38,000 fought George McClellan's army of about 75,000 at a small creek in western Maryland. The battle stopped Lee's first invasion of the North. It also remains a grim record in American history. What does Antietam still hold the record for?
answer: Bloodiest single day in American military history — about 23,000 total casualties
choices: Bloodiest single day in American military history — about 23,000 total casualties
Largest cavalry charge in American military history — about 8,000 horsemen
Longest single battle in American military history — three days and nights
Most decisive Confederate defeat in American military history — total surrender
context: About 12,400 Union and 10,300 Confederate casualties in 12 hours of fighting. Photographer Alexander Gardner's images of the dead — the first time Americans had ever seen battlefield corpses in news photographs — were displayed at Mathew Brady's New York studio in October and shocked the country. Five days after Antietam, Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation. The 'most decisive Confederate defeat with total surrender' came at Appomattox in 1865, not at Antietam.

question: On January 1, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln issued an executive order during the Civil War declaring enslaved people in Confederate-controlled territory legally free. The order changed the war's character — from a war for the Union to a war for the Union AND emancipation. What was the document called?
answer: The Emancipation Proclamation
choices: The Emancipation Proclamation
The Reconstruction Act
The Freedmen's Charter
The Equal Justice Decree
context: The Proclamation did not free slaves in border states loyal to the Union (Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri, Delaware) — Lincoln did not believe his war powers extended that far. It also did not technically free anyone immediately, since it applied to territory Lincoln could not yet reach. But it changed the war's stated purpose, blocked British and French recognition of the Confederacy, and let Black men enlist in the Union Army (about 180,000 eventually did). Full constitutional abolition came with the 13th Amendment, ratified December 1865.

question: On November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a new cemetery on a Pennsylvania battlefield, President Abraham Lincoln spoke for about two minutes after a famous orator had spoken for two hours. Lincoln himself thought his remarks had been a failure. They are now considered one of the greatest speeches in English. About how long is the Gettysburg Address?
answer: About 272 words — roughly two minutes long
choices: About 272 words — roughly two minutes long
About 850 words — roughly six minutes long
About 1,400 words — roughly twelve minutes long
About 2,100 words — roughly twenty minutes long
context: The featured speaker was Edward Everett, who spoke for two hours in classical Greek-oration style. Everett wrote to Lincoln the next day: 'I should be glad if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as you did in two minutes.' Five manuscript copies in Lincoln's hand survive, with slight variations. The address opens 'Four score and seven years ago...' — counting back from 1863 gives 1776, the Declaration of Independence.

question: On April 9 1865 Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered to Union General Ulysses S. Grant in the parlor of a Virginia farmhouse owned by a man named Wilmer McLean. McLean had moved to Appomattox Court House specifically to escape the Civil War. What was bizarre about McLean's earlier life that made his hosting the surrender a strange historical coincidence?
answer: His first farm at Manassas Junction had hosted the first major battle (First Bull Run) in July 1861
choices: His first farm at Manassas Junction had hosted the first major battle (First Bull Run) in July 1861
He had been Stonewall Jackson's commanding officer in the Mexican-American War of 1846-48
He had personally signed the Virginia ordinance of secession in April 1861
He had been imprisoned for two years in Fort Sumter before the war began
context: Wilmer McLean's farm at Manassas Junction was used as the Confederate headquarters during the First Battle of Bull Run (July 21 1861), and Union artillery shells actually landed in his kitchen. He moved his family 120 miles south to remote Appomattox Court House to escape the war. Four years later the war found him again — Lee and Grant signed the surrender documents on his parlor table on April 9 1865. Union soldiers stripped the parlor of furniture afterward as souvenirs. McLean is said to have remarked: 'The war began in my front yard and ended in my front parlor.'

question: Five days after Lee's surrender at Appomattox, on Good Friday April 14, 1865, President Abraham Lincoln was attending a comedy at Ford's Theatre in Washington when he was shot in the back of the head by an actor and Confederate sympathizer. He died the next morning. Who shot Lincoln?
answer: John Wilkes Booth
choices: John Wilkes Booth
Lewis Powell
George Atzerodt
David Herold
context: Booth was a famous Shakespearean actor from a prominent theatrical family. He jumped from Lincoln's box to the stage after firing, shouted 'Sic semper tyrannis' ('Thus always to tyrants' — Virginia's state motto), and fled. He was tracked to a Virginia tobacco barn and shot dead 12 days later. Three accomplices were hanged that summer. Lincoln died at 7:22 a.m. April 15, 1865. Secretary of War Edwin Stanton reportedly said at the bedside: 'Now he belongs to the ages.'

question: On December 17, 1903, on the windswept dunes of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, two brothers from Dayton, Ohio made the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air craft. The first flight lasted about 12 seconds and covered 120 feet. Who made the flight?
answer: Orville and Wilbur Wright
choices: Orville and Wilbur Wright
Samuel Langley and Charles Manly
Glenn Curtiss and Augustus Herring
Octave Chanute and George Spratt
context: Orville flew first — the brothers had tossed a coin in the morning. They made four flights that day; the longest was 59 seconds and 852 feet. Their genius was the three-axis control system that let the pilot maneuver in the air — derived from watching how birds twisted their wing tips. The brothers were bicycle mechanics with no formal engineering training. The Smithsonian initially denied them credit and claimed Langley's 1903 aircraft (which had crashed twice into the Potomac) was the true first; the dispute was not settled until 1942.

question: In January 1918, near the end of World War I, U.S. President Woodrow Wilson outlined 14 principles for a postwar settlement — including freedom of the seas, open diplomacy, and a general association of nations to keep the peace. The last point envisioned what international organization?
answer: The League of Nations
choices: The League of Nations
The United Nations
The North Atlantic Treaty Organization
The International Red Cross
context: Wilson got the League into the Treaty of Versailles (1919) but could not get the U.S. Senate to ratify the treaty — Senator Henry Cabot Lodge and other Republicans opposed binding America to collective defense obligations. The League of Nations began operating in 1920 without the United States; it failed to prevent World War II and was replaced by the United Nations in 1945. Wilson suffered a debilitating stroke in October 1919 during a national speaking tour for the treaty.

question: On May 20-21, 1927, a 25-year-old former U.S. Air Mail pilot flew alone, nonstop from Long Island, New York to Le Bourget Field outside Paris in a single-engine monoplane — 33.5 hours over the Atlantic with no radio. The flight made him the most famous man in the world. Who was the pilot?
answer: Charles Lindbergh
choices: Charles Lindbergh
Amelia Earhart
Wiley Post
Eddie Rickenbacker
context: Lindbergh's plane, the Spirit of St. Louis, was financed by St. Louis businessmen. He stripped it of everything non-essential — no parachute, no radio, no front windscreen (he used a periscope). He stayed awake the whole flight by leaning out the side window into the cold air. About 150,000 people swarmed Le Bourget when he landed. He collected the $25,000 Orteig Prize. His infant son was kidnapped and murdered in 1932 in one of the most famous criminal cases of the century.

question: On the morning of December 7, 1941, the Japanese Imperial Navy launched a surprise aerial attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet at its Hawaii naval base. About 2,400 Americans died, 8 battleships were sunk or damaged, and 188 American aircraft were destroyed on the ground. The next day, President Franklin Roosevelt asked Congress for a declaration of war with a famous phrase. What did Roosevelt call December 7?
answer: 'A date which will live in infamy'
choices: 'A date which will live in infamy'
'The hour when freedom called us'
'A morning of betrayal'
'The dawn of America's resolve'
context: The attack was led by Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, who had warned the Japanese cabinet that war with America was unwinnable but planned the attack on orders. The U.S. Pacific Fleet's three aircraft carriers were at sea and escaped the attack — a fact that would prove decisive at Midway six months later. Congress declared war on Japan on December 8 with one dissenting vote (Jeannette Rankin, who had also voted against entering WWI in 1917). Germany declared war on the U.S. four days later.

question: On June 6, 1944, the largest amphibious invasion in history landed about 160,000 American, British, Canadian, and Allied troops on five beaches of the Normandy coast of German-occupied France. The supreme Allied commander watched the operation he had reluctantly ordered the night before through bad weather. Who commanded?
answer: General Dwight D. Eisenhower
choices: General Dwight D. Eisenhower
General George Patton
General Omar Bradley
General Bernard Montgomery
context: Eisenhower had drafted a press statement to be released if the invasion failed, taking full personal responsibility — it survives in his papers and was not used. The five landing beaches were code-named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword. Omaha Beach was the bloodiest — about 2,400 American casualties on the first day alone. By August 25, the Allies had liberated Paris. The Normandy campaign cost roughly 73,000 Allied dead by the time it closed.

question: On July 16, 1945, the first atomic bomb was tested at a remote site in the New Mexico desert. The scientific director of the Manhattan Project watched the dawn fireball rise into a mushroom cloud and later recalled a verse from the Hindu scripture Bhagavad-Gita coming to his mind. Who was the scientific director and what did he quote?
answer: J. Robert Oppenheimer — 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds'
choices: J. Robert Oppenheimer — 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds'
Enrico Fermi — 'The chain reaction can now never be unbroken'
Leslie Groves — 'We have at last given war a final master'
Edward Teller — 'The atom has spoken to mankind today'
context: The test was code-named Trinity. The yield was about 21 kilotons. Twenty-one days later, the first atomic bomb used in war was dropped on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, killing roughly 80,000 people instantly. A second bomb destroyed Nagasaki on August 9. Japan surrendered on August 15. Oppenheimer would have his security clearance revoked in 1954 during the McCarthy era; the decision was formally voided by the Department of Energy in 2022.

question: On May 17, 1954, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racially segregated public schools were unconstitutional, overturning the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson 'separate but equal' doctrine. Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote the opinion. What was the case called?
answer: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
choices: Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka
Loving v. Virginia (interracial marriage)
Roe v. Wade (federal abortion right)
McCulloch v. Maryland (federal bank)
context: The lead plaintiff was Oliver Brown, whose daughter Linda had been required to walk past a nearby white school to attend a Black school 21 blocks away in Topeka, Kansas. The NAACP Legal Defense Fund's lead attorney was Thurgood Marshall, who would later become the first Black Supreme Court Justice (1967). The decision faced massive resistance in the South — in 1957 President Eisenhower had to send the 101st Airborne Division to Little Rock, Arkansas to enforce school integration at Central High School.

question: On December 1, 1955, a 42-year-old seamstress refused to give up her bus seat to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama. Her arrest sparked a 13-month bus boycott led by a young local minister and ended with the Supreme Court ruling Montgomery's segregated buses unconstitutional. Who was the bus rider?
answer: Rosa Parks
choices: Rosa Parks
Fannie Lou Hamer
Diane Nash
Ella Baker
context: Parks was not, as legend sometimes has it, simply tired from work — she was a longtime NAACP secretary and had been actively trained in nonviolent resistance. The 26-year-old minister who led the boycott was Martin Luther King Jr., then pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church. Black residents organized carpools and walked to work for 381 days. The Supreme Court ruled in November 1956 that bus segregation was unconstitutional. The boycott launched the modern civil rights movement.

question: On August 28, 1963, about 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. The Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered the closing address. Departing from his prepared text, he repeated a four-word phrase that became the most famous line in American oratory of the 20th century. What did King say?
answer: 'I have a dream'
choices: 'I have a dream'
'We shall overcome'
'Let freedom ring'
'The arc bends toward justice'
context: King had used the 'I have a dream' refrain in earlier speeches. According to witnesses, gospel singer Mahalia Jackson called out from the platform during his speech: 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' King set aside his prepared text and improvised the dream sequence. The Civil Rights Act passed less than a year later (July 1964) and the Voting Rights Act the year after that (August 1965). King won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 at age 35 — youngest male recipient at that time. He was assassinated on April 4, 1968 in Memphis at age 39.

question: On July 20, 1969, the lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon. Astronaut Neil Armstrong descended the ladder and stepped onto the surface six and a half hours later, speaking a sentence that an estimated 600 million people heard live by television. What did Armstrong say as he stepped onto the Moon?
answer: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'
choices: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'
'The eagle has landed and the dream is real'
'We have come in peace for all humanity'
'God speed and God bless the human race'
context: Armstrong always said he intended 'one small step for a man' — that the 'a' was lost in transmission. Audio analysis is inconclusive. Buzz Aldrin followed Armstrong onto the surface 19 minutes later; Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia. The Apollo program landed 12 men on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. No human being has been back to the Moon since Apollo 17 left in December 1972 — over 50 years.

question: In October 1962, American spy planes photographed Soviet medium-range nuclear missiles being installed in Cuba — 90 miles off Florida. For 13 days the world stood closer to nuclear war than at any other moment in history. The crisis ended when the Soviet premier agreed to remove the missiles in exchange for a secret American agreement to remove missiles from Turkey. Who were the two leaders?
answer: John F. Kennedy and Nikita Khrushchev
choices: John F. Kennedy and Nikita Khrushchev
Lyndon Johnson and Leonid Brezhnev
Dwight Eisenhower and Joseph Stalin
Richard Nixon and Yuri Andropov
context: Kennedy imposed a naval 'quarantine' (avoiding the word 'blockade' which is technically an act of war) around Cuba. The U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff strongly favored an air strike followed by invasion; Kennedy resisted. A U.S. U-2 reconnaissance plane was shot down over Cuba on October 27; the pilot Rudolf Anderson was the only American killed in the crisis. The crisis led directly to the installation of the Moscow-Washington hotline (1963) and the Limited Test Ban Treaty (also 1963).

question: On November 9, 1989, the East German government, facing massive protests and a sudden announcement of new travel rules, opened the border crossings of the Berlin Wall — the symbol that had divided the city since August 1961. East Berliners poured through; West Berliners climbed onto the wall to celebrate. About how many years had the wall stood?
answer: About 28 years — built August 1961, opened November 1989
choices: About 28 years — built August 1961, opened November 1989
About 40 years — built 1949, opened 1989
About 50 years — built 1939, opened 1989
About 60 years — built 1929, opened 1989
context: About 5,000 people are estimated to have successfully escaped over, under, or through the Berlin Wall during its 28 years; about 140 died trying. The wall's opening was triggered by East German spokesman Günter Schabowski's bungled answer at a press conference, where he said new rules would take effect 'sofort' ('immediately') — the actual plan had been for the next day. By summer 1990 East and West Germany formed a single currency union; full reunification followed in October 1990.

question: On the clear morning of September 11, 2001, 19 hijackers from al-Qaeda took control of four passenger airliners. Two struck the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York; one struck the Pentagon; one crashed in a Pennsylvania field after passengers tried to retake the plane. About 3,000 people died. Who led al-Qaeda and ordered the attacks?
answer: Osama bin Laden
choices: Osama bin Laden
Ayman al-Zawahiri
Mohammed Atta
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
context: The North and South Towers collapsed within about 100 minutes of impact. Mayor Rudy Giuliani led the city's response. The U.S. invasion of Afghanistan began less than a month later; the Iraq War followed in March 2003. Bin Laden remained at large for nearly a decade. On May 2, 2011, U.S. Navy SEALs killed him at a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan in a raid ordered by President Barack Obama. Mohammed Atta led the operational hijacker team; Khalid Sheikh Mohammed was the operational mastermind, captured in 2003.

question: In 1908, the Detroit automaker Henry Ford introduced a simple, durable car designed for the mass market. Five years later he revolutionized factory production with a moving assembly line. By the 1920s the car cost about $300 — affordable for working families. What was the car called?
answer: The Model T
choices: The Model T
The Model A
The Cadillac Eight
The Olds Curved Dash
context: Ford's moving assembly line cut Model T production time from about 12 hours to about 90 minutes per car. About 15 million Model Ts were built between 1908 and 1927. Ford famously offered the car in any color the customer wanted 'so long as it is black' — black paint dried fastest. In 1914 Ford doubled his workers' wages to $5 a day, a radical move that let his own workers afford the cars they made and revolutionized labor expectations across American industry.

question: On March 4, 1933, with the United States in the depths of the Great Depression — 25% unemployment, banks collapsing, breadlines in every city — newly inaugurated President Franklin D. Roosevelt addressed the nation in his first inaugural with a famous reassurance. What did FDR say Americans had to fear?
answer: 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself'
choices: 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself'
'Nothing but our own loss of faith in tomorrow'
'A nation broken in spirit cannot be rebuilt'
'The shadow of despair that hangs upon this land'
context: FDR launched the 'First Hundred Days' — an avalanche of legislation including the bank holiday, the Civilian Conservation Corps, the Agricultural Adjustment Act, the Tennessee Valley Authority, and the National Industrial Recovery Act. He served four terms (the only U.S. president to do so), dying in office on April 12, 1945, less than a month before V-E Day. The 22nd Amendment (ratified 1951) limited future presidents to two terms.

question: On June 4, 1942 — six months after Pearl Harbor — U.S. carrier-based dive bombers found the Japanese carrier fleet northwest of Midway Atoll. In a window of roughly five minutes, three Japanese fleet carriers were set fatally ablaze. The fourth was destroyed that afternoon. The balance of the Pacific war shifted permanently. What were the three Japanese carriers destroyed in those five minutes?
answer: Akagi, Kaga, Soryu
choices: Akagi, Kaga, Soryu
Shokaku, Zuikaku, Junyo
Hiryu, Hosho, Ryujo
Taiho, Shinano, Unryu
context: The fourth carrier Hiryu was sunk later that afternoon. Japan lost 4 fleet carriers, about 250 aircraft, and most of its veteran naval pilots — losses it could not replace. The U.S. lost the carrier Yorktown. Admiral Yamamoto, who had planned the operation, had warned the cabinet a year earlier: 'In the first six to twelve months I shall run wild and win victory after victory. But then... I have no expectation of success.' Midway came exactly at the six-month mark.

question: On June 12, 1987, U.S. President Ronald Reagan stood at the Brandenburg Gate in West Berlin and challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev with a four-word imperative that the State Department had tried to cut from the speech seven times. Two and a half years later the Berlin Wall came down. What did Reagan say?
answer: 'Tear down this wall'
choices: 'Tear down this wall'
'Liberty knows no borders'
'Open the Brandenburg Gate'
'Let Berlin be free'
context: Speechwriter Peter Robinson wrote the line after a Berlin trip where a German woman told him at dinner: 'If this man Gorbachev is serious with his glasnost and perestroika, he can prove it. He can get rid of this wall.' The State Department and National Security Council objected that it was 'unpresidential' and 'naive.' Reagan delivered it; the Berlin Wall opened on November 9, 1989, less than 30 months later.

question: In 1852, a Cincinnati author and abolitionist published a novel that depicted the cruelty of American slavery in such vivid terms that it sold 300,000 copies in its first year — second only to the Bible — and shaped Northern opinion against slavery. When Abraham Lincoln met her during the Civil War, he reportedly called her 'the little woman who wrote the book that made this great war.' Who was she?
answer: Harriet Beecher Stowe
choices: Harriet Beecher Stowe
Louisa May Alcott
Margaret Fuller
Lydia Maria Child
context: Uncle Tom's Cabin was first published as a serial in the antislavery newspaper The National Era starting in June 1851, then as a book in March 1852. Stowe was the daughter of preacher Lyman Beecher and sister of preacher Henry Ward Beecher. The novel was banned across the American South and inspired several proslavery 'anti-Tom' novels in response. Stowe was on a fixed publisher's contract that gave her only modest royalties despite the book's enormous sales.

question: On July 5, 1852 — the day after Independence Day — the escaped-slave-turned-orator Frederick Douglass delivered a speech to a Rochester, New York abolitionist audience that became one of the most powerful pieces of American oratory. He asked his audience a pointed question about what the Fourth of July meant. What did Douglass ask?
answer: 'What to the slave is the Fourth of July?'
choices: 'What to the slave is the Fourth of July?'
'Where in this land is liberty for all?'
'How can the bell ring while men are bound?'
'When will our flag stand for every man?'
context: Douglass answered his own question: 'a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.' Douglass had escaped slavery in 1838 disguised as a sailor on a train from Baltimore to New York. His autobiography (1845) became an international bestseller. He advised Lincoln during the Civil War, recruited Black soldiers for the Union army, and served as U.S. minister to Haiti in his later years. He died in 1895 at age 77.

question: In June 1752 in Philadelphia, the 46-year-old printer, inventor, and statesman Benjamin Franklin performed (or at least described) a famous experiment with a kite, a metal key, and a thunderstorm. The point was to prove a hypothesis about lightning. What did Franklin's experiment demonstrate?
answer: That lightning is a form of electricity
choices: That lightning is a form of electricity
That metal can store electric charge for hours after a strike
That clouds carry positive charge and ground carries negative
That kites are unaffected by lightning if properly wired
context: Some modern historians have questioned whether Franklin actually flew the kite as described — the experiment as commonly told would likely have electrocuted him. Whether he flew it or not, his published understanding of lightning as electrical led directly to the invention of the lightning rod, which saved countless buildings (especially church steeples, often the tallest structures in colonial towns). Franklin was also one of only six men who signed both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution.

question: From 1732 through 1758, Benjamin Franklin published an annual almanac in Philadelphia under a pen name. The almanac was the second-best-selling book in the colonies after the Bible, partly because of its concise moral and practical aphorisms ('A penny saved is a penny earned'). What was the publication called?
answer: Poor Richard's Almanack — written under the name Richard Saunders
choices: Poor Richard's Almanack — written under the name Richard Saunders
The Pennsylvania Gazette — Franklin's main newspaper
Way to Wealth — Franklin's economic essay collection
Autobiography — Franklin's life story
context: The almanac's sayings — 'Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise' — entered the English language. Franklin later collected the best of them in 'The Way to Wealth' (1758), one of the most translated works in early American literature. Franklin retired from active business at 42 to devote himself to scientific experiments and public service. He served as the first U.S. Postmaster General, the colonies' agent to Britain, ambassador to France, and finally as the elder statesman of the Constitutional Convention.

question: On January 30-31, 1968 — during the Tet (lunar new year) ceasefire — communist North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces launched simultaneous attacks on over 100 cities and military bases throughout South Vietnam, including the U.S. embassy in Saigon. American forces beat back the attacks but the offensive shattered U.S. public confidence in the war. What is the offensive called?
answer: The Tet Offensive
choices: The Tet Offensive
The Saigon Uprising
The Hanoi Plan
