question: On June 15 1215, a band of rebellious English barons forced King John to set his seal on a charter limiting royal power. The meeting took place in a meadow beside the Thames between Windsor and Staines. What is the name of this meadow?
answer: Runnymede
choices: Runnymede
Smithfield
Bosworth Field
Salisbury Plain
context: Runnymede is now owned by the National Trust; an American Bar Association memorial stands there. Magna Carta ('Great Charter') established that even the king was subject to the law. Pope Innocent III annulled it within months at John's request, but John died the next year and the charter was reissued under his son Henry III. Four original 1215 copies survive — two at the British Library, one each at Lincoln and Salisbury cathedrals.

question: Constantinople, the capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, had stood behind its triple Theodosian walls for over 1,000 years. On May 29 1453 it fell to the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II after a 53-day siege. Mehmed's success depended on a technology that made medieval stone walls suddenly obsolete. What did Mehmed bring to the siege?
answer: Massive bronze cannons cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban, firing stone balls over 1,500 pounds
choices: Massive bronze cannons cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban, firing stone balls over 1,500 pounds
Greek-fire siphons captured from the Byzantines themselves a generation earlier
A pontoon bridge of barrels chained across the Golden Horn during the assault
Trained war elephants imported from India by Persian merchants the previous year
context: Orban had offered his services to the Byzantine emperor first; they couldn't afford him. Mehmed paid four times the salary requested. The largest cannon was 27 feet long and required 60 oxen to drag it. Constantine XI Palaiologos, the last Roman emperor, died fighting in the breach. The fall ended the Roman Empire 1,000 years after Rome itself fell; many Greek scholars fled to Italy, fueling the Renaissance.

question: Joan of Arc was the illiterate peasant girl from Domrémy who at 17 convinced the French dauphin Charles to give her command of an army. She broke the English siege of Orleans in May 1429 and saw Charles crowned king at Reims that July. Captured by the Burgundians in 1430, she was sold to the English and tried by a French church court. Her execution date and age were:
answer: May 30 1431, age 19 — burned at the stake in Rouen's market square
choices: May 30 1431, age 19 — burned at the stake in Rouen's market square
January 6 1432, age 20 — burned at the stake outside the cathedral at Reims
March 4 1431, age 17 — beheaded by English soldiers without a formal trial
May 30 1431, age 24 — hanged at Calais after seven months of imprisonment
context: Joan was charged with heresy and cross-dressing, condemned, and burned on May 30 1431. Her ashes were thrown into the Seine. A retrial in 1456, ordered by Charles VII, found her innocent. She was canonized as a saint in 1920. Her birthdate is uncertain but commonly given as January 6 1412 — making her 19 at her death.

question: Augustine of Hippo (354-430) wrote the Confessions around 397-400, the first true autobiography in Western literature. He described a moment in a garden in Milan in 386 when, weeping under a fig tree, he heard a child's voice from a neighboring house chanting words that led him to open Paul's Letter to the Romans. What did the voice chant?
answer: 'Tolle, lege' — 'Take up and read'
choices: 'Tolle, lege' — 'Take up and read'
'Veni, vidi' — 'I came, I saw'
'Sursum corda' — 'Lift up your hearts'
'Pax tecum' — 'Peace be with you'
context: Augustine opened Romans 13:13-14 and read the passage about putting on the Lord Jesus Christ. He converted on the spot, was baptized at Easter 387 by Ambrose of Milan, and eventually became bishop of Hippo in North Africa. The Confessions blends autobiography with theology and philosophy. Augustine died as Hippo was being besieged by the Vandals in 430. He is one of the four original Latin Doctors of the Church.

question: From 343 to 340 BC the philosopher Aristotle was hired to tutor a 13-year-old prince at the royal palace of Macedon. The prince would, within fifteen years, conquer the largest empire the ancient world had ever seen, from Greece to the Indus River. Who was Aristotle's pupil?
answer: Alexander the Great
choices: Alexander the Great
Pyrrhus of Epirus
Philip II of Macedon
Antigonus the One-Eyed
context: King Philip II of Macedon, Alexander's father, hired Aristotle on the strength of his Athenian reputation. Aristotle had himself been the star pupil of Plato at the Academy. The exact effect of Aristotle's teaching on Alexander is disputed — Alexander carried a copy of the Iliad annotated by Aristotle on campaign, but conquered as a Macedonian warrior-king, not as a philosophical idealist. Aristotle later returned to Athens to found his own school, the Lyceum.

question: Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287-212 BC) is supposed to have discovered the principle of displacement — that an object placed in water displaces its own volume — while taking a bath. King Hiero II had asked Archimedes to determine whether a goldsmith had adulterated a votive crown with silver. Tradition says Archimedes ran naked through the streets shouting one Greek word. What was the word?
answer: 'Eureka' — 'I have found it'
choices: 'Eureka' — 'I have found it'
'Aletheia' — 'Truth'
'Sophia' — 'Wisdom'
'Logos' — 'Reason'
context: The story is told by Vitruvius, two centuries after Archimedes' death; it may be apocryphal. What is certain is that Archimedes formulated the principle that bears his name (buoyancy equals the weight of fluid displaced). He died in the Roman sack of Syracuse in 212 BC, reportedly killed at his desk drawing geometry — the Roman general Marcellus had ordered him spared. His tomb featured a sphere inscribed in a cylinder, his proudest geometric proof.

question: Napoleon's soldiers digging fortifications at Fort Julien near Rosetta in Egypt found a black basalt slab in July 1799, inscribed with the same text in three scripts. The decipherment of Egyptian hieroglyphics from this stone, completed in 1822, ranks as one of history's great philological achievements. Who deciphered it?
answer: Jean-François Champollion, a French linguist who had taught himself Coptic
choices: Jean-François Champollion, a French linguist who had taught himself Coptic
Thomas Young, the English polymath who also explained the nature of light
Henry Rawlinson, the British officer who later deciphered the cuneiform of Persia
Wilhelm von Humboldt, the Prussian philologist who founded comparative linguistics
context: Young made important early progress identifying royal names (cartouches) but Champollion published the breakthrough on September 27 1822 in his Lettre à M. Dacier. He died at 41 in 1832 of a stroke, having opened 3,000 years of Egyptian history to scholarship. The stone itself, looted from the French by the British under the 1801 Treaty of Alexandria, has been in the British Museum since 1802.

question: Summer 1666: the plague closed Cambridge and the 23-year-old Isaac Newton went home to his mother's farm at Woolsthorpe in Lincolnshire. In a single 18-month period there — his 'year of wonders' — he invented calculus, decomposed white light with a prism, and developed his theory of universal gravitation. What did Newton himself later say first set him thinking about gravity?
answer: An apple fell from a tree while he sat beneath it in the orchard at Woolsthorpe
choices: An apple fell from a tree while he sat beneath it in the orchard at Woolsthorpe
Lightning struck a tree near the farmhouse during a summer thunderstorm
A weight broke loose from his mother's kitchen scale and crashed into the floor
A meteor crossed the sky during one of his nighttime observations of Mars
context: Newton told the apple story to several visitors, including the antiquarian William Stukeley, who wrote it down. A descendant of the actual tree still grows at Woolsthorpe Manor (now owned by the National Trust). Newton waited 20 years before publishing the Principia in 1687 — partly because he had to invent better mathematics first, partly because he hated controversy with rival natural philosophers.

question: Around 1440 the Florentine sculptor Donatello unveiled a bronze David standing about 5 feet 2 inches tall, commissioned by the Medici for the courtyard of the Palazzo Medici. Viewers were shocked — not by the subject (David and Goliath was a familiar Christian image) but by a quality the sculpture had that nothing in Christian Europe had had for a thousand years. What was unprecedented about it?
answer: It was the first freestanding nude sculpture made since Roman antiquity
choices: It was the first freestanding nude sculpture made since Roman antiquity
It was the first life-sized bronze cast in northern Italy in over 200 years
It was the first sculpture displayed openly outdoors rather than inside a church
It was the first statue Donatello signed on the base with his full Christian name
context: Donatello had earlier carved a marble David in 1408, but it was clothed. The bronze nude broke a thousand-year absence — medieval Christian art avoided the nude form. The work passed through the hands of the Medici, the Republic, and the Signoria. It now stands in the Bargello Museum in Florence. Michelangelo's larger marble David (1504) directly answered Donatello's bronze.

question: Antoine Lavoisier was the father of modern chemistry — he established combustion as a reaction with oxygen, named hydrogen, and proved conservation of mass. He was also a fermier général, a private tax collector for the French crown. The Reign of Terror swept him up. Sentenced to death on May 8 1794, the judge reportedly dismissed pleas for the great scientist's life with a famous line. What did the judge supposedly say?
answer: 'The Republic has no need of savants'
choices: 'The Republic has no need of savants'
'Science kneels before the Republic's law'
'No labor exempts a man from the guillotine'
'A chemist's measurements cannot weigh treason'
context: The exact quote is disputed by historians — but it has become the symbolic phrase for revolutionary anti-intellectualism. The mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange said the next day: 'It took them only an instant to cut off that head, and a hundred years may not give us another like it.' Lavoisier was 50. His wife Marie-Anne survived and edited his collected works for publication.

question: James Watt's 1769 separate-condenser patent revolutionized the steam engine, multiplying its fuel efficiency several times over and making the Industrial Revolution possible. According to the famous (probably embellished) story, Watt's insight came as he watched something common in his aunt's kitchen as a boy. What had he observed?
answer: Steam lifting the lid of a boiling kettle on the kitchen stove
choices: Steam lifting the lid of a boiling kettle on the kitchen stove
Hot air rising up the chimney over the hearth as a draft
A whistling teapot building pressure on the stove ring
A bellows pumping air into the kitchen fire to brighten it
context: The kettle anecdote is told by Watt's biographer François Arago in 1839, decades after Watt's death — it is probably more parable than literal history. What is documented is that Watt was a Glasgow University instrument maker repairing a model Newcomen engine in 1763 when he realized that cooling the cylinder for each stroke wasted enormous heat. His separate condenser, patented 1769, kept the cylinder hot and cooled the steam in a separate chamber.

question: On December 17 1903 at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright successfully flew the first powered, heavier-than-air, controlled aircraft in history. Orville took the first flight while Wilbur ran alongside. About how long was that first flight in distance and duration?
answer: About 120 feet, lasting 12 seconds
choices: About 120 feet, lasting 12 seconds
About 850 feet, lasting roughly one minute
About 50 feet, lasting under 4 seconds
About 1,700 feet, lasting nearly two minutes
context: The brothers made four flights that day; the longest, by Wilbur, covered 852 feet in 59 seconds. A photographer captured the first flight, producing one of history's most famous images. The Wrights — bicycle mechanics from Dayton, Ohio, with no formal engineering education — beat the better-funded Samuel Pierpont Langley of the Smithsonian, whose own aircraft had crashed into the Potomac nine days earlier.

question: Charles Darwin spent five weeks in the Galápagos Islands aboard HMS Beagle in 1835, collecting specimens that would later illustrate his theory of natural selection. The famous Galápagos finches — over a dozen species with different beaks for different food sources — became the textbook example of adaptation. When did Darwin actually realize the finches were the key?
answer: Months later in London — the ornithologist John Gould identified them as distinct species in 1837
choices: Months later in London — the ornithologist John Gould identified them as distinct species in 1837
Immediately on the islands — he noted in his journal that each island had its own finch
After the Origin was published — a Cambridge colleague pointed out his collection from 1859
Never personally — Alfred Russel Wallace identified the finches' significance after Darwin's death
context: Darwin had not even labeled his finch specimens by island — he had to reconstruct the geographic distribution from Captain FitzRoy's collection and his own mockingbird notes. The finches were identified by John Gould of the London Zoological Society in March 1837. Darwin's Origin of Species was published 22 years later, on November 24 1859 — the first 1,250 copies sold out the same day.

question: Gregor Mendel, an Augustinian friar at the monastery of Brno in Moravia, cross-bred pea plants from 1856 to 1863 and statistically tracked their inherited traits, publishing the laws of inheritance in 1866. His work was almost completely ignored for decades. When was Mendel finally rediscovered?
answer: In 1900 — three botanists independently rediscovered his paper while doing similar experiments
choices: In 1900 — three botanists independently rediscovered his paper while doing similar experiments
In 1882 — Darwin himself praised Mendel in a footnote to a revised edition of the Origin
In 1869 — Mendel won the Royal Society's Copley Medal during his own lifetime
In 1925 — Thomas Hunt Morgan's Drosophila lab at Columbia tracked down Mendel's reprint
context: Hugo de Vries (Netherlands), Carl Correns (Germany), and Erich von Tschermak (Austria) all rediscovered Mendel's paper independently in 1900. Mendel had sent reprints to several leading biologists in the 1860s — Karl Wilhelm von Nägeli's reply was discouraging, and Mendel turned to monastery administration. He died in 1884 with his life's scientific work essentially unknown. Modern genetics is sometimes dated from the 1900 rediscovery.

question: Thomas Edison invented the phonograph in 1877 — a tin-foil cylinder rotated under a stylus that vibrated with the speaker's voice. Edison made the first recording himself, reciting four words from a children's nursery rhyme into the horn. What four words did Edison record?
answer: 'Mary had a little lamb'
choices: 'Mary had a little lamb'
'Twinkle twinkle little star'
'Hickory dickory dock there'
'Old MacDonald had a farm'
context: Edison's recording of 'Mary had a little lamb' is one of the most famous first events in technology history. The original tin-foil cylinder did not survive; Edison rerecorded the phrase decades later. The phonograph patent (US 200,521) was granted February 19 1878. Edison later developed the wax cylinder for commercial sale. Émile Berliner's flat disc (1887) eventually replaced cylinders entirely as the basis for recorded music.

question: On April 26 1937 the German Condor Legion, fighting for Franco in the Spanish Civil War, bombed the Basque town of Guernica for three hours. About 1,650 civilians died. Pablo Picasso, then living in Paris, was commissioned by the Spanish Republican government to paint a mural for the Spanish pavilion at the 1937 Paris World's Fair. What did he paint?
answer: Guernica — a 25-foot black-and-white mural of fragmented figures and a screaming horse
choices: Guernica — a 25-foot black-and-white mural of fragmented figures and a screaming horse
Massacre at Chios — a colored remake of Delacroix's 1824 image of Greek slaughter
The Bombing of Madrid — an Expressionist scene of falling planes over the city
The Republic's Lament — a Cubist Madonna mourning over a fallen soldier
context: Guernica is now in the Reina Sofía museum in Madrid; it was kept at MoMA in New York from 1939 until 1981, with Picasso's instruction that it not return to Spain until democracy was restored. The painting measures 11 by 25 feet. Picasso reportedly told a Gestapo officer who asked, while seeing a photograph of Guernica in his Paris studio during the occupation: 'No, you did this.'

question: Brunelleschi built his Florence cathedral dome (1420-1436) without scaffolding from below — the 138-foot opening was too vast to span. His four million bricks had to lock each course in place as the dome rose. What brick pattern did Brunelleschi use to make this work?
answer: Herringbone — alternating vertical bricks pinning horizontal courses together
choices: Herringbone — alternating vertical bricks pinning horizontal courses together
Roman opus reticulatum — diagonal grid of small square stones
Catalan basket-weave — flat tiles in interlocking ovals
Byzantine cushion-fill — coarse cores faced with thin marble sheets
context: Each horizontal ring of brick was pinned by vertical bricks set at regular intervals, locking the curve as it rose. Brunelleschi had studied Roman ruins in his youth, but the herringbone solution is his own — possibly inspired by Persian or Islamic precedents he could have seen in Genoa or Venice. The dome remains the largest masonry dome in the world. The lantern atop the dome was completed by Brunelleschi's pupil Michelozzo in 1461.

question: Around 1450 a goldsmith in Mainz, Germany, named Johannes Gutenberg combined three existing technologies — movable metal type, oil-based ink, and the wine-press — into a printing press that could mass-produce books. His masterwork, finished around 1455, is one of the most valuable books in the world. What was it?
answer: The 42-line Bible (Vulgate), so called for the number of lines per column on most pages
choices: The 42-line Bible (Vulgate), so called for the number of lines per column on most pages
The Mainz Psalter, dated August 14 1457, the first dated printed book
The Catholicon, a Latin dictionary printed in 1460 in over 700 pages
The 36-line Bible, an earlier and rarer prototype edition
context: Gutenberg's 42-line Bible was printed in two volumes of about 640 pages each. About 49 copies survive in whole or in fragments; about 21 are essentially complete. A complete copy has not sold publicly since 1978, when one fetched $2.2 million (over $10 million in today's terms). Gutenberg himself was sued by his financial backer Johann Fust and lost both his press and his profits; he died poor around 1468.

question: Christopher Columbus sailed from Palos, Spain, on August 3 1492 with three ships — Niña, Pinta, and Santa María — searching for a westward route to Asia. On the night of October 11 1492 a lookout aboard the Pinta sighted land. Columbus made landfall the next morning on an island in the Bahamas that the inhabitants called Guanahani. What name did Columbus give the island?
answer: San Salvador — 'Holy Savior'
choices: San Salvador — 'Holy Savior'
Hispaniola — 'Little Spain'
Trinidad — 'Trinity'
Santo Domingo — 'Saint Dominic'
context: The exact identity of Guanahani is debated; the leading modern candidate is Watling's Island (renamed San Salvador in 1925). Columbus made four voyages to the Americas (1492, 1493, 1498, 1502) and died in 1506 in Valladolid, Spain, convinced he had reached the outer islands of Asia. The continents were named in 1507 by the German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller after Amerigo Vespucci, who had correctly identified them as a new world.

question: Francis Drake, English privateer, set sail from Plymouth in December 1577 in his 100-ton ship the Pelican, which he renamed mid-voyage to honor his patron Sir Christopher Hatton. He raided Spanish ports along the Pacific coast of South America, captured immense treasure, and returned to England in September 1580 — the second man to complete what feat?
answer: Circumnavigate the globe — first was Magellan's expedition, completed by Elcano in 1522
choices: Circumnavigate the globe — first was Magellan's expedition, completed by Elcano in 1522
Cross the equator going east — first was the Portuguese navigator Cabral in 1500
Land a European ship in California — first was Spaniard Cabrillo in 1542
Map the Strait of Magellan — first was the Portuguese pilot Estêvão Gomes in 1525
context: Drake's renamed ship was the Golden Hind. Magellan had been killed in the Philippines in 1521; only Juan Sebastián Elcano and 17 survivors returned to Spain in 1522 of the original 270-man expedition. Drake returned with treasure worth more than the English Crown's annual revenue. Queen Elizabeth knighted him aboard the Golden Hind at Deptford on April 4 1581 in defiance of furious Spanish protests.

question: King Richard III of England was killed at the Battle of Bosworth Field on August 22 1485, ending the Wars of the Roses. His body was buried in haste at the Greyfriars Church in Leicester, which was later demolished during the Reformation. Where were Richard III's bones discovered in 2012?
answer: Under a Leicester car park — Greyfriars Church's site had been built over
choices: Under a Leicester car park — Greyfriars Church's site had been built over
In the Tower of London — DNA testing matched bones found in the White Tower
Behind a panel at Westminster Abbey — hidden during Henry VIII's reign
In a Bosworth churchyard — long marked but uncovered only by ground-radar survey
context: Historian Philippa Langley led the Looking for Richard project; the dig under the Leicester Social Services car park began August 25 2012. The skeleton — with severe scoliosis matching contemporary descriptions, multiple battle wounds, and DNA matched to a living descendant of Richard's sister — was confirmed in February 2013. Richard III was reinterred at Leicester Cathedral on March 26 2015.

question: Louis XIV of France reigned for 72 years (1643-1715) — the longest reign of any major European monarch. He moved his court to a former hunting lodge his father had built and transformed it into the most magnificent palace in Europe, where he could keep France's quarrelsome nobility under his eye. What was the palace?
answer: Versailles, southwest of Paris
choices: Versailles, southwest of Paris
Fontainebleau, southeast of Paris
Schönbrunn, on the outskirts of Vienna
Het Loo, in the eastern Netherlands
context: Louis XIV's father Louis XIII had built the original hunting lodge in 1624. Louis XIV began the great expansion in the 1660s and moved the court there permanently in 1682. Versailles housed about 10,000 people. The Sun King — so called for the iconography of his personal absolutism (he reportedly never said 'L'État, c'est moi,' but it captures his theory) — outlived both his son and grandson; he was succeeded by his great-grandson Louis XV at the age of five.

question: On November 1 1755 (All Saints' Day) a massive earthquake struck Lisbon, Portugal, followed by a tsunami and a six-day fire. Roughly 40,000–60,000 died in a city of 200,000. The catastrophe profoundly shook Enlightenment European confidence that the natural world was rationally ordered. One major French response was a 1759 satirical novella. Who wrote it and what was it called?
answer: Voltaire wrote Candide, attacking Leibnizian optimism through a naive hero
choices: Voltaire wrote Candide, attacking Leibnizian optimism through a naive hero
Rousseau wrote Émile, blaming urban civilization rather than nature for the disaster
Diderot wrote La Religieuse, arguing the disaster proved no benevolent God existed
Montesquieu wrote The Spirit of the Laws, attributing the loss to bad city planning
context: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet) had been close friends with Frederick the Great of Prussia. Candide (1759) follows a young man whose tutor Pangloss insists 'all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds' through cumulative disasters that include the Lisbon quake. The novel ends with the famous line 'Il faut cultiver notre jardin' ('we must cultivate our garden'). Lisbon was rebuilt under the Marquis of Pombal with one of the first earthquake-resistant urban grids.

question: Carl Linnaeus, Swedish botanist (1707-1778), published the Systema Naturae in 1735 — a tiny eleven-page first edition that he expanded across 13 editions over his lifetime. His system gave every living thing a two-part Latin name that taxonomists still use. What is this naming system called?
answer: Binomial nomenclature — genus and species, e.g. Homo sapiens
choices: Binomial nomenclature — genus and species, e.g. Homo sapiens
Plinian nomenclature — three Latin descriptors for every species
Aristotelian taxonomy — only animals classified, in eleven categories
Cuvierian comparison — species named by their fossil ancestors first
context: Linnaeus also organized the hierarchy of kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. The Systema Naturae's first edition fit on a single folded sheet; the 1758 tenth edition is the official starting point for zoological nomenclature. Linnaeus named over 12,000 species; he also coined the name Homo sapiens (Latin 'wise man') for our own species. He died with a personal collection that was later sold to England and forms the foundation of the Linnean Society's holdings.

question: In April 1874 a group of French painters — refused by the official Salon — organized their own exhibition in Paris at the studio of the photographer Nadar. A critic named Louis Leroy wrote a mocking review for the satirical magazine Le Charivari, taking the title of one painting by Claude Monet to insult the entire group. The mocking name stuck and became the movement's accepted label. What was the painting?
answer: Impression, Sunrise (Impression, soleil levant) — Monet's view of Le Havre harbor
choices: Impression, Sunrise (Impression, soleil levant) — Monet's view of Le Havre harbor
Sunset on the Seine — Monet's evening study at Argenteuil
Foggy Morning in Rouen — Monet's first cathedral fragment
The Bathers at La Grenouillère — Monet's joint canvas with Renoir
context: Leroy's article was titled 'L'Exposition des Impressionnistes' — Exhibition of the Impressionists — using Monet's painting title as a synonym for unfinished, sketch-like work. The group included Monet, Renoir, Degas, Pissarro, Cézanne, Sisley, and Berthe Morisot. Impression, Sunrise was painted in 1872 from Monet's hotel window in Le Havre. It was stolen from the Marmottan Museum in 1985 and recovered in 1990.

question: Richard Wagner spent 26 years (1848-1874) composing his Ring of the Nibelung — a cycle of music dramas based on Germanic mythology. He persuaded King Ludwig II of Bavaria to fund construction of a special opera house at Bayreuth specifically designed for the cycle, with a hidden orchestra pit and other innovations. How many operas form the Ring cycle?
answer: Four — Das Rheingold, Die Walküre, Siegfried, and Götterdämmerung
choices: Four — Das Rheingold, Die Walküre, Siegfried, and Götterdämmerung
Three — performed over three consecutive evenings with intermissions
Six — including the prologues now performed separately
Two — a long opening and a longer climax
context: The four operas total roughly 15 hours of music. Bayreuth opened with the first complete Ring on August 13 1876 — Wagner himself in the audience watching King Ludwig and other royal guests. Wagner's hidden 'mystic gulf' orchestra pit blended the sound and let audiences focus on the stage. The Bayreuth Festival has run continuously since 1876, with breaks only for the two World Wars; it is still run by Wagner family descendants.

question: Frédéric Chopin (1810-1849), Polish-born composer of the Romantic era, spent his last 18 years in exile in Paris, dying of tuberculosis at age 39 in a fourth-floor apartment on the Place Vendôme. His funeral at the Madeleine featured Mozart's Requiem performed at his own request. Where was Chopin buried, and what specific Polish element was placed with him?
answer: Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris, with a jar of Polish soil sprinkled on his coffin
choices: Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris, with a jar of Polish soil sprinkled on his coffin
Wawel Cathedral in Kraków, the burial place of Polish kings
Powązki Cemetery in Warsaw, alongside Polish national poets
The Madeleine vaults in Paris, beneath the church of his funeral
context: Chopin had left Warsaw before the 1830 Uprising and never returned to his homeland. His sister Ludwika brought Polish soil to Paris for his burial. Per his request, his heart was removed before burial, preserved in cognac, and smuggled back to Warsaw — it rests today in a pillar of the Holy Cross Church in Warsaw. The Père Lachaise grave became a Polish patriotic shrine; the Nazis tried unsuccessfully to remove the headstone in 1940.

question: Adam Smith, Scottish moral philosopher and customs official, published his treatise on political economy in March 1776 — the same year as the American Declaration of Independence. The book ran to over 1,000 pages and laid the foundation for modern economic analysis. What was the book's full title?
answer: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
choices: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
The Theory of Moral Sentiments and Their Economic Causes
A Treatise on the Division of Labour and Free Markets
Principles of Political Economy and the Liberty of Trade
context: Smith argued that self-interested actors in competitive markets, guided by an 'invisible hand,' often produce social benefits unintended by any individual. He had earlier published The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759), the philosophical foundation for the Wealth of Nations. Smith was a friend of David Hume and tutored the future Prime Minister William Pitt the Younger. He died in Edinburgh in 1790; on his deathbed he had most of his manuscripts burned.

question: On July 3 1863 Robert E. Lee ordered 12,500 Confederate soldiers across an open mile of ground at Gettysburg, against the Union line on Cemetery Ridge. Half were killed, wounded, or captured. As broken survivors streamed back, Lee rode out alone to meet them. He took personal responsibility on the spot. What did Lee say to the survivors?
answer: 'It is all my fault — General Pickett, your men have done all that men could do'
choices: 'It is all my fault — General Pickett, your men have done all that men could do'
'Rally to me on the ridge — we will hold this ground until darkness falls'
'God knows we have done our duty — He will give us another chance tomorrow'
'Virginia has lost her finest sons — let the world mark how they fell today'
context: Pickett's Charge is the 'high water mark of the Confederacy' — the closest the Confederate Army ever came to breaking the Union line. About 6,000 of 12,500 became casualties; the 26th North Carolina took 85% casualties. Lee offered his resignation to Jefferson Davis days later; Davis refused. Pickett himself, asked years later why the charge failed, replied: 'I always thought the Yankees had something to do with it.'

question: On November 15 1864 Union General William Tecumseh Sherman left burning Atlanta with 62,000 men and began marching toward the Atlantic coast — abandoning his supply lines, living off the land, and destroying everything of military value across a 60-mile-wide path of devastation. Six weeks later he reached the sea. What city did he capture as his 'Christmas gift' to Lincoln?
answer: Savannah, Georgia — taken without a fight on December 21 1864
choices: Savannah, Georgia — taken without a fight on December 21 1864
Charleston, South Carolina — the symbolic birthplace of the Confederacy
Wilmington, North Carolina — the Confederacy's last major Atlantic port
Mobile, Alabama — captured after Farragut's August naval victory
context: Sherman telegraphed Lincoln on December 22: 'I beg to present you as a Christmas gift the city of Savannah, with one hundred and fifty heavy guns and plenty of ammunition, and also about twenty-five thousand bales of cotton.' The march broke the Confederacy's will to continue. Sherman then turned north into the Carolinas, where his army was even harsher than in Georgia. The war ended four months later at Appomattox.

question: On July 5 1852 the formerly enslaved abolitionist Frederick Douglass — invited by the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society — delivered a speech in Corinthian Hall, Rochester, New York. He did not speak on July 4 because he refused to celebrate Independence Day while millions of Americans remained enslaved. What did Douglass call his speech?
answer: 'What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?'
choices: 'What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?'
'On the Hypocrisy of American Liberty'
'A Free Man's Lament on the Birthday of the Nation'
'The Slave's Verdict on American Freedom'
context: The speech is now considered one of the greatest American addresses. Douglass thundered: 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine. You may rejoice, I must mourn.' He had escaped slavery in Maryland in 1838, become a leading abolitionist orator, published his autobiography in 1845, and would go on to advise Lincoln during the Civil War. He died in 1895 at age 77.

question: On May 2 1863 the Confederate general Stonewall Jackson executed one of the most brilliant flank attacks in American military history at Chancellorsville, Virginia — marching 28,000 men around the Union right and smashing it at sunset. That night, riding back to his lines, Jackson was shot. Who shot him?
answer: His own North Carolina troops, in the dark, mistaking his party for Union cavalry
choices: His own North Carolina troops, in the dark, mistaking his party for Union cavalry
Union skirmishers, hidden in the woods and tracking his party through firelight
A Pennsylvania sharpshooter, who later confessed to identifying Jackson by his cap
A Confederate sentry, who panicked when Jackson failed to give the password
context: Jackson was hit by three bullets — two in the left arm, one in the right hand. His left arm was amputated. Lee said: 'He has lost his left arm; I have lost my right arm.' Pneumonia set in. Jackson died eight days later on May 10 1863. His last words: 'Let us cross over the river, and rest under the shade of the trees.' Chancellorsville was Lee's tactical masterpiece, but he had lost his most valuable subordinate; the loss is often credited with making possible the disaster at Gettysburg two months later.

question: On the night of October 16 1859, the abolitionist John Brown led 21 men in an attack on the federal armory and arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia. He planned to seize the arms inside and ignite a slave uprising across the South. The raid was crushed within 36 hours by U.S. Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee. Brown was hanged on December 2. What was Brown's last written statement, handed to a jail guard on the gallows?
answer: 'I am quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood'
choices: 'I am quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood'
'God forgive a country that has driven me to this end without granting me peace'
'My soul has done its work; let those who follow finish what I began here today'
'Tell my wife the cause is just and the day of reckoning is closer than they know'
context: Brown handed the prophecy to a guard as he walked to the scaffold at Charles Town, Virginia. Seventeen months later the Civil War began. Brown was hanged in the presence of John Wilkes Booth (then a Virginia militia private), Robert E. Lee, and Stonewall Jackson. The raid radicalized opinion in both the North (where Brown was hailed by some as a martyr) and the South (where it fueled secessionist arguments that Northern abolitionists meant war).

question: On the night of December 16 1773 about 100 Sons of Liberty, some disguised as Mohawk Indians, boarded three British ships in Boston harbor — the Dartmouth, the Eleanor, and the Beaver — and destroyed their cargo to protest a Parliamentary tax. They dumped a specific commodity into the harbor. What did they destroy?
answer: 342 chests of tea — about 92,000 pounds, worth approximately £10,000
choices: 342 chests of tea — about 92,000 pounds, worth approximately £10,000
180 bales of cotton — bound for British textile mills in Manchester
45 hogsheads of molasses — to protest the Molasses Act of 1733
12 crates of stamped paper — for the Stamp Act of 1765 distribution
context: The 'tea' was Chinese tea (about £18,000 in 1773 pounds; perhaps $2 million today). Parliament responded with the Coercive Acts (called the Intolerable Acts in the colonies), which closed Boston's port and effectively ended self-government in Massachusetts. The harshness of the response united the other colonies behind Massachusetts and led to the First Continental Congress in September 1774.

question: On April 19 1775, British regulars marched out of Boston to seize colonial militia stores at Concord, Massachusetts. They were met first at Lexington Green, then turned back at Concord's North Bridge. Ralph Waldo Emerson's 1837 'Concord Hymn' gave the day's opening shots their famous title. What did Emerson call the shot fired at Concord's North Bridge?
answer: 'The shot heard 'round the world'
choices: 'The shot heard 'round the world'
'The first flash of liberty's torch'
'The dawn of America's freedom'
'The voice of awakened justice'
context: Emerson's hymn was written for the 1837 dedication of the Concord battle monument. The British column took heavy casualties retreating to Boston as militia harassed them from cover the entire 16 miles. Within weeks militia from every New England colony had surrounded Boston. The Revolutionary War had begun.

question: On October 17 1777 a British army of 5,800 under General John Burgoyne surrendered to American forces under Horatio Gates at Saratoga, New York. The victory had immediate strategic consequences far beyond New York — convincing one major European power to enter the war on the American side. Which power?
answer: France — Louis XVI signed the alliance treaty in February 1778
choices: France — Louis XVI signed the alliance treaty in February 1778
Spain — Charles III declared war on Britain in 1779 as France's ally
The Dutch Republic — joined the League of Armed Neutrality in 1780
Russia — Catherine the Great threatened British shipping
context: The French alliance was the war's true turning point — bringing France's navy, regular army, and (eventually) $1.3 billion livres in loans. France formally entered the war in summer 1778. Spain joined in 1779. The Dutch were dragged into war with Britain in 1780. Without French naval support, Yorktown in 1781 would have been impossible. Burgoyne's surrender resulted from a strategic blunder — he marched south from Canada expecting support from General Howe that never materialized (Howe sailed for Philadelphia instead).

question: On October 19 1781 the British army of Lord Cornwallis — 7,000 men — surrendered at Yorktown, Virginia, after a three-week siege by combined American and French forces under Washington and Rochambeau. The French navy under Admiral de Grasse had cut off escape by sea. According to a famous (and disputed) story, the British military band played a specific song as they marched out to lay down their arms. What song was supposedly played?
answer: 'The World Turned Upside Down' — an English ballad of mockery and reversed fortune
choices: 'The World Turned Upside Down' — an English ballad of mockery and reversed fortune
'God Save the King' — a final defiant statement of British loyalty
'The Liberty Song' — a sarcastic concession to American patriotic anthems
'Yankee Doodle' — chosen by Cornwallis himself as a parting insult
context: Cornwallis pleaded illness and sent General Charles O'Hara to surrender his sword. Washington, in response, refused the sword and directed O'Hara to his own second-in-command, General Benjamin Lincoln. The 'world turned upside down' story dates from after the war — there is no contemporary documentary evidence. The British government of Lord North fell in March 1782; peace negotiations began. The Treaty of Paris was signed September 3 1783.

question: On March 23 1775, a month before the shots at Lexington, the Virginia attorney Patrick Henry rose before the Second Virginia Convention at St. John's Church in Richmond. He moved that Virginia raise a militia force. His speech ended with a four-word quotation that became the most famous American war cry of the Revolution. What four words did Henry shout?
answer: 'Give me liberty or death!'
choices: 'Give me liberty or death!'
'Liberty stands above all!'
'Free men or bondsmen!'
'Death before submission!'
context: Henry's exact words are reconstructed; no contemporary transcript survives. The version we know was written by William Wirt in his 1817 biography of Henry. Henry had earlier (1765) opposed the Stamp Act in the House of Burgesses with his 'If this be treason, make the most of it' speech. He was Virginia's first governor and refused to attend the 1787 Constitutional Convention, opposing the strong national government it produced.

question: On the morning of July 11 1804 the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Alexander Hamilton and the sitting Vice President Aaron Burr met for a duel across the Hudson River at Weehawken, New Jersey — the same spot where Hamilton's son Philip had died in a duel three years earlier. Burr's shot struck Hamilton in the abdomen. Hamilton died the next afternoon. What was the underlying cause of the duel?
answer: Hamilton's relentless political attacks had cost Burr the New York governorship that spring
choices: Hamilton's relentless political attacks had cost Burr the New York governorship that spring
Hamilton had refused to repay a $20,000 loan Burr had personally guaranteed
Hamilton had insulted Burr's adult daughter Theodosia at a dinner party in Albany
Burr had publicly accused Hamilton of an affair with Burr's own niece Sarah
context: Burr believed (correctly) that Hamilton had blocked his political advancement for years and had specifically derailed his April 1804 New York governor's race with private letters that became public. The challenge cited a derogatory remark Hamilton had supposedly made at an Albany dinner. Burr fled to South Carolina, was later tried for treason (and acquitted) after his Western adventures, and died in obscurity in 1836. Hamilton's widow Eliza outlived him by 50 years.

question: On August 24 1814, British troops under General Robert Ross marched into Washington D.C. and burned the Capitol, the White House, and the Treasury. The First Lady Dolley Madison, with the British less than two hours away, refused to leave the White House until she had saved one specific item. What did she save?
answer: Gilbert Stuart's full-length portrait of George Washington — cut from its frame and carried out
choices: Gilbert Stuart's full-length portrait of George Washington — cut from its frame and carried out
The original 1776 Declaration of Independence — rolled and hidden in a wagon
The Constitution and Bill of Rights — sewn into the lining of her traveling cloak
George Washington's personal sword — wrapped in a velvet cloth from her parlor
context: Dolley Madison wrote to her sister that day describing the rescue: the frame was broken and the canvas cut from the stretcher by an enslaved man named Paul Jennings and a French steward. The portrait now hangs in the East Room of the rebuilt White House. President James Madison was with American troops outside the city. The British also burned the Library of Congress; Jefferson sold his personal library to start it over.

question: In 1830 President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act. The Supreme Court ruled in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) that the Cherokee Nation was sovereign and could not be removed; Jackson reportedly said 'John Marshall has made his decision, now let him enforce it.' In 1838 the U.S. Army forced 16,000 Cherokee to march from Georgia to present-day Oklahoma. About how many died on the march from cold, hunger, and disease?
answer: Roughly 4,000 — about a quarter of those who began the march
choices: Roughly 4,000 — about a quarter of those who began the march
Roughly 800 — most survivors reached the Indian Territory by 1839
Roughly 9,500 — over half of those who started in the South
Roughly 150 — primarily elderly travelers in the worst weather
context: The Cherokee called it Nunna daul Tsuny — 'the trail where they cried.' The Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw, and Seminole were also forcibly removed, often with similar death rates. About 1,000 Cherokee evaded the roundup by hiding in the Smoky Mountains; their descendants form the Eastern Band of Cherokee. Jackson had built his political career partly on military victories against the Creek in 1814 (Horseshoe Bend) and the Seminole in 1818.

question: From February 23 to March 6 1836, about 200 Texan defenders held the Alamo mission at San Antonio against a Mexican army of perhaps 2,000 under Antonio López de Santa Anna. On the morning of March 6 the mission was overrun; nearly every defender died, including Davy Crockett, Jim Bowie (in his sick bed), and William Travis. Six weeks later the Texan general Sam Houston defeated Santa Anna at the battle of San Jacinto, securing Texan independence. What was the Texan battle cry at San Jacinto?
answer: 'Remember the Alamo!' — alongside 'Remember Goliad!' for the massacre of prisoners
choices: 'Remember the Alamo!' — alongside 'Remember Goliad!' for the massacre of prisoners
'Liberty or Death!' — adopted from Patrick Henry by Houston's officers
'God Save Texas!' — the war cry of the Texas Rangers since 1823
'Death to the Tyrant!' — Houston's personal motto of the campaign
context: Houston attacked Santa Anna's siesta camp on April 21 1836; the battle lasted 18 minutes. The Texans captured Santa Anna himself. Texas remained an independent republic until 1845, when it was annexed by the United States — which triggered the Mexican-American War (1846-1848). The 'Goliad' part of the war cry referred to Santa Anna's March 27 1836 execution of about 400 Texan prisoners after the battle of Goliad.

question: On November 19 1863 the Massachusetts orator Edward Everett spoke for two hours at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery at Gettysburg — a classical-style oration the audience expected to be the day's main event. President Abraham Lincoln spoke afterward for about two minutes from a single sheet of paper. About how many words long was Lincoln's address?
answer: Approximately 272 words — beginning 'Four score and seven years ago...'
choices: Approximately 272 words — beginning 'Four score and seven years ago...'
Approximately 850 words — taking roughly seven minutes to deliver
Approximately 1,400 words — close to Everett's length on a smaller scale
Approximately 2,100 words — Lincoln's longest formal address as President
context: Lincoln spoke from a single sheet, took about 2 minutes, and was followed by applause that he and his secretaries thought was muted. Everett wrote to Lincoln the next day: 'I should be glad if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as you did in two minutes.' Five manuscript copies in Lincoln's hand survive, with minor variations. The address has been carved at the Lincoln Memorial.

question: On Palm Sunday, April 9 1865, Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Ulysses S. Grant at the McLean House in Appomattox Court House, Virginia. Grant's surrender terms were considered remarkably generous. What did Grant allow the Confederate soldiers to do?
answer: Keep their horses for spring plowing and go home on parole if they pledged not to fight again
choices: Keep their horses for spring plowing and go home on parole if they pledged not to fight again
Retain their unit organization as territorial militias under Union officer oversight
Receive full back pay in Union currency for their service in the Confederate army
March home under their regimental colors with full military honors and weapons
context: Grant later wrote that he felt 'sad and depressed at the downfall of a foe who had fought so long and valiantly.' Lee left wearing a dress uniform and his ceremonial sword. The Union soldiers were ordered not to celebrate. Grant's generous terms helped set the tone for postwar reconciliation, which Lincoln's assassination five days later would severely complicate. Lee accepted the presidency of Washington College (now Washington and Lee) and died in 1870.

question: On the evening of Good Friday, April 14 1865 — five days after Lee's surrender — Abraham Lincoln attended a comedy called 'Our American Cousin' at Ford's Theatre in Washington D.C. with his wife Mary Todd Lincoln. During the play the actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth shot the President in the back of the head at point-blank range. What did Booth shout from the stage after jumping from the presidential box?
answer: 'Sic semper tyrannis!' — 'Thus always to tyrants' (the Virginia state motto)
choices: 'Sic semper tyrannis!' — 'Thus always to tyrants' (the Virginia state motto)
'Hoc voluerunt!' — 'They wanted this!' (a paraphrase of Caesar's last words)
'Memento mori!' — 'Remember your death!' (a classical funeral motto)
'Mors tyrannis!' — 'Death to the tyrant!' (Booth's own private maxim)
context: Booth broke his leg in the jump from the box to the stage but escaped on horseback. Lincoln was carried across the street to the Petersen House, where he died at 7:22 the next morning. Secretary of War Edwin Stanton's words: 'Now he belongs to the ages.' Booth was killed in a tobacco barn in Virginia 12 days later. The conspiracy had also attacked Secretary of State William Seward (badly wounded) and was meant to kill Vice President Andrew Johnson (whose attacker lost his nerve).

question: Washington's Continental Army survived the brutal winter of 1777-78 at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, about 20 miles outside British-occupied Philadelphia. Roughly 2,000 of the 12,000 soldiers died of cold, hunger, and disease. In February 1778 a Prussian volunteer arrived and began drilling the surviving men into a professional army. Who was the drillmaster?
answer: Baron Friedrich von Steuben — former staff officer to Frederick the Great
choices: Baron Friedrich von Steuben — former staff officer to Frederick the Great
The Marquis de Lafayette — French aristocrat who had funded his own passage
Tadeusz Kościuszko — Polish military engineer who designed Saratoga's defenses
Johann de Kalb — Bavarian-born general who died at Camden in 1780
context: Von Steuben spoke no English; his drilling commands were translated and spread through the camp by his aides. His Regulations for the Order and Discipline of the Troops of the United States (1779) became the army's drill manual for decades. He died on his New York land grant in 1794. The Marquis de Lafayette was at Valley Forge but as a major general, not as drillmaster; the others arrived later.

question: On January 17 1781 the American general Daniel Morgan, with about 1,000 mostly militia troops, won one of the most tactically perfect battles of the Revolutionary War at Cowpens, South Carolina, against the British cavalry officer Banastre Tarleton's 1,100 regulars. Morgan used a deliberate fake retreat by his militia to set up his veterans. The maneuver that destroyed Tarleton's command is the same one Hannibal had used at Cannae 1,400 years earlier. What is it called?
answer: Double envelopment — encircling the enemy from both flanks simultaneously
choices: Double envelopment — encircling the enemy from both flanks simultaneously
Refused flank attack — holding one wing while the other strikes
Wedge formation — driving a narrow point through the enemy center
Echelon attack — units advancing one at a time in a stepped line
context: Morgan instructed his militia to fire two volleys and then deliberately fall back as if routed. Tarleton charged after them straight into Morgan's regulars on either side and the Continental cavalry behind. Tarleton lost 850 of 1,100 men in less than an hour. Cowpens was studied at West Point and helped Nathanael Greene's southern strategy push Cornwallis toward Yorktown.

question: From May 25 to September 17 1787, 55 delegates from 12 states (Rhode Island sent none) met at the Pennsylvania State House (now Independence Hall) in Philadelphia. Their stated purpose was to revise the Articles of Confederation, but they ended by writing an entirely new Constitution. Who presided over the convention?
answer: George Washington — chosen unanimously on the first day as president of the convention
choices: George Washington — chosen unanimously on the first day as president of the convention
Benjamin Franklin — at 81 the oldest delegate and the convention's senior statesman
James Madison — 'Father of the Constitution' and chief recorder of the debates
Roger Sherman — only person to sign all four founding documents 1774-1789
context: Washington's presence gave the convention legitimacy; his presiding role kept him largely silent on specific proposals. James Madison sat near the front and took the detailed notes that are our primary record of the debates — published only after his death in 1840. The Constitution was signed September 17 1787, ratified by the ninth state (New Hampshire) on June 21 1788, and took effect March 4 1789. Of the 55 delegates, 39 signed.

question: George Washington's Farewell Address — actually a printed letter, never delivered as a speech — was published in September 1796. It warned the young nation against several specific dangers in foreign policy. What is its most famous foreign-policy warning?
answer: Against permanent entangling alliances with any foreign power
choices: Against permanent entangling alliances with any foreign power
Against any war with European powers for the next twenty years
Against trade tariffs higher than ten percent on any imported goods
Against accepting any foreign-born citizen in elected federal office
context: Washington's exact phrase was that the United States should have 'as little political connection as possible' with foreign nations and steer clear of 'permanent alliances.' The 'entangling alliances' phrase comes from Jefferson's first inaugural in 1801. The document was drafted by Hamilton and Madison and revised by Washington. The advice shaped American foreign policy for over a century until the Spanish-American War (1898) began continental empire-building, and World War II ended American isolationism.

question: On December 2 1823 President James Monroe's annual message to Congress announced a foreign-policy principle drafted largely by Secretary of State John Quincy Adams. The principle warned European powers against further colonization or political intervention in the Western Hemisphere. What was the U.S. promising in return?
answer: Non-interference in existing European colonies or in Europe's own internal affairs
choices: Non-interference in existing European colonies or in Europe's own internal affairs
American military aid to any newly independent Latin American republic against Spain
American troops and naval support for the suppression of all Atlantic slave trading
American support for a free-trade compact with Britain to be enforced jointly
context: The doctrine was prompted by fears of Russian expansion in the Pacific Northwest and possible Spanish reconquest of newly independent Latin American republics. The British Royal Navy actually enforced it for decades — Britain had its own commercial interests in keeping other European powers out of the Americas. The doctrine was extended by Theodore Roosevelt's 1904 corollary asserting an American right of intervention in the Caribbean.

question: The phrase 'manifest destiny' was coined in 1845 by the journalist John L. O'Sullivan, editor of the Democratic Review. He used it twice in 1845 articles arguing for the annexation of Texas and (separately) for American claims to Oregon. What did O'Sullivan say it was Americans' manifest destiny to do?
answer: 'To overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions'
choices: 'To overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions'
'To carry the torch of constitutional government from coast to coast within fifty years'
'To wash our hands clean of European entanglements through territorial expansion'
'To assert sovereignty over the Pacific Ocean as Britain has done with the Atlantic'
context: O'Sullivan's specific phrase was meant to claim divine sanction for territorial expansion. The Mexican War (1846-48) and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo brought California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, and parts of Colorado and New Mexico under American control. The Oregon Treaty (1846) settled the northern boundary at the 49th parallel. By 1853 the Gadsden Purchase had completed the lower 48. The territorial cost to Mexico was about half its national land area.

question: From July 19-20 1848, about 300 people met at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, for the first American convention on the rights of women. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott had planned it during the 1840 World's Anti-Slavery Convention in London, where as women they had been seated behind a curtain. What document did the Seneca Falls convention produce?
answer: The Declaration of Sentiments — modeled directly on the Declaration of Independence
choices: The Declaration of Sentiments — modeled directly on the Declaration of Independence
The Address to the Nation — a 22-page indictment of American patriarchy
The Women's Manifesto — calling for armed resistance to all property laws
The Petition of Rights — a single-page list of nine constitutional amendments
context: The Declaration of Sentiments began 'We hold these truths to be self-evident: that all men and women are created equal.' It listed 18 specific grievances paralleling Jefferson's list against George III. 68 women and 32 men signed. Frederick Douglass spoke in support of the resolution demanding the vote — the most controversial single resolution. The women's suffrage movement that began at Seneca Falls would take 72 years to win the 19th Amendment in 1920.

question: In March 1857 Chief Justice Roger Taney delivered the Supreme Court's majority opinion in Dred Scott v. Sandford, ruling against the enslaved Missouri man Dred Scott who had sued for freedom on the basis of years spent in free territory. Taney's ruling went beyond Scott's individual case to make two sweeping declarations. What were they?
answer: Black people could not be U.S. citizens — and Congress could not ban slavery from federal territories
choices: Black people could not be U.S. citizens — and Congress could not ban slavery from federal territories
Free states must return escaped slaves under federal law — and Congress could not protect free-state citizens
Slave property crossed state borders without restriction — and state courts had no jurisdiction
The Constitution implicitly endorsed perpetual slavery — and abolitionism was a federal crime
context: Taney's ruling invalidated the Missouri Compromise of 1820, ruled that no Black person had ever been or could be a U.S. citizen, and declared that slaveowners' Fifth Amendment property rights followed them into any territory. The decision intensified the sectional crisis and helped Lincoln to the 1860 election. The 14th Amendment (1868) explicitly overturned Taney's citizenship ruling. Taney died the same day Maryland voted to abolish slavery in October 1864.

question: At 5:29 a.m. on July 16 1945, the world's first atomic bomb detonated atop a 100-foot tower in the New Mexico desert near Alamogordo — codename 'Trinity.' The flash was visible 200 miles away. According to a film interview decades later, the scientific director J. Robert Oppenheimer recalled a phrase from the Bhagavad Gita as he watched the fireball. What did Oppenheimer say came to his mind?
answer: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds'
choices: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds'
'I have seen the dawn of a thousand suns'
'The atom has spoken; the world is silent'
'God has shown what man may do with fire'
context: Oppenheimer cited the line in a 1965 NBC documentary; the exact moment he thought of it is debated. The Trinity bomb was a plutonium implosion device of about 21 kilotons. Three weeks later the Hiroshima bomb (uranium gun-type, ~15 kilotons) killed roughly 70,000 instantly on August 6; the Nagasaki bomb (plutonium implosion, ~21 kilotons) killed roughly 40,000 instantly on August 9. Japan announced surrender on August 15.

question: In a June 5 1947 commencement address at Harvard, Secretary of State George Marshall proposed massive American aid to rebuild war-shattered Europe — eventually $13 billion (over $150 billion in modern terms) from 1948 to 1952. The Soviet Union refused to participate and forbade its satellite states from accepting. By what name did the program become known?
answer: The Marshall Plan — formally the European Recovery Program
choices: The Marshall Plan — formally the European Recovery Program
The Truman Doctrine — extended from Greece and Turkey to all of Europe
The Lend-Lease Renewal — a peacetime extension of wartime supply contracts
The Acheson Initiative — named for Marshall's State Department successor
context: The Marshall Plan supplied 16 Western European nations. The economist Paul Hoffman administered the program. Recipients were required to coordinate spending plans, an exercise that contributed to the postwar European integration that became the European Union. Marshall, the WWII Army chief of staff who had organized victory, received the 1953 Nobel Peace Prize — the only career soldier ever to win it.

question: On June 24 1948 the Soviet Union sealed off all road and rail access to West Berlin, hoping to force the Western Allies out of the city. President Harry Truman ordered a massive airlift instead. For 11 months U.S. and British aircraft delivered up to 12,000 tons of supplies per day to 2.5 million West Berliners. One American pilot became famous for a personal addition to the cargo. What did Lt. Gail Halvorsen do?
answer: Dropped candy bars on small parachutes to Berlin children as he approached the airport
choices: Dropped candy bars on small parachutes to Berlin children as he approached the airport
Carried a piano into Berlin in his cargo bay for a 1949 Christmas concert
Flew a daily route over East Berlin scattering propaganda leaflets in German
Trained Berlin orphans to operate ham radios to communicate with the West
context: Halvorsen wiggled his C-54's wings as a signal to children watching the planes approach Tempelhof airport, then dropped handkerchief parachutes loaded with chocolate. He became 'Uncle Wiggly Wings' and 'the Candy Bomber.' By 1949 American children had donated thousands of pounds of candy to the operation. Halvorsen died in 2022 at age 101. The Berlin Blockade ended May 12 1949; the airlift had moved 2.3 million tons of supplies.

question: On October 14 1962 a U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet medium-range ballistic missiles being installed in Cuba, 90 miles from Florida. For 13 days the world stood at the brink of nuclear war as President John F. Kennedy negotiated with Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev. How was the crisis resolved on October 28?
answer: Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles; Kennedy secretly pledged to remove U.S. missiles from Turkey
choices: Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles; Kennedy secretly pledged to remove U.S. missiles from Turkey
Kennedy ordered a full naval blockade and U-2 reconnaissance until the missiles rusted in place
Khrushchev surrendered the missiles publicly; the United States made no concession in return
Kennedy authorized a limited airstrike on the launch sites, after which Khrushchev backed down
context: The Cuban-missile resolution included a public Kennedy promise not to invade Cuba and a secret Kennedy promise to withdraw American Jupiter missiles from Turkey within six months — a concession that was only fully declassified decades later. The crisis led to the 1963 Moscow-Washington hotline. Khrushchev was ousted by his Politburo colleagues in October 1964, partly for the Cuban humiliation.

question: On April 12 1963 Martin Luther King Jr. was arrested in Birmingham, Alabama, for marching in defiance of a court injunction. While in jail he read a published statement by eight white Alabama clergymen calling his nonviolent campaign 'unwise and untimely.' He wrote a long reply in the margins of the newspaper, on toilet paper, and on scraps smuggled in by his lawyer. What is the document called?
answer: Letter from Birmingham Jail
choices: Letter from Birmingham Jail
The Birmingham Manifesto
Reply to the Alabama Clergymen
A Plea from the Cell
context: King's letter argued that the moral law stands above unjust civil law — drawing on Augustine, Aquinas, and the natural-law tradition. 'One has not only a legal but a moral responsibility to obey just laws. Conversely, one has a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws.' He wrote it over April 16-20 1963. It is now considered one of the great documents of American moral argument. King won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 and was assassinated April 4 1968 in Memphis at age 39.

question: On August 28 1963 about 250,000 people gathered on the National Mall in Washington for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Martin Luther King Jr. spoke from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. Partway through his prepared remarks, the gospel singer Mahalia Jackson — seated behind him — called out a specific encouragement. What did Mahalia Jackson shout?
answer: 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' — prompting King to set his text aside
choices: 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' — prompting King to set his text aside
'Sing it from your heart, brother!' — urging him toward a sermon style
'Let the people hear you!' — when the loudspeakers seemed to fade
'Speak for our children, Martin!' — referring to her own foster son
context: King had used the 'I have a dream' refrain in earlier speeches, most recently in Detroit two months before. He set aside his prepared text and improvised the final four minutes from memory. The speech is widely considered the greatest American speech of the 20th century. Mahalia Jackson sang at King's funeral in April 1968.

question: At 10:56:15 p.m. Eastern Time on July 20 1969, Neil Armstrong stepped off the Lunar Module Eagle's ladder onto the surface of the Moon at the Sea of Tranquility. About 600 million people worldwide watched the live broadcast. What did Armstrong say as he stepped off?
answer: 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind'
choices: 'That's one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind'
'The eagle has landed, and humanity has touched the heavens'
'This is the first foot of the future of mankind'
'I am here in peace for all the people of Earth'
context: Armstrong always insisted he said 'one small step for a man' — without the 'a' the sentence makes no sense. Audio analysis is divided. He had drafted the line himself only hours before the EVA. He and Buzz Aldrin spent 2 hours 31 minutes on the surface; Michael Collins remained in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia. The mission planted an American flag, set up scientific experiments, and brought back 21.5 kg of lunar samples.

question: On August 8 1974 President Richard Nixon announced his resignation in a televised address from the Oval Office, effective at noon the next day. He became the first U.S. president to resign. The scandal that brought him down had begun with a June 17 1972 break-in at a specific Washington building. What was that building?
answer: The Watergate complex — Democratic National Committee headquarters
choices: The Watergate complex — Democratic National Committee headquarters
The Pentagon — to retrieve missing Vietnam-strategy documents
The Library of Congress — to steal personal files on Senator George McGovern
The Brookings Institution — Nixon's 1971 plan to firebomb the think tank
context: Five burglars connected to Nixon's reelection committee were caught inside DNC offices at the Watergate. The cover-up, not the original burglary, brought Nixon down — the 'smoking gun' tape of June 23 1972 caught him discussing using the CIA to obstruct the FBI's investigation. Vice President Gerald Ford was sworn in August 9; Ford pardoned Nixon a month later. Two Washington Post reporters — Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein — broke much of the story.

question: On Christmas Eve 1968 the three astronauts of Apollo 8 — Frank Borman, James Lovell, and William Anders — became the first humans to orbit the Moon. On their ninth orbit they broadcast live to Earth. Roughly one billion people watched or listened in 64 countries. What did the astronauts read on their Christmas Eve broadcast?
answer: The first ten verses of Genesis from the King James Bible
choices: The first ten verses of Genesis from the King James Bible
A Christmas message from President Lyndon Johnson
Selections from John Milton's 'Paradise Lost'
A poem composed for the mission by Robert Frost before his 1963 death
context: Anders read verses 1-4 of Genesis 1, Lovell read 5-8, and Borman read 9-10. Borman closed: 'And from the crew of Apollo 8 we close with good night, good luck, a Merry Christmas, and God bless all of you — all of you on the good Earth.' Earlier in the orbit Anders had taken the Earthrise photograph, one of the most influential photographs in history. The 1968 broadcast aired during a year of assassinations (MLK, RFK), Tet, Prague Spring's crushing, and the My Lai Massacre.

question: From May 1804 to September 1806 the Corps of Discovery — about 33 men under Meriwether Lewis and William Clark — explored the new Louisiana Purchase from St. Louis to the Pacific and back. Their guide and interpreter through much of the Rockies was a 16-year-old Shoshone woman, kidnapped years earlier and married to a French-Canadian trapper. What was her name?
answer: Sacagawea — whose brother Cameahwait turned out to be the Shoshone chief who supplied horses
choices: Sacagawea — whose brother Cameahwait turned out to be the Shoshone chief who supplied horses
Pocahontas — daughter of Powhatan and adopted into a different exploration
Wahunsenacah — princess of the Cayuse who later married Marcus Whitman
Winema — daughter of a Modoc chief who guided Lieutenant Frémont's expedition
context: Sacagawea joined the expedition at the Mandan villages in present-day North Dakota with her husband Toussaint Charbonneau. She carried her infant son Jean Baptiste (Pomp) across the continent. Her presence as a woman with a baby signaled the expedition's peaceful intent to Indigenous peoples they encountered. Her Shoshone language skills proved critical at the Continental Divide. She died in 1812 at about age 25.

question: On March 9 1862 the first battle between two ironclad warships in history was fought at Hampton Roads, Virginia. The Union's USS Monitor — designed by John Ericsson with a single rotating turret — faced the Confederate CSS Virginia, rebuilt from the burned hulk of a steam frigate. What was the original frigate the Virginia had been built from?
answer: USS Merrimack — burned by the Union when Norfolk Navy Yard was abandoned in 1861
choices: USS Merrimack — burned by the Union when Norfolk Navy Yard was abandoned in 1861
USS Cumberland — sunk by the Virginia on the previous day, March 8 1862
USS Congress — burned by the Virginia on the previous day's rampage
USS Constitution — recovered from Boston naval reserve and rebuilt
context: The Confederates had pulled the burned USS Merrimack from the bottom and rebuilt it as the ironclad Virginia — but Northern writers called the battle 'Monitor versus Merrimack' and the name stuck. The battle was tactically a draw; both ships withdrew. The Virginia was scuttled by the Confederates in May 1862 to prevent capture; the Monitor sank in a December 1862 storm off Cape Hatteras. The duel ended the age of wooden warships worldwide.

question: On Sunday morning December 7 1941 the Japanese Imperial Navy launched 353 aircraft from six aircraft carriers in a surprise attack on the U.S. Pacific Fleet anchorage at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. Eight battleships were sunk or damaged; 2,403 Americans died. The next day President Franklin Roosevelt asked Congress for a declaration of war with a famous opening phrase. How did Roosevelt characterize December 7?
answer: 'A date which will live in infamy'
choices: 'A date which will live in infamy'
'The blackest day in our national memory'
'A morning of treachery the world will not forget'
'The opening of the cruelest war yet known to man'
context: Congress declared war 388-1 in the House (the lone dissent: Jeannette Rankin, who had also voted against U.S. entry into WWI). Roosevelt had drafted the speech personally on December 7, originally writing 'a date which will live in world history,' then crossing it out and writing 'infamy.' Germany and Italy declared war on the U.S. on December 11. The U.S. carriers — the actual Japanese targets — had been at sea on December 7 and survived.

question: On the morning of June 6 1944 — Operation Overlord — Allied forces landed on five beaches of the Normandy coast of German-occupied France. Over 156,000 troops crossed the Channel in the largest amphibious assault in history. American forces had two of the five beaches. The bloodiest American beach was a sector defended by entrenched German positions on the bluffs above the sand. Which beach was it?
answer: Omaha — where the U.S. 1st Infantry Division took roughly 2,400 casualties on June 6
choices: Omaha — where the U.S. 1st Infantry Division took roughly 2,400 casualties on June 6
Utah — the western American beach, taken with relatively light casualties
Sword — the easternmost beach, where Free French commandos landed first
Juno — assaulted by the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division, not Americans
context: Omaha was held by the German 352nd Infantry Division, a higher-quality unit than Allied intelligence had identified. The beach defenses included concrete bunkers, machine guns, and pre-sighted artillery. By nightfall the Americans had a tenuous foothold. Total Allied casualties on June 6 1944 were about 10,000 killed, wounded, or missing. The Normandy campaign would last until late August.

question: On March 4 1933 — the depths of the Great Depression, with 25% unemployment, hundreds of bank failures, and millions homeless — Franklin Delano Roosevelt was sworn in as the 32nd President of the United States. His first inaugural address contained one phrase that became among the most famous of the 20th century. What did Roosevelt say Americans had to fear?
answer: 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself'
choices: 'The only thing we have to fear is fear itself'
'Despair is the deepest enemy of any republic'
'Doubt in our purpose, not the cost of meeting it'
'Hesitation in the hour of national peril'
context: Roosevelt would deliver three more inaugurals — the only president elected to more than two terms (the 22nd Amendment, ratified 1951, established the two-term limit). The inaugural launched the 100-day legislative blitz that created the New Deal — bank-holiday, CCC, AAA, TVA, NRA, all enacted in three months. Roosevelt died in office on April 12 1945 at Warm Springs, Georgia, less than a month before V-E Day.

question: On the morning of September 11 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers seized four U.S. commercial airliners. Two struck the World Trade Center towers in New York; one struck the Pentagon in Virginia. The fourth, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed in a Pennsylvania field after passengers attempted to retake the cockpit. About how many people died on September 11 2001 total?
answer: Roughly 2,977 — the largest foreign attack on American soil in history
choices: Roughly 2,977 — the largest foreign attack on American soil in history
Roughly 1,200 — primarily in the WTC South Tower's first collapse
Roughly 6,500 — initial estimates that were later sharply revised down
Roughly 850 — passengers, hijackers, and a small number of WTC staff
context: The 19 hijackers also died and are usually counted separately. The Twin Towers collapsed within two hours of the strikes; about 2,750 died at the WTC alone, including 343 New York firefighters. Flight 93 crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania; passenger Todd Beamer's recorded call to a phone operator included the phrase 'Let's roll' as the passengers stormed the cockpit. The U.S. invaded Afghanistan on October 7 2001. Osama bin Laden was killed by U.S. Navy SEALs in Pakistan on May 2 2011.

question: In September 480 BC, with Athens evacuated and the Persian fleet of about 1,200 ships hunting the smaller Greek fleet (~370 ships), Athenian commander Themistocles needed to force a battle in the narrow waters of the Salamis strait where Persian numbers wouldn't help. He sent a slave named Sicinnus across with a secret message to the Persian king Xerxes. What did the message tell Xerxes?
answer: That the Greeks were about to flee — Xerxes should block the strait that night before they escaped
choices: That the Greeks were about to flee — Xerxes should block the strait that night before they escaped
That a Greek captain would defect — he would signal where to attack the weakest squadron
That a winter storm was coming — Xerxes should attack at dawn before weather ruined the chance
That the oracle priests at Delphi had spoken — the gods now favored Persia in the sea battle
context: Xerxes took the bait. The Persian fleet rowed all night to bottle up the Greeks, then entered the narrows at dawn — exhausted, where Persian numerical advantage meant nothing. The Greeks destroyed roughly 200-300 Persian ships and lost about 40. Xerxes watched the disaster from a golden throne set up on Mount Aigaleo overlooking the strait. The playwright Aeschylus, who fought in the battle, dramatized it eight years later in 'The Persians.'

question: From February 21 to December 18 1916 — 10 months — the German and French armies bled themselves white at Verdun, France. The Germans hoped to force the French to defend the symbolic fortress city until the French army broke. The French commander Philippe Pétain organized the defense around a single supply road — la Voie Sacrée. What three-word French phrase became the defining slogan of the Verdun defense?
answer: 'Ils ne passeront pas' — 'They shall not pass'
choices: 'Ils ne passeront pas' — 'They shall not pass'
'Vive la France' — 'Long live France'
'Patrie ou mort' — 'Fatherland or death'
'À la baïonnette' — 'To the bayonet'
