question: After capturing Atlanta on September 2, 1864 — a victory that secured Lincoln's November re-election — Union Major General William Tecumseh Sherman cut his army loose from supply lines, burned Atlanta's military stores (much of the city followed), and led 62,000 men southeast through Georgia. For five weeks the army lived off the land, destroyed railroads, factories, and resources in a 60-mile-wide swath, and arrived at Savannah December 22, 1864. Sherman sent President Lincoln a telegram offering the captured city as what?
answer: 'A Christmas gift — the city of Savannah, with 150 heavy guns and plenty of ammunition, and also about 25,000 bales of cotton'
choices: 'A Christmas gift — the city of Savannah, with 150 heavy guns and plenty of ammunition, and also about 25,000 bales of cotton'
'A holiday tribute — the city of Savannah, intact and undamaged, with its fortifications and naval stores'
'A wartime greeting — the city of Savannah, surrendered without battle, ready for federal administration'
'A New Year's offering — the city of Savannah and all the cotton wealth of the Lower South'
context: Sherman's March to the Sea (Atlanta to Savannah, November 15 - December 21, 1864) was a deliberate demonstration that the Confederate government could not protect its citizens — a campaign of 'hard war' aimed at breaking civilian morale and the South's capacity to fight. From Savannah Sherman turned north through the Carolinas in early 1865, burning Columbia (SC) and forcing Joseph Johnston's surrender at Bennett Place, NC, on April 26, 1865 — 17 days after Appomattox. The march remains controversial; Confederate descendants describe it as terrorism, Union historians as the war-shortening strategic necessity that saved tens of thousands of lives.

question: By spring 1942 the U.S. Navy's code-breaking team at Station Hypo in Pearl Harbor — led by Lt. Commander Joseph J. Rochefort — had broken enough of the Japanese fleet code JN-25 to read about 10-15% of intercepted traffic. Hypo intercepted messages referring to an operation against 'AF.' To confirm AF was Midway Atoll, Rochefort had the Midway base radio in the clear that its desalination plant had broken. Within hours Japanese traffic reported 'AF is short of fresh water.' What did Admiral Chester Nimitz then do?
answer: Concentrated his three available carriers north of Midway to ambush the Japanese carrier force
choices: Concentrated his three available carriers north of Midway to ambush the Japanese carrier force
Reinforced Midway's garrison with the entire 7th Marine Regiment as a defensive measure
Diverted MacArthur's southwestern fleet to Hawaii to reinforce the carrier task force
Mined the western approaches to Pearl Harbor as protection against carrier attack
context: Yorktown (damaged at Coral Sea two weeks earlier and given 90 days for repair) was patched and back to sea in 48 hours. Enterprise and Hornet completed the three-carrier task force. On June 4, 1942, U.S. carrier dive bombers caught the four Japanese fleet carriers rearming aircraft on deck and sank Akagi, Kaga, Soryu (in the same five-minute window) and Hiryu later that day. Yamamoto lost four carriers, 250 aircraft, and most of his veteran naval pilots — irreplaceable losses. The Pacific war's offensive initiative shifted permanently to the United States.

question: From February 23 to March 6, 1836, about 200 Texan defenders held the converted San Antonio mission known as the Alamo against a Mexican army of perhaps 1,800 under General Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna. On approximately the eleventh day of siege, Lt. Colonel William B. Travis — knowing relief was not coming and the position was lost — reportedly drew a line in the sand with his sword and asked those willing to stay and fight to the death to step across. All but one (Moses Rose) crossed. The Alamo fell at dawn on March 6, 1836; all defenders were killed including James Bowie (sick in bed) and Davy Crockett. What was the cry that became the Texas Revolution's rallying call?
answer: 'Remember the Alamo' — Sam Houston's army shouted it at San Jacinto six weeks later
choices: 'Remember the Alamo' — Sam Houston's army shouted it at San Jacinto six weeks later
'Liberty or the grave' — Travis's last appeal to the Texan settlements for support
'No surrender, no quarter' — Santa Anna's red-flag order and the Texans' defiant reply
'Death to the tyrant' — the Texas legislators' phrase taken up by army recruiters
context: On April 21, 1836 at San Jacinto, Sam Houston's army of about 900 Texans surprised Santa Anna's larger Mexican force during an afternoon siesta. The battle lasted 18 minutes; Texas casualties were 11 killed, 30 wounded; Mexican casualties were over 600 killed and 700 captured (including Santa Anna himself the next day). Houston signed the Treaties of Velasco gaining Texas independence. The Republic of Texas existed for nine years before joining the United States in 1845; the Mexican-American War (1846-48) followed, ending with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo and the Mexican Cession.

question: On the evening of June 5, 1944, with weather windows closing and 156,000 Allied troops about to embark for the Normandy invasion, Supreme Commander Dwight D. Eisenhower drafted a brief message on a small pad that he kept in his wallet. The letter was meant to be released if the landing failed. It began: 'Our landings... have failed to gain a satisfactory foothold and I have withdrawn the troops.' He continued with a remarkable sentence. What did Eisenhower commit to?
answer: Personal sole responsibility — 'If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone'
choices: Personal sole responsibility — 'If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone'
Resignation as Supreme Commander — 'I shall return immediately to the United States'
Demanding congressional inquiry — 'A complete investigation is the public's right'
Refusing further field command — 'I am unfit for the trust placed in me by the President'
context: Eisenhower's letter (which he never had to release) is one of the most studied documents in leadership literature. By the end of June 6, 1944, about 156,000 Allied troops were ashore on five Normandy beaches — Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, Sword — with about 4,400 killed (about 2,500 of them American, the worst losses at Omaha). The breakout from Normandy took until late July (Operation Cobra); Paris was liberated August 25, 1944. The Wehrmacht in the West would never recover. Eisenhower became Army Chief of Staff (1945), Supreme Allied Commander Europe (1951), president of Columbia University (1948), and 34th President of the United States (1953-1961).

question: On Good Friday evening, April 14, 1865 — five days after Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox — President Abraham Lincoln and Mary Todd Lincoln attended a performance of the comedy 'Our American Cousin' at Ford's Theatre in Washington. Around 10:15 PM, during a moment of audience laughter, actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth slipped into the presidential box from the rear, fired a single .44-caliber Derringer ball into Lincoln's left occipital lobe, leaped to the stage, broke his fibula on landing, and reportedly shouted a famous Latin phrase before escaping out the back. What did Booth reportedly shout?
answer: 'Sic semper tyrannis' — 'Thus always to tyrants' — the Virginia state motto
choices: 'Sic semper tyrannis' — 'Thus always to tyrants' — the Virginia state motto
'Pro patria mori' — 'To die for the country' — a phrase from Horace
'Veni, vidi, vici' — 'I came, I saw, I conquered' — Caesar's report
'In hoc signo vinces' — 'In this sign you shall conquer' — Constantine's vision
context: Lincoln was carried across the street to the Petersen boarding house, where he died at 7:22 AM on April 15, 1865 — Easter Saturday — without regaining consciousness. Secretary of War Edwin Stanton at the deathbed: 'Now he belongs to the ages.' Booth was tracked through southern Maryland and northern Virginia for 12 days; cornered in a tobacco barn near Port Royal, Virginia on April 26, he was shot dead by Sergeant Boston Corbett against orders to take him alive. Four other conspirators were hanged July 7, 1865.

question: On December 1, 1955 in Montgomery, Alabama, a 42-year-old seamstress who had spent decades as secretary of the local NAACP chapter — and who had attended training at the Highlander Folk School the previous summer — refused to give up her seat on a city bus to a white passenger after the colored section had filled. She was arrested. The local Women's Political Council and a young 26-year-old Baptist minister organized a one-day boycott for December 5. It lasted 381 days, until the U.S. Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional on December 17, 1956. Who was the young minister?
answer: Martin Luther King Jr.
choices: Martin Luther King Jr.
Ralph David Abernathy
Vernon Johns
Edgar Daniel Nixon
context: Rosa Parks's refusal was not (as later mythology had it) the spontaneous protest of a tired seamstress; she was a deliberate, prepared, and trained NAACP officer. Earlier in 1955 a 15-year-old Claudette Colvin had been arrested for the same offense, but movement leaders judged her circumstances (pregnant, unmarried) bad for a test case. The Montgomery Improvement Association elected the new young pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church — Martin Luther King Jr., who had moved to Montgomery the previous September — its president. The boycott launched both the modern civil rights movement and King's national leadership.

question: On October 19, 1781 at Yorktown, Virginia, after a 21-day siege by a combined Franco-American force of about 17,000 under Washington and Rochambeau, supported by the French fleet under Admiral de Grasse that blocked British relief, the British commander Lieutenant General Charles Cornwallis — claiming illness — sent his subordinate Brigadier General Charles O'Hara to surrender 8,000 men. Tradition holds the British military band played a particular tune as the Redcoats marched out to lay down arms — a wry comment on the inversion of expected outcomes. What tune did the band reportedly play?
answer: 'The World Turned Upside Down' — a popular ballad fitting the unprecedented British surrender
choices: 'The World Turned Upside Down' — a popular ballad fitting the unprecedented British surrender
'God Save the King' — a final assertion of royal sovereignty despite battlefield defeat
'Yankee Doodle' — defiantly playing the song Americans had adopted as their own
'Hearts of Oak' — the Royal Navy march asserting British naval honor in the moment
context: The 'World Turned Upside Down' anecdote first appears in print in the 1820s; modern historians regard it as plausible but unverifiable. The defeat ended major combat operations in the American Revolution; the Treaty of Paris (September 3, 1783) recognized American independence. Cornwallis went on to a long and respectable career — Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, Governor-General of India. The American military victory was won by a combination of Continental Army discipline (forged at Valley Forge), French naval and military intervention, and Washington's persistence after seven years.

question: Tuesday, September 11, 2001: at 8:46 AM Eastern, American Airlines Flight 11 (Boston to Los Angeles) struck the North Tower of the World Trade Center in Manhattan. At 9:03 AM United Flight 175 struck the South Tower. At 9:37 AM American Flight 77 struck the western face of the Pentagon. At 10:03 AM United Flight 93 — its passengers having voted to charge the hijackers — crashed in a Pennsylvania field. The Twin Towers collapsed at 9:59 AM and 10:28 AM. The combined death toll exceeded 2,977 civilians killed plus the 19 al-Qaeda hijackers. Among the dead were 343 New York City firefighters and 60 NYPD and Port Authority police officers — many killed when the towers collapsed. What had they been doing?
answer: Climbing the stairwells of the towers to help evacuate civilians trapped above the fires
choices: Climbing the stairwells of the towers to help evacuate civilians trapped above the fires
Securing the streets around the towers to keep crowds back from falling debris
Forming a perimeter around the Pentagon's western facade to assist Defense Department staff
Coordinating the FAA national ground-stop that grounded all 4,000 commercial flights
context: The 343 FDNY dead are the largest loss of life of any single emergency-services unit in U.S. history. Above-impact floors of the towers were essentially un-evacuable; firefighters were doing what they could anyway. Father Mychal Judge, the FDNY chaplain, was killed administering last rites at the scene and was officially Victim 0001. The Bush administration's response — Afghanistan invasion (October 2001), Iraq invasion (March 2003), the global war on terror — defined American foreign policy for two decades. Osama bin Laden was killed by U.S. Navy SEALs at his Abbottabad compound on May 2, 2011.

question: In 1953-54, with the Cold War deepening and McCarthy hearings raging, J. Robert Oppenheimer — Manhattan Project scientific director, Trinity test hero, former AEC adviser — was investigated by a personnel security board over his opposition to the hydrogen bomb program (he had favored arms control), past leftist associations (his brother Frank was an ex-Communist), and 1943 statements about Soviet contacts. The board found him 'loyal' but a 'security risk' and revoked his clearance on June 29, 1954. What was the broader significance?
answer: It signaled that even decorated scientific service did not protect against ideological investigation in Cold War America
choices: It signaled that even decorated scientific service did not protect against ideological investigation in Cold War America
It established the principle that all federal scientific advisers must publicly endorse current weapons programs
It eliminated civilian advisers from the AEC structure, transferring authority entirely to military officials
It prompted Congress to pass a law requiring loyalty oaths from all federally funded scientific researchers
context: Oppenheimer's clearance revocation ended his role in nuclear policy. He spent the rest of his career at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, dying in 1967 of throat cancer. In December 2022, the U.S. Department of Energy formally vacated the 1954 decision, calling it the product of a 'flawed process.' Edward Teller, who had testified against Oppenheimer, was ostracized by much of the physics community for the rest of his life. Christopher Nolan's 2023 film Oppenheimer renewed broad public engagement with the episode.

question: From 1838-1839 under President Van Buren and General Winfield Scott, the U.S. Army forcibly removed about 16,000 Cherokee from their ancestral homelands in Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and Alabama to Indian Territory (modern Oklahoma) — about 1,200 miles, mostly on foot. This implemented the 1830 Indian Removal Act signed by Andrew Jackson, even though the Supreme Court's Worcester v. Georgia (1832) had ruled Georgia's removal laws unconstitutional (Jackson reportedly: 'John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it'). What is the conventional estimate of Cherokee deaths during the removal?
answer: Approximately 4,000 — about one-quarter of the Cherokee removed died of cold, hunger, and disease
choices: Approximately 4,000 — about one-quarter of the Cherokee removed died of cold, hunger, and disease
Approximately 250 — most casualties were elderly people who could not endure the march
Approximately 800 — primarily children under five and pregnant women lost during transit
Approximately 12,000 — losses included most Cherokee who had refused the official removal
context: The Trail of Tears removed not only Cherokee but also Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), Chickasaw, and Seminole — the 'Five Civilized Tribes' — under the same 1830 Act. Combined deaths likely exceeded 12,000. A small Cherokee remnant (the Eastern Band) hid in the Smoky Mountains and survives today as a federally recognized tribe in North Carolina. The Cherokee in Oklahoma rebuilt their nation, including written constitutions, schools, and the syllabary developed by Sequoyah before removal. Jackson's image on the $20 bill has become controversial.

question: By late January 1943 the German 6th Army was trapped at Stalingrad on the Volga, encircled since November by Operation Uranus, starving and frostbitten. Hitler promoted commander Friedrich Paulus to Generalfeldmarschall on January 30 with a specific message implied by the promotion itself: Hitler had calculated that no German field marshal in history had ever done a particular thing. The promotion was meant to ensure Paulus did not become the first. What was Hitler signaling Paulus to do?
answer: To commit suicide rather than surrender — no German field marshal had ever been taken alive
choices: To commit suicide rather than surrender — no German field marshal had ever been taken alive
To break out westward alone — only a field marshal could rally the remaining troops
To negotiate personal terms — only a field marshal had rank to deal with Soviet commanders
To return to Germany personally — a field marshal could not be held as a prisoner of war
context: Paulus surrendered the next day, January 31, 1943 — becoming the first German field marshal ever taken prisoner. About 91,000 starving German troops surrendered; only about 5,000 survived Soviet captivity and returned to Germany after the war. The siege cost roughly 750,000 German + Axis casualties and possibly 1.1 million Soviet. Paulus eventually broadcast anti-Nazi radio addresses from Soviet captivity. He died in East Germany in 1957. Stalingrad is generally regarded as the turning point of the European war.

question: Johann Sebastian Bach died in Leipzig in 1750. By the time of his death his style was already considered old-fashioned; for the next 79 years much of his work — including the towering St. Matthew Passion of 1727 — was unknown outside small German Lutheran circles. In March 1829, in Berlin, a public concert revived the Passion and ignited the modern Bach revival that has made him a pillar of Western music. The conductor who organized and led the revival was only 20 years old. Who was he?
answer: Felix Mendelssohn
choices: Felix Mendelssohn
Robert Schumann
Franz Liszt
Hector Berlioz
context: Mendelssohn's grandmother Bella Salomon had given him a manuscript copy of the St. Matthew Passion for his 14th birthday. The 1829 Berlin performance used roughly 400 singers and players. Mendelssohn cut about a third of the score to fit modern concert format. Goethe attended a related concert. The revival spread across Europe within a decade; Bach went from a regional Lutheran kapellmeister to one of the central composers of Western music.

question: On the night of November 23 1654, the French mathematician Blaise Pascal had an experience lasting roughly two hours that he believed was a direct encounter with God. He scribbled a record on a small piece of parchment headed with a date, a time, and one word in capitals. For the remaining eight years of his life until his death at 39, he carried the parchment sewn into the lining of his coat — transferring it from coat to coat — where a servant found it after his death. What single word did Pascal write at the top under the date?
answer: 'FIRE' — Feu
choices: 'FIRE' — Feu
'GOD' — Dieu
'GRACE' — Grace
'LIGHT' — Lumiere
context: The 'Memorial' is one of the most famous personal documents in the history of religion. It opens: 'The year of grace 1654 / Monday, 23 November... From about half past ten in the evening until about half past twelve at night / FIRE / God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, not of the philosophers and scholars.' Pascal had already invented mechanical calculation, modern probability theory, and major work in fluid dynamics. After this night he largely abandoned mathematics for theology, producing the Pensees.

question: In the Cornaro Chapel of Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome stands one of the central monuments of Baroque sculpture: Gian Lorenzo Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, completed 1652. Bernini carved Teresa of Avila in mystic rapture, an angel about to plunge a fiery arrow into her heart, the whole tableau lit by a hidden window above so that gilded rays seem to pour real sunlight onto stone. Sculptors had thought one particular feat impossible in marble before Bernini. What does the sculpture famously achieve?
answer: Teresa's robes appear weightless and fluid — heavy marble carved to look like wind-blown cloth
choices: Teresa's robes appear weightless and fluid — heavy marble carved to look like wind-blown cloth
Teresa's face shows three distinct expressions — depending on the angle of the viewer's approach
The angel's wings cast a real shadow on the wall — calculated to match the chapel's window angle
The arrow tip changes color through the day — different mineral veins react to the changing light
context: Bernini was the dominant artist of 17th-century Rome — sculptor, architect, painter, designer of fountains, urban planner. The Cornaro family commissioned the chapel; family members in marble box-seats watch Teresa's vision from the side walls like opera spectators. Teresa of Avila (1515-1582) was a Spanish Carmelite mystic and Doctor of the Church; her autobiography describes the angelic vision Bernini depicts. The work fuses sculpture, architecture, and theatrical lighting into a single multimedia experience.

question: On May 7 1824, in Vienna's Karntnertor Theater, Ludwig van Beethoven premiered his 9th Symphony — the first major symphony to incorporate vocal soloists and chorus, setting Schiller's Ode to Joy. Beethoven, completely deaf for years, stood at the front beside the actual conductor, beating time several bars off from the orchestra. At the end of the final movement, with the audience erupting in applause, Beethoven did not turn around. A specific person stepped forward and physically intervened so that the deaf composer could finally see what was happening behind him. Who turned Beethoven around?
answer: The contralto soloist Caroline Unger
choices: The contralto soloist Caroline Unger
The concertmaster Michael Umlauf
Beethoven's nephew Karl van Beethoven
The conductor's young assistant Franz Schubert
context: Caroline Unger sang the contralto solo part. By multiple eyewitness accounts she walked over to Beethoven, took his shoulder, and turned him to face the audience — who were waving hats and handkerchiefs because the deaf composer could not hear their cheering. The audience reportedly broke into a fifth ovation, exceeding even the customary three rounds reserved for the Imperial family. Beethoven died less than three years later in March 1827.

question: On April 26 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, German and Italian aircraft of the Condor Legion bombed the Basque town of Guernica on a market day, killing hundreds of civilians and destroying most of the town. Pablo Picasso, then living in Paris, had been commissioned by the Spanish Republican government to produce a mural for the Spanish Pavilion at the 1937 Paris International Exposition. Reading the newspaper reports from Guernica, he abandoned his planned subject. The huge black-white-and-grey canvas he produced over the next six weeks is widely considered the most famous anti-war painting of the 20th century. What is unusual about Guernica's color palette?
answer: It is painted entirely in greys, black, and white — no color at all on the eleven-foot canvas
choices: It is painted entirely in greys, black, and white — no color at all on the eleven-foot canvas
Each victim figure is painted in a different single color — the bull alone is monochrome
The flames are painted in real gold leaf — the only ornamentation on an otherwise grey ground
The canvas was painted entirely in blue tones — later darkened to grey by Picasso's request
context: The painting is 11 ft tall and 25 ft wide. Picasso said the monochrome palette evoked newspaper photographs — the way most of Europe was learning of the bombing. The canvas toured Europe and America raising awareness for the Republican cause; Picasso refused to allow it to be displayed in Spain while Franco lived. It hung in MoMA in New York from 1939 until 1981, when it finally went home to Madrid after Spain's transition to democracy. It now hangs in the Reina Sofia.

question: Pope Julius II forced the Sistine Chapel ceiling commission on Michelangelo in 1508 over his protests — Michelangelo insisted he was a sculptor, not a painter. Working alone on a custom scaffold he designed himself, he painted roughly 5,000 square feet of fresco — Genesis, the Prophets, the Creation of Adam — over four years, finishing October 31 1512. The job left him with one specific lasting physical change he later wrote about in a sonnet to a friend. What had four years on the scaffold done to his body?
answer: His neck stayed permanently twisted upward — for months afterward he could read letters only by holding them above his head
choices: His neck stayed permanently twisted upward — for months afterward he could read letters only by holding them above his head
Lead in the pigments poisoned him — he lost most of his hair and several teeth within a year of finishing the ceiling
His right eye went partially blind — from constant paint dripping into his face during work overhead
His back stiffened so badly — he could not bow before the Pope at the October 1512 unveiling without assistance
context: Michelangelo's own sonnet to Giovanni da Pistoia describes the deformation: 'My beard turns up to heaven; my nape falls in / Fixed on my spine: my breast-bone visibly / Grows like a harp: a rich embroidery / Bedews my face from brush-drops thick and thin.' The ceiling was unveiled October 31 1512. He returned 22 years later to paint The Last Judgment on the altar wall. He died in 1564 at age 88, still working on St. Peter's Basilica.

question: On June 22 1633, after months of interrogation by the Roman Inquisition for teaching Copernican heliocentrism in his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, Galileo Galilei knelt before his judges in the Dominican convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva and formally abjured — recited a prepared statement renouncing the doctrine that the Earth moves around the Sun. He was 69, threatened with torture, and would spend the remaining nine years of his life under house arrest. Legend says that as he rose from his knees he muttered four words in Italian. What words has tradition assigned him?
answer: 'Eppur si muove' — 'And yet it moves'
choices: 'Eppur si muove' — 'And yet it moves'
'Vincet veritas' — 'Truth will conquer'
'Dio mi vede' — 'God sees me'
'Pazienza, pazienza' — 'Patience, patience'
context: The eppur si muove story is almost certainly apocryphal — no contemporary source records it, and Galileo would have been mad to mutter such a thing in earshot of the Inquisition. The earliest attested telling is from 1757 in Giuseppe Baretti's Italian Library, more than a century after the event. But the phrase captures the truth of the situation: Galileo had recanted under duress, the heliocentric Earth still moved regardless, and the Church's 1633 condemnation would eventually have to be reversed. Pope John Paul II formally acknowledged the Galileo affair as an error in 1992.

question: Isaac Newton invented calculus and the laws of motion and universal gravitation during his 1665-67 plague years at Woolsthorpe but did not publish. For 20 years the work sat in his desk. In 1684 the young astronomer Edmond Halley visited Newton in Cambridge with a problem: what curve does a planet trace under an inverse-square attraction to the Sun? Newton answered 'an ellipse — I have calculated it.' Halley spent the next three years coaxing Newton through the writing of the Principia. The Royal Society had run out of money on a fish-anatomy book the year before. How did the Principia of 1687 get printed?
answer: Halley paid the printing costs personally from his own modest income
choices: Halley paid the printing costs personally from his own modest income
Charles II provided a royal subsidy after a private audience with Halley
Cambridge University printed it from college funds at Trinity
A subscription was raised among London merchants who admired Newton
context: Halley was 28 when he met Newton on the comet question. He paid for the Principia out of pocket because the Royal Society had spent its book budget on Francis Willughby's De Historia Piscium, a heavily illustrated fish book that flopped commercially. Halley even fronted Newton parts of the royalties. Halley's comet — which Halley correctly predicted would return in 1758 — bears his name. The Principia is widely considered the most important work in the history of physical science.

question: On June 15 1215, in a meadow at Runnymede beside the Thames, an angry coalition of English barons forced King John to seal a list of feudal demands. Most of the 63 clauses dealt with narrow medieval concerns — fish-weirs, the size of grain measures, payments for inheriting fiefs — and the agreement collapsed within months as John repudiated it. But two clauses, later renumbered 39 and 40 in the 1297 statute version, became foundational to the entire English-speaking legal tradition over the following 800 years. What did those two clauses establish?
answer: No free man could be imprisoned or stripped of his rights except by lawful judgment of his peers, and justice could not be sold, denied, or delayed
choices: No free man could be imprisoned or stripped of his rights except by lawful judgment of his peers, and justice could not be sold, denied, or delayed
The king could not levy any tax without the consent of all his bishops and barons assembled in person
The king's eldest son inherited the crown automatically and could not be removed except by trial
All free men could bear arms in their own defense without any royal license or restriction at all
context: The full clauses (in the 1297 statute version): 'No free man shall be taken or imprisoned... except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land. To no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice.' Edward Coke, in his early-17th-century commentaries, made Magna Carta the foundation of his argument that even the king was under the law — a doctrine the American colonists invoked against George III in the 1770s. The phrase 'due process of law' descends from the chapter 39 language.

question: On April 17-18 1521, summoned before Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and the imperial diet at Worms, the Augustinian friar Martin Luther was shown his books and ordered to recant. He asked for a day to consider. He returned April 18 and delivered a speech refusing — saying his conscience was bound by Scripture and that to act against conscience was neither right nor safe. Tradition assigns him a closing four-word German phrase. The actual transcripts vary, but the phrase has stood for 500 years as the founding line of Protestant conscience. What does the famous phrase say?
answer: 'Hier stehe ich' — 'Here I stand'
choices: 'Hier stehe ich' — 'Here I stand'
'Gott helfe mir' — 'God help me'
'Christus ist Herr' — 'Christ is Lord'
'Ich habe gesprochen' — 'I have spoken'
context: The longer attributed ending: 'Hier stehe ich, ich kann nicht anders. Gott helfe mir. Amen.' ('Here I stand, I can do no other. God help me. Amen.') The 'Hier stehe ich' line appears in the earliest printed German edition of Luther's speech but not in the official Latin minutes — historians treat it as plausibly authentic but uncertain. Luther was excommunicated and outlawed; Frederick the Wise of Saxony hid him at Wartburg Castle, where he translated the New Testament into German in eleven weeks.

question: William Wilberforce entered the British Parliament in 1780. In 1787, partly under the influence of the former slave-ship captain John Newton (composer of 'Amazing Grace'), the young Anglican MP took up the cause of abolition. For the next 20 years he introduced an annual bill to abolish the British slave trade; for 20 years Parliament voted it down or buried it in committee. On February 23 1807 the Commons finally passed the Slave Trade Act by 283-16, and the House rose to give Wilberforce a standing ovation while he wept. How many days before his death did Wilberforce receive word that Parliament had also passed final abolition of slavery itself throughout the British Empire?
answer: Three days before he died — he died July 29 1833, the Slavery Abolition Act passed July 26
choices: Three days before he died — he died July 29 1833, the Slavery Abolition Act passed July 26
Several months before — the Slavery Abolition Act passed January 1833 and he lingered until autumn
About a year before — he lived to see compensation negotiations conclude in early 1832
Just hours before — the Lords passed final reading the same morning he died
context: The 1807 Slave Trade Act only outlawed British participation in the trade; it did not free anyone already enslaved. Wilberforce and the Clapham Sect continued for another 26 years for full emancipation. The Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 freed about 800,000 people in the British Caribbean; the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron suppressed the trans-Atlantic trade through the 1860s. Wilberforce is buried in Westminster Abbey near his friend William Pitt the Younger.

question: On May 29 1913, the Ballets Russes premiered a new work at the brand-new Theatre des Champs-Elysees in Paris: Igor Stravinsky's Le Sacre du Printemps (The Rite of Spring), choreographed by Vaslav Nijinsky. The plot was a pagan Russian ritual culminating in a chosen maiden dancing herself to death. The music's hammering dissonances and irregular rhythms, paired with Nijinsky's deliberately ugly turned-in choreography, produced one of the most famous public reactions in concert history. What happened in the auditorium during the performance?
answer: The audience rioted — fistfights broke out, police were called, the music was barely audible
choices: The audience rioted — fistfights broke out, police were called, the music was barely audible
The audience walked out en masse — leaving the theater nearly empty by the second tableau
The audience laughed continuously — the orchestra reportedly stopped twice from embarrassment
The audience refused to applaud — sat in silence so prolonged that Stravinsky fled the building
context: Eyewitnesses described a melee in the aisles within minutes of the curtain rising. Stravinsky himself left his seat in fury and went backstage where Nijinsky was shouting numbers to the dancers because they could not hear the orchestra. The riot made Stravinsky famous overnight. Within a year the music was being performed as a concert piece without ballet to enthusiastic audiences. The Rite became the most influential single score of 20th-century classical music — Pierre Boulez called it the moment musical modernity began.

question: Marie Sklodowska Curie, working in a converted shed in Paris with her husband Pierre, processed tons of pitchblende ore from Bohemian uranium mines to isolate two new radioactive elements they had identified spectroscopically in 1898. The first element they named for her native Poland. The second they named for the property they had themselves discovered — a word she coined to describe the spontaneous emission of energy from these atoms. What second element did the Curies isolate and name in 1898?
answer: Radium — named from the Latin radius for 'ray'
choices: Radium — named from the Latin radius for 'ray'
Actinium — named from the Greek aktis for 'beam'
Thorium — named for the Norse god Thor
Francium — named for her adopted country France
context: Marie isolated about one decigram of pure radium chloride in 1902 — from roughly a ton of pitchblende. She and Pierre won the 1903 Nobel in Physics with Henri Becquerel; Pierre was killed by a horse-drawn wagon in 1906. Marie won a second Nobel, in Chemistry, in 1911 — the first person ever to win in two sciences. Her notebooks remain so radioactive they are stored in lead-lined boxes and handled in protective clothing. She died of aplastic anemia in 1934 from cumulative radiation exposure.

question: On November 24 1859, John Murray's London bookshop released Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species. Darwin had delayed publication for more than two decades since his Galapagos voyage of 1835, refining his theory of evolution by natural selection in private and anxiously corresponding with friends about how to present it. A 1858 letter from Alfred Russel Wallace describing essentially the same theory finally forced Darwin's hand. The first print run sold out on the publication day. How many copies did that first edition contain?
answer: 1,250 copies — sold out to booksellers on the first day
choices: 1,250 copies — sold out to booksellers on the first day
Roughly 5,000 copies — gone within the first week of release
12,000 copies — Murray had anticipated controversy and printed heavily
Only about 250 copies — printed as a private subscription edition for naturalists
context: Murray initially proposed 500 copies; Darwin pushed for 1,250. All went to booksellers on November 22 1859 (subscribers' day, two days before the official publication date). A second edition of 3,000 followed quickly. Origin has remained continuously in print ever since. Darwin had Alfred Russel Wallace's letter from the Malay archipelago in 1858; the two men's joint paper was presented at the Linnean Society in July 1858 with neither author present. Wallace had identified the same mechanism Darwin had worked on for 20 years.

question: Filippo Brunelleschi laid his last brick on the dome of Florence's cathedral, Santa Maria del Fiore, in 1436 — after 16 years of construction. The roughly four million bricks were laid in a herringbone pattern that locked each course in place; no centering scaffold was built from below because the opening was too vast to span. The dome stands roughly 142 feet across at its inner diameter. Nearly 600 years later, what record does Brunelleschi's dome still hold today?
answer: It remains the largest masonry dome ever built — no later structure has matched the span without steel reinforcement or modern concrete
choices: It remains the largest masonry dome ever built — no later structure has matched the span without steel reinforcement or modern concrete
It remains the tallest dome in Italy — Saint Peter's dome in Rome is wider but slightly lower
It remains the only dome in Europe constructed entirely without iron tie-rings — the herringbone substituted for metal
It remains the most-visited cathedral in continental Europe — averaging more annual visitors than Saint Peter's
context: Santa Maria del Fiore's dome is roughly 142 ft inner diameter, 376 ft to the lantern peak. Saint Peter's dome (Michelangelo + della Porta, 1593) is slightly larger by some measures but used iron chains for tension reinforcement. Hagia Sophia's dome (537) is older but smaller in span. Brunelleschi's solution — double shell, herringbone brick courses, gradual self-supporting taper — was an engineering problem nobody had solved since the Roman Pantheon (118-128 AD) and the formula for Roman concrete had been lost for 1,000 years.

question: Joan of Arc, the illiterate peasant girl from Domremy who claimed visions of saints, led French royal armies to lift the English siege of Orleans in May 1429 and crowned Charles VII at Reims that July. Captured by Burgundians in 1430 and sold to the English, she was tried at Rouen for heresy and cross-dressing. On May 30 1431 she was burned at the stake in the Old Market Square. How old was Joan when she died?
answer: Nineteen — she was about 13 when she said the visions began
choices: Nineteen — she was about 13 when she said the visions began
Twenty-three — she had been campaigning for several years before capture
Seventeen — captured in her first year of military command
Twenty-six — only the last three years of her life were public
context: Joan was born in Domremy around January 1412 and died May 30 1431 — aged 19. Her ashes were thrown in the Seine to prevent relic-collecting. A retrial under Pope Callixtus III in 1455-56 declared her innocent. She was canonized in 1920 — almost 500 years later. Mark Twain spent twelve years researching his historical novel about her, published 1896, which he considered his best book.

question: On August 24 410 AD, after a three-day siege, the Visigoth army of Alaric I sacked Rome — the first time the city had fallen to a foreign enemy in nearly 800 years. The shock reverberated across the Mediterranean world; pagan critics blamed the disaster on Rome's recent abandonment of the old gods for Christianity. In Hippo Regius in North Africa, Bishop Augustine — already author of the Confessions — began writing a massive theological reply that would take him 13 years to finish (completed 426 AD). What book did Augustine write in response to the sack of Rome?
answer: The City of God (De Civitate Dei)
choices: The City of God (De Civitate Dei)
On Christian Doctrine (De Doctrina Christiana)
Against the Pagans (Contra Paganos)
On the Trinity (De Trinitate)
context: The City of God argues there are two cities — the earthly city built on self-love and the City of God built on love of God — and that the Christian's true loyalty is to the latter, which no Visigoth can sack. The book runs to 22 books and is one of the foundational texts of Western political and theological thought. Augustine died in 430 AD as Vandals besieged Hippo. His Confessions and City of God shaped medieval Christian thought; in the Reformation both Luther (an Augustinian friar) and Calvin built on Augustinian themes.

question: On May 29 1453, after a 53-day siege, Sultan Mehmed II's Ottoman army entered Constantinople through breaches in the Theodosian land walls — the triple-layered fortifications that had protected the Byzantine capital since 408 AD. The 21-year-old sultan rode through the Hagia Sophia and ordered its conversion to a mosque. Emperor Constantine XI was killed in the fighting, ending the Roman Empire 1,480 years after its founding. The Ottoman victory was made possible by one specific technological innovation that finally broke walls that had repelled every previous siege. What did Mehmed deploy?
answer: Massive bronze cannon — including the Basilica, 27 feet long, throwing 1,200-pound stone balls
choices: Massive bronze cannon — including the Basilica, 27 feet long, throwing 1,200-pound stone balls
Greek fire delivered by tunneling — sappers brought the incendiary up under the wall foundations
Naval blockade with chained galleys — starvation finally forced the city to open the gates
Mining of the seawall — Mehmed's engineers undermined the Golden Horn defenses overnight
context: The Basilica cannon was cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban — who had first offered his services to the Byzantines but they could not afford his fees. The gun fired about seven times a day; reloading took two hours; it had to be cooled with oil between shots. Conventional fortified walls were now obsolete. The fall of Constantinople is often cited as the close of the Middle Ages. Greek scholars fleeing west with Byzantine manuscripts fed the Italian Renaissance; the Ottoman blockade of land routes to Asia spurred the European search for sea routes east.

question: James Watt was a Glasgow instrument-maker repairing a Newcomen steam engine for the university in 1763 when he saw that the engine wasted enormous amounts of heat — each piston stroke had to alternately heat and cool the entire cylinder. The fix came to him during a Sunday walk on Glasgow Green in 1765: keep the working cylinder permanently hot, and condense the steam in a separate chamber. He patented the design in 1769. Compared to the Newcomen engine it replaced, how much fuel did Watt's separate-condenser engine use per unit of work?
answer: Roughly one-quarter as much fuel — a fourfold improvement in efficiency
choices: Roughly one-quarter as much fuel — a fourfold improvement in efficiency
Roughly half as much fuel — about a twofold improvement
Roughly one-tenth as much fuel — a tenfold improvement
About the same fuel — but with faster cycling and more reliable operation
context: The roughly 75% reduction in coal consumption made steam engines economically viable far from coalfields — pumping mines, driving mills, eventually powering ships and locomotives. Watt partnered with Birmingham manufacturer Matthew Boulton from 1775; the Boulton & Watt firm dominated steam engine manufacture for a generation. The unit of power 'watt' (and the kilowatt) is named for him. The Industrial Revolution is sometimes dated from Watt's separate condenser; some economic historians prefer Stephenson's Rocket (1829) or Bessemer steel (1856) as the inflection point.

question: Aristotle (384-322 BC), the most influential philosopher of the ancient world, founded the Lyceum at Athens around 335 BC. Two decades earlier, around 343 BC, King Philip II of Macedon had hired him for a specific tutoring assignment that would shape world history. Aristotle taught the future king for roughly three years at Mieza in Macedon, covering literature, ethics, politics, medicine, and philosophy. Who was Aristotle's most famous student?
answer: Alexander the Great
choices: Alexander the Great
Ptolemy I Soter, founder of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty
Cleomenes III of Sparta
Demetrius of Phalerum
context: Aristotle was about 41 when he took the post; Alexander was 13. The tutoring was at the Temple of the Nymphs at Mieza. Alexander reportedly slept with a copy of Homer's Iliad and a dagger under his pillow on his campaigns. He sent biological specimens back to Aristotle from Asia, which Aristotle used in his zoological works. Alexander succeeded his father at 20 (336 BC), conquered the Persian Empire over the next decade, and died in Babylon at 32 in 323 BC. Aristotle died the following year.

question: In 399 BC the Athenian assembly tried Socrates on charges of impiety and corrupting the youth. He defended himself in the speech later written down by his student Plato as the Apology, was convicted by a narrow majority, and was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock. He had thirty days between sentence and execution because of a religious festival. His students, including the wealthy Crito, had bribes ready and an escape boat waiting. Why did Socrates refuse to escape, according to Plato's Crito?
answer: He had lived under Athens's laws his entire life — to flee them when they turned against him would be to break the implicit contract that had made his life possible
choices: He had lived under Athens's laws his entire life — to flee them when they turned against him would be to break the implicit contract that had made his life possible
He believed the gods had ordained his execution — to escape would be to commit a worse impiety than the one he was charged with
He was 70 and ill — old age would soon kill him anyway and a public death would shame his accusers
His wife Xanthippe forbade flight — she would not raise their children in exile and dishonor
context: The Crito is one of the foundational documents of Western political philosophy on the duty of obedience to law. Socrates argues that if a citizen has lived under the city's protection for 70 years and could have left at any time, the citizen has tacitly consented to the laws. To break them when they harm him is to corrupt the laws themselves. He drank the hemlock and died on the day the religious envoy returned from Delos.

question: In summer 1665 plague closed Cambridge University. Twenty-two-year-old Isaac Newton went home to his mother's farm at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire. Over the following 18 months — what he later called his annus mirabilis — he invented the calculus, worked out the laws of motion, formulated the law of universal gravitation, and decomposed white light with a prism into its component colors. He published none of this for two decades. Newton told the apple-falling-on-his-head story (or rather, an apple-falling-near-him story) to William Stukeley in 1726, the year before his death. Where did Newton say he sat when the apple fell?
answer: Under an apple tree in his mother's orchard at Woolsthorpe
choices: Under an apple tree in his mother's orchard at Woolsthorpe
On a wooden bench outside his Trinity College rooms
In a chair beside the laboratory window at Woolsthorpe
Beneath an old oak tree on the Cambridge college backs
context: Newton told Stukeley (Memoirs of Sir Isaac Newton's Life, 1752): 'It was occasion'd by the fall of an apple, as he sat in a contemplative mood... why should that apple always descend perpendicularly to the ground.' A direct descendant of the original tree still grows at Woolsthorpe Manor; cuttings have been planted at Trinity College, Cambridge and at NASA centers. The Principia, which laid out the system, did not appear until 1687 — 20 years after the apple year.

question: On December 17 1903 at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first sustained powered controlled flights of a heavier-than-air machine. They made four flights that morning, taking turns. Orville went first because they had flipped a coin. The first flight covered 120 feet in 12 seconds; the fourth, by Wilbur, covered 852 feet in 59 seconds. Almost no newspaper reported the event correctly for years. About how long did Orville's first flight last?
answer: Roughly 12 seconds — covering about 120 feet of ground
choices: Roughly 12 seconds — covering about 120 feet of ground
Roughly two minutes — covering nearly half a mile
Roughly 30 seconds — covering about 300 feet down the dune
Roughly 5 seconds — covering only about 30 feet of skipping motion
context: The Wright Flyer was photographed at the moment of liftoff by John T. Daniels of the local lifesaving station — the most famous aviation photograph ever taken. The Wrights brought the original 1903 Flyer home and stored it in a shed; a 1913 flood damaged it. Repaired, it hung in the Science Museum in London from 1928 to 1948 as a protest over Smithsonian credit-giving to Samuel Langley's failed flyer. It now hangs in the National Air and Space Museum in Washington DC.

question: Johannes Kepler worked as Tycho Brahe's assistant in Prague from 1600 until Tycho's death in 1601. He inherited Tycho's voluminous and highly accurate planetary observation data — particularly for Mars. After eight years of laborious calculation, Kepler published Astronomia Nova in 1609, announcing that Mars's orbit was not a perfect circle as ancient astronomers had insisted for 2,000 years. He had identified the true shape. The discovery is now known as Kepler's first law of planetary motion. What is the orbital shape Kepler proved?
answer: An ellipse — with the Sun at one of the two foci
choices: An ellipse — with the Sun at one of the two foci
A circle — but offset so the Sun was not at its center
A spiral — gradually approaching and receding from the Sun
A perfect circle — Kepler confirmed the ancient view with new precision
context: Kepler had to abandon a 2,000-year-old assumption — that celestial motion must be circular as the perfect shape — to fit Tycho's data. Mars's orbit is elliptical (eccentricity 0.093). The second law (equal areas in equal times) appeared in the same 1609 book; the third law (period squared proportional to semi-major axis cubed) followed in 1619 in Harmonices Mundi. Newton's Principia (1687) would derive all three laws from his law of universal gravitation, completing what Kepler had begun a century before.

question: On August 10 1519 the Portuguese navigator Ferdinand Magellan left Seville with five ships and 270 men, sailing for the Spanish crown in search of a westward route to the Spice Islands. Three years later, on September 6 1522, one ship and 18 survivors returned — the first circumnavigation of the globe. Magellan himself never completed the voyage. What happened to him?
answer: Killed in a skirmish with islanders on Mactan in the Philippines, April 27 1521
choices: Killed in a skirmish with islanders on Mactan in the Philippines, April 27 1521
Died of scurvy in mid-Pacific, March 1521, halfway through the crossing
Killed by mutineers in Patagonia, April 1520, after he ordered an execution
Drowned in a storm rounding the Cape of Good Hope on the return voyage, 1522
context: Magellan led 60 men ashore on Mactan to enforce Spanish-Christian authority over a local chief named Lapu-Lapu. The Spaniards in armor were overwhelmed in the surf; Magellan was killed by a bamboo spear and Lapu-Lapu's warriors. The expedition continued under Juan Sebastian Elcano, who brought the Victoria back to Seville in 1522. Antonio Pigafetta's diary is the chief surviving account. The strait at the southern tip of South America still bears Magellan's name.

question: On October 19 1781, after a three-week siege, the British army of General Charles Cornwallis surrendered to combined American and French forces at Yorktown, Virginia. The defeat was so total that Lord North, on hearing the news in London, walked back and forth crying 'O God! It is all over.' Tradition holds that as the defeated British troops marched out to lay down their arms, the British military band played a specific tune — symbolic of the historical reversal taking place. What did the British band reportedly play?
answer: 'The World Turned Upside Down' — a 17th-century English ballad
choices: 'The World Turned Upside Down' — a 17th-century English ballad
'God Save the King' — out of defiance toward the new republic
'Yankee Doodle' — at the demand of the American commanders
'A Soldier's Dirge' — a slow funeral march of the regimental tradition
context: The story comes from American officer Henry Dearborn's journal and other 19th-century memoirs; some modern historians doubt the band-tune detail. Cornwallis pleaded illness and sent General Charles O'Hara to make the surrender. Washington refused to receive a deputy and directed O'Hara to surrender to Benjamin Lincoln (whom the British had humiliated at Charleston the previous year). The Treaty of Paris ending the war was signed September 3 1783. Cornwallis went on to a distinguished career governing Ireland and India.

question: On November 19 1863, at the dedication of the new national cemetery on the Gettysburg battlefield, the day's announced featured orator was Edward Everett, the most famous public speaker of the age. Everett delivered a two-hour Greek-style oration the audience expected to be the main event. Abraham Lincoln rose afterward and spoke for about two minutes from a single sheet of paper. The press response the next day was mixed — even Lincoln thought the address had failed. Today it is regarded as one of the finest speeches in English. About how many words did Lincoln's address contain?
answer: Approximately 272 words
choices: Approximately 272 words
Approximately 850 words
Approximately 1,400 words
Approximately 2,100 words
context: Everett wrote to Lincoln the next day: 'I should be glad if I could flatter myself that I came as near to the central idea of the occasion in two hours as you did in two minutes.' Five manuscript copies in Lincoln's hand survive, with slight word-by-word variations. The address opens 'Four score and seven years ago' (87 years before 1863 places the founding at 1776, the Declaration, not 1787, the Constitution — a deliberate choice). Lincoln's text reframed the war from preserving the Union to fulfilling the Declaration's 'all men are created equal.'

question: On March 21 1861, three weeks before Fort Sumter, Confederate Vice President Alexander Stephens addressed a large crowd at the Athenaeum in Savannah, Georgia. His speech laid out what he said was the founding principle of the new Confederate government — the principle he said distinguished it from the federal Constitution. The text was published in the Savannah Republican and quickly known across both North and South as the Cornerstone Speech. The speech is essential to understanding what the Civil War was actually fought over, because Confederate leaders themselves said it explicitly. What did Stephens identify as the Confederacy's cornerstone?
answer: Slavery — the new government rested on 'the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man'
choices: Slavery — the new government rested on 'the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man'
States' rights — the principle that each state retained ultimate authority against federal overreach
Free trade — the Northern protective tariff was the central injustice the South was leaving over
Christian government — the new republic was explicitly a Christian commonwealth unlike the secular North
context: Stephens, quoted directly: 'Our new government is founded upon exactly the opposite idea [from the Declaration]; its foundations are laid, its cornerstone rests, upon the great truth that the negro is not equal to the white man; that slavery — subordination to the superior race — is his natural and normal condition. This, our new government, is the first, in the history of the world, based upon this great physical, philosophical, and moral truth.' The four Confederate states that issued formal 'declarations of causes of secession' — South Carolina, Mississippi, Georgia, Texas — each named slavery as the central reason. The Cornerstone Speech is the standing rebuttal to all later 'it was about tariffs and states' rights' revisionism.

question: On May 14 1804 Captains Meriwether Lewis and William Clark left St. Charles, Missouri with about 33 men and the teenage Shoshone interpreter Sacagawea — the Corps of Discovery commissioned by Thomas Jefferson to explore the lands the United States had just bought from France through the Louisiana Purchase. They returned to St. Louis on September 23 1806 — two years and four months later. Only one man died on the expedition (probably of a ruptured appendix). About how many miles did the Corps cover on its round trip?
answer: About 8,000 miles — from St. Louis to the Pacific and back
choices: About 8,000 miles — from St. Louis to the Pacific and back
About 3,200 miles — only the outbound westward leg was documented in detail
About 15,000 miles — including extensive northern and southern reconnaissance loops
About 1,200 miles — much of the trip was by Missouri River rather than overland
context: Lewis and Clark followed the Missouri to its source, crossed the Continental Divide at Lemhi Pass, descended the Clearwater-Snake-Columbia, and reached the Pacific near Astoria, Oregon in November 1805. Sacagawea (about 16 when she joined, carrying her infant son Jean Baptiste 'Pomp') was crucial to peaceful contacts with western Indians. Lewis became governor of Louisiana Territory but died in 1809 — either suicide or murder, still disputed. Clark served as superintendent of Indian affairs and lived until 1838.

question: On July 20 1969, at 20:17 UTC, the lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility on the Moon. Six hours later, at 02:56 UTC on July 21, Neil Armstrong descended the ladder and stepped onto the lunar surface, becoming the first human being on another world. His first words were transmitted live to roughly 600 million viewers on Earth. Armstrong later said he had meant to include a one-letter word that radio static dropped. With the lost letter restored, what did he intend to say?
answer: 'That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind'
choices: 'That's one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind'
'That's one small step for our nation, one giant leap for humanity'
'One small step from this lander, one giant leap for the human race'
'A small step for me here, a giant leap for all the world'
context: Armstrong said he intended 'a man' (one man, the indefinite article) — the version without 'a' makes 'man' and 'mankind' synonymous and breaks the contrast. Acoustic analysis of the original radio tape is inconclusive; Armstrong insisted he had said 'a man' but couldn't hear it in the playback. The Eagle was on the lunar surface for 21 hours; Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked outside for about 2.5 hours. Michael Collins orbited above in Columbia. They returned safely to Earth on July 24 1969.

question: In December 1783, after the Treaty of Paris ended the Revolutionary War, General George Washington traveled to Annapolis, Maryland where Congress was sitting. On December 23 he appeared before the assembled members, delivered a brief speech, formally handed over his commission as commander-in-chief, and went home to Mount Vernon to spend Christmas with Martha. When the act was reported in London, King George III made a famous prediction about Washington's place in history. What did George III reportedly say?
answer: That if Washington really resigned and went home, he would be 'the greatest man in the world'
choices: That if Washington really resigned and went home, he would be 'the greatest man in the world'
That Washington could be expected to seize the crown himself within five years
That the new American government would not last more than a decade without a king
That a man who would resign such power must be either a fool or a saint
context: Source: the artist Benjamin West, who served as court painter to George III, told the story to several visitors and the painter John Trumbull recorded it. The act of voluntarily surrendering supreme military power — going home like Cincinnatus from his plow — was without modern precedent. Cromwell had become Lord Protector; Caesar had crossed the Rubicon. Washington went home. He would be called back to the presidency in 1789, then resign that office too after two terms — a precedent that held until 1940 and was enshrined in the 22nd Amendment in 1951.

question: On the evening of April 14 1865 — five days after Robert E. Lee's surrender at Appomattox — President Abraham Lincoln and his wife Mary Todd attended a performance at Ford's Theatre in Washington. Their guests in the presidential box were Major Henry Rathbone and his fiancee Clara Harris. At about 10:15 PM, during a single laugh-line in the play, the actor John Wilkes Booth slipped into the box and shot Lincoln in the back of the head with a derringer. Lincoln died the following morning. What was the title of the play Lincoln was watching?
answer: Our American Cousin — a popular British comedy by Tom Taylor
choices: Our American Cousin — a popular British comedy by Tom Taylor
She Stoops to Conquer — Goldsmith's 18th-century comedy of manners
The Rivals — Sheridan's enduring comedy of crossed lovers
The School for Scandal — Sheridan's drawing-room satire of London society
context: Booth knew the play and chose the moment of the loudest single laugh — Asa Trenchard's line 'you sockdologizing old man-trap!' Lincoln died at 7:22 AM the next morning, April 15 1865, in a boarding house across the street. Booth broke a leg leaping from the box but escaped on horseback. He was tracked to a barn in Virginia and shot dead on April 26. Major Rathbone tried to stop Booth and was stabbed in the arm; he later murdered his wife in 1883 and died in an asylum.

question: George Washington's Farewell Address was published in the American Daily Advertiser of Philadelphia on September 19 1796 — never delivered as a speech. Drafted with help from Hamilton and Madison, the letter announced Washington's refusal to seek a third term and laid out a list of warnings for the young republic. One specific phrase about foreign policy entered American political thought as a foundational warning for the next 150 years. What did Washington warn against?
answer: Entangling alliances — particularly permanent alliances with European powers
choices: Entangling alliances — particularly permanent alliances with European powers
Standing armies in peacetime — which inevitably consume republics from within
Direct election of senators — which would surrender the states' role to popular passion
Public debt — which mortgages future generations to present-day extravagance
context: Washington's actual phrase: 'It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world.' Jefferson refined this in his 1801 inaugural as 'peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations — entangling alliances with none.' The doctrine of avoiding permanent European entanglements held — with arguments over its application — until the U.S. joined NATO in 1949. The Farewell Address also warns against political factionalism and 'the baneful effects of the spirit of party.'

question: On July 5 1852, the abolitionist Frederick Douglass — escaped slave, newspaper editor, the most famous African-American of his age — gave a Fourth of July address (postponed one day) to the Rochester Ladies' Anti-Slavery Society at Corinthian Hall in Rochester, New York. Roughly 600 people attended. The speech is one of the most powerful uses of the holiday's own rhetoric against itself in American history. What question did Douglass put to his audience?
answer: 'What to the slave is the Fourth of July?' — and answered that the day's celebration of liberty was a mockery to the enslaved
choices: 'What to the slave is the Fourth of July?' — and answered that the day's celebration of liberty was a mockery to the enslaved
'When shall America be true?' — and traced the gap between the Declaration's promise and the practice of the slave states
'Who shall break these chains?' — and laid the duty on Christians of every section
'Where is the Founding now?' — and challenged the audience to claim the Founders' real legacy
context: The full opening line: 'What, to the American slave, is your Fourth of July? I answer; a day that reveals to him, more than all other days in the year, the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim.' Douglass had been born into slavery in Maryland around 1818, escaped in 1838, and become one of the most-traveled lecturers in the Anglo-American world. His three autobiographies (1845, 1855, 1881) are landmark American literature. He lived to see emancipation and the 13th-15th Amendments and died in 1895.

question: Through the bitter winter of 1777-78 the Continental Army camped at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania while the British army wintered comfortably in occupied Philadelphia twenty miles away. About 2,500 of Washington's 12,000 men died of disease and exposure. In February 1778 a Prussian officer arrived at camp, recommended by Benjamin Franklin from Paris, speaking no English and demanding to be addressed by an imaginary aristocratic title he had invented. He transformed the surviving Continental troops in two months of relentless drill in the snow. Who was the Prussian drillmaster of Valley Forge?
answer: Baron Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben
choices: Baron Friedrich Wilhelm von Steuben
Baron Johann de Kalb of the Continental line
General Casimir Pulaski of the Polish cavalry
Marquis Marie-Joseph de Lafayette of the French
context: Von Steuben was not actually a baron and his Prussian rank had been only captain — Franklin and Silas Deane embellished his credentials to get him a commission. He drilled the Continental Army from dawn to dusk through March-April 1778, often demonstrating each movement himself with his men. He wrote the army's first standard drill manual ('Blue Book,' 1779). The Continentals who marched out of Valley Forge in June 1778 were essentially a new army; they fought the British at Monmouth Court House on equal terms three weeks later.

question: On October 17 1777, British General John Burgoyne surrendered his entire army of about 5,800 men to American General Horatio Gates at Saratoga, New York, ending a British strategic effort to split off New England by driving south from Canada along the Hudson. The American victory had a specific decisive consequence in European diplomacy. France had been secretly supplying the rebels with arms for over a year; now French foreign minister Vergennes pushed for formal alliance. What did the Saratoga victory directly produce?
answer: The Franco-American Treaty of Alliance, signed February 6 1778 — bringing France openly into the war
choices: The Franco-American Treaty of Alliance, signed February 6 1778 — bringing France openly into the war
The Spanish entry into the war alongside France, mid-1778 — adding the Spanish fleet to the equation
The Dutch declaration of armed neutrality, autumn 1778 — opening Atlantic shipping to the rebels
The Russian armed-neutrality declaration of 1780 — closing the Baltic to British naval supplies
context: France's open entry transformed the war from a colonial rebellion into a world conflict — fought from the West Indies to India. Spain joined in 1779; the Netherlands in 1780. By 1781 the British fleet was stretched too thin to relieve Cornwallis at Yorktown, where the French Navy under de Grasse and a French expeditionary force under Rochambeau combined with Washington's army to end the war. Saratoga is conventionally called the war's turning point for this reason. Burgoyne's army was paroled rather than imprisoned; Congress later repudiated the parole terms.

question: On September 17 1862, in cornfields and lanes outside Sharpsburg, Maryland, Robert E. Lee's invading Army of Northern Virginia fought George B. McClellan's Army of the Potomac to a tactical draw — but Lee was forced to withdraw south of the Potomac, ending his first invasion of the North. Five days later, with a Union victory finally in hand, Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation. Antietam holds a specific terrible distinction in American military history. What is it?
answer: It remains the bloodiest single day in American history — about 23,000 total casualties
choices: It remains the bloodiest single day in American history — about 23,000 total casualties
It was the largest battle Lee ever fought — about 100,000 men engaged on each side
It was the longest single battle of the Civil War — fighting continued for three full days
It was the only battle of the war fought entirely on a Sunday — Lee took advantage of Union observance
context: Roughly 3,650 killed outright, 17,000 wounded, 2,000 missing — a combined total above 23,000 in one day. The Confederate field army numbered about 38,000; the Union about 87,000 (only some actually engaged). Lee fought McClellan to a draw against odds that should have destroyed the Confederate army. McClellan failed to pursue. The Antietam battlefield is among the best-preserved Civil War sites; Bloody Lane and Burnside Bridge remain visible. The battle's outcome gave Lincoln the Union 'victory' he needed to issue the Emancipation Proclamation September 22 1862.

question: On the morning of December 7 1941, six Japanese carriers launched 353 aircraft against the U.S. Pacific Fleet at anchor in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. The two-wave attack sank or damaged eight battleships and three cruisers, destroyed 188 American aircraft, and killed about 2,400 sailors, soldiers, and civilians. One specific class of American warship escaped the attack entirely — they were all out at sea on December 7 — and would prove decisive in the Pacific war within six months. What ships were not at Pearl Harbor that morning?
answer: The U.S. Pacific Fleet's three aircraft carriers — Enterprise, Lexington, Saratoga
choices: The U.S. Pacific Fleet's three aircraft carriers — Enterprise, Lexington, Saratoga
The Pacific Fleet's heavy cruiser force — out on a training exercise off Wake Island
The Pacific Fleet's submarine force — already deployed forward to Manila Bay
The Pacific Fleet's destroyer screen — escorting transports to the West Coast
context: Enterprise was ferrying aircraft to Wake Island; Lexington was bound for Midway; Saratoga was on the West Coast. The Japanese attack destroyed obsolete battleships and missed the carriers, which had completely replaced battleships as the decisive naval weapon by mid-1942. Within six months — at Coral Sea (May 1942) and Midway (June 1942) — American carrier-based aircraft would destroy four of the six carriers that hit Pearl Harbor. Admiral Yamamoto had warned the cabinet a year before Pearl Harbor: 'I shall run wild for six months — after that, I have no expectation of success.'

question: On June 4 1942, six months and three days after Pearl Harbor, U.S. Navy carrier aircraft destroyed four Japanese fleet carriers off Midway Atoll in a single afternoon — the decisive engagement of the Pacific War. The Japanese commander of the entire Combined Fleet operation, Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, had personally warned the Japanese cabinet before Pearl Harbor about exactly this risk. What had Yamamoto told the Japanese government in 1940-41?
answer: That he could run wild in the Pacific for six to twelve months but had no expectation of success against America after that
choices: That he could run wild in the Pacific for six to twelve months but had no expectation of success against America after that
That war with America was militarily winnable but only if Hawaii were occupied within thirty days
That a single decisive battle could force American surrender before America's industrial base mobilized
That Japan should preempt by destroying the Panama Canal before any war with the U.S. began
context: Yamamoto's exact statement to Prime Minister Konoye in autumn 1940: 'In the first six to twelve months of a war with the United States and Great Britain I will run wild and win victory upon victory. But then, if the war continues after that, I have no expectation of success.' The six-month mark from Pearl Harbor was June 7 1942 — three days after Midway. Yamamoto was killed April 18 1943 when American P-38s, alerted by code-breaking, ambushed his transport plane over Bougainville.

question: On October 14 1962, a U-2 reconnaissance flight over western Cuba photographed Soviet medium-range ballistic missiles being assembled at San Cristobal — capable of reaching Washington with nuclear warheads in five minutes. For thirteen days the Kennedy administration weighed responses. The Joint Chiefs of Staff pushed for immediate air strikes followed by invasion. Kennedy chose a different option that left Khrushchev a way to back down without humiliation. What did Kennedy announce in his televised speech of October 22 1962?
answer: A naval quarantine of Cuba — to block further Soviet shipments while leaving room for negotiation
choices: A naval quarantine of Cuba — to block further Soviet shipments while leaving room for negotiation
A bombing campaign against the Soviet missile sites — to begin within 48 hours unless dismantled
An immediate full ground invasion of Cuba — with the goal of removing the Castro government within a week
A unilateral withdrawal of all U.S. forces from Turkey — as a public offer to defuse the standoff
context: A blockade in international law is an act of war; Kennedy used the word 'quarantine' for political-legal reasons. Khrushchev agreed October 28 to remove the Cuban missiles in exchange for a public U.S. pledge not to invade Cuba and a private agreement to remove American Jupiter missiles from Turkey within six months. The world had come the closest it has ever come to nuclear war. Robert Kennedy's memoir Thirteen Days (1969) and the declassified ExCom tapes are the primary sources. The hotline between the White House and Kremlin was established in 1963 as a direct result.

question: On August 28 1963 about 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial for the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. Martin Luther King Jr. was the closing speaker. He had a prepared text that built toward a peroration about 'going back to our homes' — but partway through, the gospel singer Mahalia Jackson, standing behind him on the platform, called out 'Tell them about the dream, Martin!' King set his prepared text aside and improvised the final third of the speech. What recurring four-word phrase did King use across the improvised closing?
answer: 'I have a dream'
choices: 'I have a dream'
'Let freedom ring out'
'We shall overcome'
'I have been there'
context: King had used variants of the 'I have a dream' formula in earlier speeches that summer in Detroit and elsewhere. The Lincoln Memorial version on national television made it iconic. The famous closing — 'Free at last, free at last, thank God almighty, we are free at last' — quotes the Negro spiritual. King was 34. The speech is now widely regarded as one of the greatest American orations alongside the Gettysburg Address. Eight months later President Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, ending Jim Crow segregation in public accommodations.

question: On April 18 1942, four months after Pearl Harbor, sixteen B-25 medium bombers under Lieutenant Colonel James Doolittle took off from the deck of the U.S. carrier Hornet, 650 miles off the Japanese coast, and conducted the first American air raid on Japan. The damage to military targets was modest; the strategic effect was enormous, forcing the Japanese to commit four carriers to defending the home islands and partly motivating Yamamoto's drive to fight a decisive battle at Midway. The takeoff itself was unprecedented in military aviation. Why?
answer: B-25 medium bombers had never before taken off from an aircraft carrier — the carrier deck was too short for normal procedure
choices: B-25 medium bombers had never before taken off from an aircraft carrier — the carrier deck was too short for normal procedure
The bombers carried no fighter escort — Doolittle ordered radio silence the entire 650 miles inbound
All sixteen pilots had volunteered knowing there was no plan for them to return to the carrier — they had to fly on to China
All sixteen — B-25s had never carrier-launched before AND the entire raid was one-way without return option
context: B-25s normally needed 1,200 feet for takeoff; Doolittle's planes had about 470 feet from spot to deck-edge on Hornet. Doolittle had spent weeks training with shortened-runway takeoffs in Florida. The raiders bombed Tokyo, Yokohama, and Nagoya, then flew on toward Free China hoping for friendly airfields; most crashed or were force-landed. Of 80 raiders, 64 eventually returned via China; 8 were captured by Japanese forces (3 executed, 1 died of beatings); 3 died in crash landings. Doolittle expected court-martial for losing all 16 aircraft; he received the Medal of Honor and promotion to Brigadier General.

question: On February 23 1945, on the fifth day of the U.S. Marine Corps assault on the Japanese-held volcanic island of Iwo Jima, a 40-man patrol from the 28th Marines fought their way to the summit of Mount Suribachi at the island's southern tip. They raised a small American flag at about 10:30 AM. A few hours later a second, larger flag replaced the first; the second flag-raising was photographed by Associated Press photographer Joe Rosenthal in what became the most reproduced photograph in American history. Three of the six Marines in Rosenthal's photograph were dead before the battle of Iwo Jima ended. About how long did the fighting on Iwo Jima continue after the flag-raising?
answer: About one more month — the island was declared secured March 26 1945
choices: About one more month — the island was declared secured March 26 1945
About one more week — organized resistance collapsed within days of the flag
About three more months — Japanese garrisons fought into the rainy season
