context: The Haitorei (Sword Abolishment Edict) of March 28 1876 banned the carrying of swords in public except by serving military and police. The samurai class — about 5-7% of Japan's population — lost their hereditary stipends in 1873-76 (commuted to government bonds), their right to bear arms (1876), and their distinctive topknot hairstyle (1871 cropping decree). The Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 led by Saigo Takamori was the last samurai revolt against the modernization process; defeated by the new conscript Imperial Japanese Army. The samurai class formally dissolved by 1885. The Meiji modernization was so fast that Japan defeated China in 1894-95 and Russia in 1904-05 within a generation of starting it.

question: On July 8 1853, U.S. Commodore Matthew C. Perry sailed four U.S. Navy steam-and-sail warships into Edo Bay and demanded that the Tokugawa Shogunate end the 220-year policy of national isolation (sakoku) that had restricted foreign contact to a Dutch trading post at Dejima in Nagasaki harbor. Perry presented a letter from President Millard Fillmore demanding relations. He returned February 1854 with nine warships; Japan signed the Convention of Kanagawa opening two ports. What did Perry's steam warships become known as in Japanese?
answer: Kurofune — 'Black Ships' — for their iron-coated black hulls and the dark coal smoke from their steam engines
choices: Kurofune — 'Black Ships' — for their iron-coated black hulls and the dark coal smoke from their steam engines
Tetsubune — 'Iron Ships' — for the European armor plating that Japanese observers noted with alarm
Tsumetai-fune — 'Cold Ships' — for the Western reserve of Perry's officers in their dealings with Japanese hosts
Yokai-fune — 'Demon Ships' — for the supernatural appearance to coastal observers who had never seen steamships
context: The Black Ships (Kurofune) of 1853-54 shocked Japan into recognizing the gap between Tokugawa technology and the industrialized West. The Tokugawa system collapsed within 15 years; the Meiji Restoration of 1868 began the rapid modernization that produced an industrialized Japan within a generation. Perry's expedition is one of the textbook examples of asymmetric coercive diplomacy. Japan's response — the choice of selective modernization rather than colonial submission — is the textbook contrast with China's contemporary failure to reform under similar Western pressure (the Opium Wars 1839-42 and 1856-60). The Black Ships' arrival is commemorated annually at Shimoda in Shizuoka Prefecture.

question: Ibn Sina (Avicenna, about 980-1037), born in Bukhara in present-day Uzbekistan, was the most influential medical author of the Islamic Golden Age and one of the dominant figures of medieval medicine in both the Islamic and Christian worlds. His five-volume medical encyclopedia, completed about 1025, became the standard medical textbook in Latin translation across Western Europe. For approximately how long did Ibn Sina's Canon serve as the basic medical textbook in European universities?
answer: About 600 years — used at universities such as Bologna, Montpellier, and Padua from the 12th century through the 17th century
choices: About 600 years — used at universities such as Bologna, Montpellier, and Padua from the 12th century through the 17th century
About 100 years — superseded by the 13th-century Latin translations of Galen
About 1,500 years — still recommended as a working textbook at Cairo's al-Azhar through the 1800s
About 50 years — quickly displaced by 12th-century anatomical work of Salerno
context: Ibn Sina's Canon (al-Qanun fi al-Tibb) was translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona around 1175 and remained a basic medical text at European universities through the 17th century. He drew on Greek (Galen, Hippocrates), Persian, and Indian medical traditions and added his own substantial clinical observations. He is also a major philosopher — his metaphysical works influenced both Aquinas (Christian) and Maimonides (Jewish). The conventional Western teleological story that ancient learning was rediscovered at the Italian Renaissance ignores the Islamic and Jewish chain of transmission from late antiquity through Iberian (Toledo) and Sicilian translators who brought texts into Latin Europe across the 12th-13th centuries.

question: Ibn Battuta (1304-1377) of Tangier in modern Morocco set out in 1325 at age 21 on what was intended as a one-year pilgrimage to Mecca. He returned home about 24 years later, having traveled across most of the known Islamic world plus China, Sumatra, and parts of West Africa. His travels covered an estimated distance unprecedented in pre-modern times for an individual traveler. About how many miles did Ibn Battuta cover across his travel career?
answer: About 75,000 miles — across about 44 modern countries from Tangier to China
choices: About 75,000 miles — across about 44 modern countries from Tangier to China
About 5,000 miles — primarily within the Islamic Mediterranean from Morocco to Egypt
About 250,000 miles — comparable to a modern long-haul truck driver across decades
About 1,200 miles — limited to a single Hajj from Tangier to Mecca and back
context: Ibn Battuta's Rihla ('The Travels'), dictated to scholar Ibn Juzayy in Fez after his return, is one of the great works of pre-modern travel literature. He visited Mecca multiple times, lived in Delhi (serving the Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq), traveled to Sumatra, China, and West Africa (including Mali). Some of the more remote sections (especially China and East Africa) are debated for first-hand accuracy. Approximately 75,000 miles is the standard scholarly estimate; the actual distance might be somewhat less if some claimed journeys were drawn from secondary sources. By contrast Marco Polo had covered about 15,000 miles over 24 years (1271-1295).

question: Ibn Khaldun (1332-1406), born in Tunis to a family of Andalusian Muslim refugees from the Christian reconquest of Iberia, served as a senior administrator and judge across the courts of the western Islamic world. In 1377, in a Berber fortress in present-day Algeria where he had retired briefly, he wrote the Muqaddimah ('Introduction') to his planned history of the Berbers and Arabs. The Muqaddimah developed a systematic theory of history, civilization, and the rise and fall of states. What is the central thesis of the Muqaddimah?
answer: Civilizations rise from tribal solidarity (asabiyya), reach urban refinement, then decline as that solidarity erodes — a roughly four-generation cycle
choices: Civilizations rise from tribal solidarity (asabiyya), reach urban refinement, then decline as that solidarity erodes — a roughly four-generation cycle
All historical events fulfill divine providence — the patterns of rise and fall reveal God's hidden plan
Climate determines civilization — Mediterranean cultures dominate because of their geographical and meteorological advantages
Trade routes determine history — civilizations rise and fall as the geography of commercial exchange shifts beneath them
context: Ibn Khaldun's analysis of asabiyya ('group feeling' or 'tribal solidarity') as the underlying engine of state formation, combined with his observations of how urban refinement erodes the original asabiyya across about four generations, anticipates substantial themes in modern sociology and political economy. The Muqaddimah is widely cited as the earliest systematic philosophy of history, anticipating Vico (1725), Hegel (1820s), Toynbee (1934-61). Arnold Toynbee called it 'undoubtedly the greatest work of its kind that has ever yet been created by any mind in any time or place.' Ibn Khaldun also developed economic theory including the principle that low tax rates can produce higher revenue than high rates (a thesis later associated with Arthur Laffer).

question: The Ottoman Empire from roughly the late 14th through the 17th century operated a distinctive elite recruitment system called the devshirme ('blood tax' or 'collection') — periodic levies of Christian boys from Balkan and Anatolian villages, who were converted to Islam, given intensive education, and trained for service in either the imperial administration or the elite military corps. The elite military corps recruited through this system became the Sultan's standing infantry and his most reliable troops for several centuries. What was the corps called?
answer: The Janissaries (Yeni Ceri, 'new troops') — at peak about 50,000 men, the first standing salaried infantry in any post-Roman European or West Asian state
choices: The Janissaries (Yeni Ceri, 'new troops') — at peak about 50,000 men, the first standing salaried infantry in any post-Roman European or West Asian state
The Mamluks — though the Mamluk slave-soldier system was a separate parallel institution centered in Egypt
The Sipahis — though the Sipahis were the Ottoman feudal cavalry rather than the devshirme infantry
The Bektashi — though the Bektashi were a Sufi religious order associated with the Janissaries but not identical to them
context: The Janissaries were the world's first modern professional standing army — salaried, drilled, equipped uniformly with firearms (matchlock muskets from the 16th century). The devshirme drew about 1 in 40 Christian boys from a village periodically; conversion to Islam was forced. The system simultaneously imposed real human costs on Christian Balkan families and provided extraordinary opportunities for the boys taken (many rose to senior government posts; the Grand Vizier was often of devshirme origin). The devshirme was discontinued in the late 17th century; the Janissary corps was massacred in 1826 when Mahmud II destroyed them in the 'Auspicious Incident' to make way for a modernized army.

question: The largest stone ruins in sub-Saharan Africa south of the Sahara — about 240 miles south of present-day Harare, Zimbabwe — are the remains of a major medieval African trading city known as Great Zimbabwe. The granite walls of the Great Enclosure rise about 36 feet without mortar; the city housed perhaps 18,000-20,000 people at its peak around 1300-1450 and traded gold across the Indian Ocean with Kilwa, India, and China (Chinese Ming pottery has been excavated at the site). What people built and inhabited Great Zimbabwe?
answer: The Shona — Bantu-speaking ancestors of present-day Zimbabweans, building the city from about 1100 to 1450
choices: The Shona — Bantu-speaking ancestors of present-day Zimbabweans, building the city from about 1100 to 1450
The Phoenicians — building a colonial trading post in the medieval period as part of their late commercial empire
The Persians — Sassanian merchants building a southern trade entrepot from the 6th-9th centuries AD
The Portuguese — building a 15th-century stone factory analogous to their coastal forts on the Indian Ocean trade routes
context: Great Zimbabwe was built by Shona-speaking ancestors of modern Zimbabweans across about 350 years. Colonial-era racist historiography (Cecil Rhodes's company, white-rule Rhodesia) repeatedly tried to attribute the stone city to non-African builders (Phoenicians, Sabaeans, Portuguese, anyone but Black Africans) — a position thoroughly refuted by archaeological and DNA evidence. The city declined after about 1450 — possibly due to environmental degradation, salt depletion, shifting trade routes, or political fragmentation. The name 'Zimbabwe' derives from the Shona dzimba dza mabwe ('houses of stones'). UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. The country was renamed Zimbabwe in 1980 on independence, replacing the colonial name Rhodesia.

question: Polynesian navigators settled the Polynesian triangle from Hawaii in the north to New Zealand in the southwest to Easter Island in the southeast — about 10 million square miles of mostly empty ocean. They reached Easter Island by about 1200 AD and New Zealand by about 1280, using double-hulled voyaging canoes (waka in Maori) and a sophisticated navigation tradition. Western 'discovery' came in the 20th century when Mau Piailug of the Carolines taught the methods to the Hawaiian renaissance. What instruments did traditional Polynesian navigators NOT use?
answer: No compass, no chart, no chronometer, no sextant — navigation by stars, ocean swell patterns, cloud formations, water color, and seabird flight paths
choices: No compass, no chart, no chronometer, no sextant — navigation by stars, ocean swell patterns, cloud formations, water color, and seabird flight paths
No sails — relying entirely on paddling and oceanic current drift across vast distances
No outriggers — using only single-hull canoes that limited safe ocean range to coastal waters
No knowledge of stars — relying entirely on day-time navigation by sun position and ocean swell
context: Polynesian wayfinders memorized star compasses for rising and setting of about 220 named stars, learned the characteristic swell patterns produced by distant landmasses interrupting trade-wind seas, observed cloud formation over islands beyond the horizon, color shifts in water near land, and the homeward flight paths of frigate birds and other seabirds at dusk. Mau Piailug (1932-2010) guided the Hawaiian-built voyaging canoe Hokule'a from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 — the first traditional navigation crossing of those distances in centuries — establishing that the methods had not in fact been lost. The Hokule'a circumnavigated the globe 2014-17 under indigenous navigation including Mau's student Nainoa Thompson.

question: On July 15 1799, a French Army engineering officer named Pierre-Francois Bouchard found a black granodiorite stone slab during fortification work near the Egyptian port of Rosetta (Rashid). The slab bore the same inscription in three scripts — Egyptian hieroglyphs at top, demotic Egyptian script in the middle, ancient Greek at bottom — the priestly decree of King Ptolemy V (196 BC). After Britain defeated France in Egypt, the Rosetta Stone went to the British Museum where it has been displayed since 1802. About how long did it take for hieroglyphic script to be successfully deciphered using the stone?
answer: About 23 years — Jean-Francois Champollion announced his decipherment in September 1822
choices: About 23 years — Jean-Francois Champollion announced his decipherment in September 1822
About 80 years — the decipherment was published in Berlin in 1879 by Heinrich Brugsch
About 5 years — Thomas Young of England published the decipherment in 1804
About 150 years — only in 1949 did Bernard Bothmer finalize the modern reading
context: Champollion (1790-1832) had been studying Coptic (the modern descendant of ancient Egyptian written in Greek-derived characters) as a teenager. The Englishman Thomas Young had made important preliminary progress 1814-19 but did not crack the system; Champollion published the key step in his Lettre a M. Dacier (September 1822), showing that hieroglyphs combined phonetic and ideographic elements rather than being purely symbolic as 17th-18th century European theories had assumed. The decipherment opened ancient Egyptian texts to historical study and founded modern Egyptology. The Rosetta Stone has been controversially held by the British Museum throughout the post-colonial era; Egyptian repatriation requests have repeatedly been declined.

question: Through the early 19th century, Fiji was widely known to Western mariners as the 'Cannibal Isles' — not as sensational exaggeration but as a literal description of regular practice. Ritual cannibalism was embedded in Fijian warfare and chieftaincy: enemy warriors killed in battle were typically eaten. European missionary records, indigenous oral traditions, and 20th-century archaeological evidence at chiefly residence sites all confirm the practice. When did large-scale Fijian cannibalism effectively end?
answer: Within a generation after mid-1800s — paramount chief Ratu Seru Cakobau's conversion to Christianity in 1854 led to formal renunciation across Fiji
choices: Within a generation after mid-1800s — paramount chief Ratu Seru Cakobau's conversion to Christianity in 1854 led to formal renunciation across Fiji
Around 1300 AD — with the formation of the first proto-state across the major Fijian islands under the early Bauan chiefly lineage
In 1953 — with the post-WWII independence movement repudiating colonial-era cultural restrictions imposed by the British administration
Never officially — the practice continues in modified form among traditional Fijian rural communities today across several remote districts
context: Ratu Seru Cakobau, the paramount chief of Bau, formally embraced Methodist Christianity on April 30 1854 and renounced cannibalism. Other Fijian chiefdoms followed across the next decade. The Methodist missionaries (the Wesleyan Methodist Mission Society) had been working in Fiji since 1835. Cakobau ceded Fiji to Britain in 1874 as the islands' first king. The practice's end was driven by Christian missionary work in cooperation with indigenous Fijian Christian converts; this is the Fijian counterpart to the suttee abolition in India, the foot-binding abolition in China, and the Aztec sacrifice abolition under Spanish conquest. Fiji gained independence from Britain in 1970.

question: The West African Kingdom of Dahomey (in present-day Benin) — a powerful slave-trading state from the early 18th through the late 19th century — practiced regular human sacrifice as part of state ceremonies known as the 'Annual Customs' (Xwetanu in Fon). Hundreds of slaves (most originally captured in raids on neighboring peoples and held in royal compounds for the purpose) were killed each year in elaborate court ceremonies — beheaded, with the heads displayed in walls around the palace at Abomey. King Ghezo (reigned 1818-1858) at peak reportedly executed thousands annually. The practice ended with French conquest of Dahomey in what specific year?
answer: 1894 — France defeated King Behanzin and dissolved the Kingdom of Dahomey in the Second Franco-Dahomean War
choices: 1894 — France defeated King Behanzin and dissolved the Kingdom of Dahomey in the Second Franco-Dahomean War
1807 — under Anglo-French pressure following the British abolition of the slave trade
1953 — with French recognition of Dahomean political autonomy
1960 — with Dahomean (Benin) independence from France
context: France conquered Dahomey in 1892-94, ending the kingdom and its slave-trading and human-sacrifice practices. Burton's mid-19th-century mission to Dahomey documented the Annual Customs in detail. The famous Dahomean amazons (Mino) — an all-female military regiment of about 6,000 — fought a noted resistance to the French invasion. Honest history of pre-modern West African states includes both the substantial achievements of states like Mali (Sankore manuscripts, Mansa Musa's wealth) and the brutal practices of others like Dahomey (state human sacrifice, slave-raiding). Modern Benin (independence 1960) honors its precolonial Dahomean heritage selectively.

question: The Iroquois Confederacy (Haudenosaunee — the 'People of the Longhouse') of upstate New York comprised five (later six) member nations and represented one of the most sophisticated indigenous political structures in pre-Columbian North America — the basis for some elements of later American federal theory. The Iroquois were also feared across the Eastern Woodlands for the ritual torture and execution of captives taken in war (the 'mourning wars' that replaced lost relatives). Jesuit missionary observers in New France documented the practices in extensive 17th-century writings. About how long could the torture rituals last?
answer: Often several days — captives were burned with embers and progressively dismembered before death; survivors might be eaten in part
choices: Often several days — captives were burned with embers and progressively dismembered before death; survivors might be eaten in part
About 30 minutes — relatively quick execution after public display
About a week — but the captive was kept alive comfortably until the public execution
Several years — captives were held as servants before eventual ritual execution
context: The Jesuit Relations (annual reports of Jesuit missions in New France, 1632-73) contain detailed accounts of Iroquois torture of captives — sometimes lasting several days, including burning, partial dismemberment, and ritual cannibalism of parts of the dead. Adoption of captives into the tribe in place of lost relatives was an alternative outcome; many adopted captives became fully assimilated. The Iroquois pattern is documented but should not be sensationalized in isolation: the same period in Europe saw Protestant-Catholic atrocities on equally horrifying scale. The torture practices ended with the broader 18th-19th century transition of indigenous societies under European-American pressure and Christian missionary work; the Iroquois political structure adapted across the colonial and U.S. periods.

question: In 1271 the 17-year-old Marco Polo of Venice left on a four-year overland journey to Khanbaliq (present-day Beijing) with his father Niccolo and uncle Maffeo, who had visited Kublai Khan's court on an earlier trip and were returning with letters from Pope Gregory X. They reached Kublai's court in 1275 and Marco stayed about 17 years, traveling extensively across Mongol-ruled China as a court official before returning to Venice in 1295. He dictated his Travels (Il Milione) while in a Genoese prison in 1298-99 to fellow prisoner Rustichello of Pisa. The book is one of the most important pre-modern travel accounts. What specific Chinese technology did Marco Polo report having seen — that startled European readers as fiction?
answer: Paper currency — circulated across Mongol China under imperial seal, accepted everywhere on pain of death for refusing it
choices: Paper currency — circulated across Mongol China under imperial seal, accepted everywhere on pain of death for refusing it
Movable-type printing — used to produce identical state edicts across the empire
Magnetic compass navigation — used by Chinese merchant junks for coastal trade
Gunpowder weaponry — used by Mongol armies in their late 13th-century campaigns
context: The Mongol Yuan dynasty had inherited from Song China the system of paper currency under state guarantee — astonishing to Western European readers whose monarchs still depended on the weight of gold and silver coin. Marco Polo describes the bark-paper bills, the imperial vermilion seal, and the legal penalty (death) for refusing the bills as payment. He also reports the use of coal as fuel ('black stones from the mountains'), the Mongol postal system, and the wealth of the great city of Hangzhou ('Kinsay'). Many medieval European readers (and some modern scholars) doubted Marco Polo had visited China at all; the consensus today is that the journey was real even if some details were exaggerated or embellished.

question: On November 26 1922, in the Valley of the Kings on the west bank of the Nile at Luxor (ancient Thebes), British Egyptologist Howard Carter peered by candlelight through a hole he had cut in the sealed door of an obscure New Kingdom royal tomb (KV62). His financial backer Lord Carnarvon — beside him — asked what Carter could see. Carter's reply has become one of the iconic moments of 20th-century archaeology. What did Carter say?
answer: 'Yes, wonderful things'
choices: 'Yes, wonderful things'
'Beyond all imagining'
'A king sleeping in gold'
'The tomb is intact'
context: Carter, asked by Carnarvon 'Can you see anything?', replied 'Yes, wonderful things.' The tomb of Tutankhamun — a minor pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty who reigned about 1332-1323 BC and died at about age 19 — was the only essentially intact royal tomb ever found in the Valley of the Kings. About 5,000 grave goods including the solid gold inner coffin (about 250 lb) and the famous gold death mask were catalogued over the following decade. Lord Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite (later complications) in April 1923, triggering decades of newspaper-driven 'curse of the pharaohs' folklore. The objects are housed at the Grand Egyptian Museum near Cairo and the Egyptian Museum in Tahrir Square.

question: Evariste Galois was 20, twice expelled from the Ecole Normale Superieure for political activity, on parole for an arms-and-uniform offense, and scheduled to fight a duel at dawn on May 31 1832 over a love affair. He spent the previous night writing mathematics in the margins of a letter to his friend Auguste Chevalier. He sketched proofs of theorems that would not be fully understood for another forty years and would eventually become the foundation of group theory and modern algebra. Across the bottom of one page, in French, he wrote a famous five-word phrase. What did Galois write?
answer: 'Je n'ai pas le temps' — 'I have not time'
choices: 'Je n'ai pas le temps' — 'I have not time'
'Adieu, ma mere' — 'Farewell, mother'
'Vive la Republique' — 'Long live the Republic'
'La posterite jugera' — 'Posterity will judge'
context: Galois was shot in the abdomen at dawn and died in a Paris hospital the next morning, May 31 1832. He was buried in a common grave; the exact location is lost. The letter to Chevalier asked Carl Gauss and Carl Gustav Jacobi to give their public opinion on the theorems' importance — 'not as to whether they are true, but as to whether they are important.' Joseph Liouville finally published Galois's collected works in 1846, fourteen years after his death. Group theory now underlies particle physics, crystallography, and modern cryptography. Galois had been politically active in the Republican movement; he had been imprisoned in 1831 for proposing a toast 'To Louis-Philippe' while holding a dagger.

question: On January 16 1913 the Cambridge mathematician Godfrey Harold Hardy received a 10-page letter from Madras, India written by an unknown 25-year-old shipping-office clerk with no formal university training. The letter contained about 120 mathematical theorems and conjectures, including several Hardy could not even formulate, let alone prove. Hardy showed the letter to his colleague John Edensor Littlewood. Together they recognized they were reading something unprecedented. Who had written the letter?
answer: Srinivasa Ramanujan — Hardy arranged his passage to Cambridge within months
choices: Srinivasa Ramanujan — Hardy arranged his passage to Cambridge within months
Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar — Hardy arranged a scholarship to Cambridge for the young astrophysicist
Satyendra Nath Bose — the Calcutta physicist whose 1924 paper to Einstein would generate Bose-Einstein statistics
Meghnad Saha — the Dhaka astrophysicist whose stellar ionization equation would appear in 1920
context: Ramanujan (1887-1920) had derived much of modern analytic number theory independently in isolation in Madras, working from secondhand 19th-century textbooks. Hardy: 'They must be true, because if they were not true, no one would have had the imagination to invent them.' Ramanujan arrived at Cambridge in April 1914; he was elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1918 — the first Indian Fellow elected primarily for mathematics. His Cambridge stay was crippled by malnutrition (vegetarian diet hard to maintain in wartime Britain) and tuberculosis. He returned to India in 1919 and died at age 32 in 1920. His 'lost notebook' of late work was rediscovered in 1976; mathematicians are still proving his conjectures.

question: Lise Meitner (1878-1968), Austrian-Swedish physicist, had worked with German chemist Otto Hahn in Berlin on nuclear physics for 30 years. As a Jewish Austrian she fled Nazi Germany in summer 1938 for Sweden. At Christmas 1938 with her nephew physicist Otto Frisch, she received Hahn's letter describing a strange result: bombarding uranium with neutrons produced barium. Walking in the snow, Meitner worked out the physics — uranium nuclei were splitting. She and Frisch coined 'nuclear fission' in their February 1939 Nature paper. Who got the 1944 Nobel in Chemistry?
answer: Otto Hahn alone — Meitner was infamously omitted, in what is widely regarded as one of the most egregious Nobel oversights
choices: Otto Hahn alone — Meitner was infamously omitted, in what is widely regarded as one of the most egregious Nobel oversights
Hahn and Meitner jointly — the prize was awarded equally to both for the chemistry and the theoretical interpretation
Hahn and Fritz Strassmann jointly — Meitner was omitted but the radiochemist co-discoverer received credit
Meitner and Otto Frisch jointly — the Nobel Committee recognized the theoretical interpretation as the prize-worthy element
context: The Nobel Committee's omission of Meitner has been widely criticized since the prize was awarded; some commentators have called it the most consequential Nobel oversight ever made. Hahn collected the chemistry credit; the necessary physical theory had been Meitner's. Element 109 was named meitnerium in her honor in 1997. Meitner refused to participate in the Manhattan Project despite recruitment offers; she said 'I will have nothing to do with a bomb!' She died in Cambridge, England in 1968 at age 89. The Hahn-Meitner Institute in Berlin (founded 1959) was named for both after Meitner's death; in 2009 it was renamed the Helmholtz Center.

question: Niels Bohr (1885-1962, Copenhagen) and Albert Einstein (1879-1955, Princeton) — the two most influential physicists of their generation — debated the foundations of quantum mechanics across more than a decade at successive Solvay Conferences in Brussels and in extensive correspondence. Einstein could never accept the radical interpretation of quantum measurement that Bohr's Copenhagen Interpretation had institutionalized. Einstein's most famous summary objection to quantum mechanics was a one-line aphorism. What did Einstein famously say about quantum indeterminacy?
answer: 'God does not play dice with the universe'
choices: 'God does not play dice with the universe'
'The Almighty has more sense than to roll dice'
'I cannot believe the moon is not there when no one looks at it'
'A theory may be useful without being true'
context: Einstein's 'God does not play dice' was offered repeatedly in letters and in conference exchanges from the 1920s onward. Bohr's reply at the Sixth Solvay Conference (1930): 'Einstein, stop telling God what to do.' The Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paper of 1935 (the EPR paradox) was Einstein's most sophisticated objection — arguing that quantum mechanics must be incomplete because it predicted 'spooky action at a distance.' John Stewart Bell's 1964 theorem and subsequent experimental tests (Alain Aspect 1982, 2022 Nobel Prize) decisively confirmed quantum predictions and refuted local-hidden-variable theories of the kind Einstein had hoped for. The debates are widely cited as the most consequential intellectual exchange in 20th-century physics.

question: Alan Turing (1912-1954), the founder of modern computer science and a central figure in the British code-breaking effort at Bletchley Park during WWII, was arrested in January 1952 for homosexual acts (illegal in Britain under the 1885 Criminal Law Amendment Act). At his trial in March 1952 he chose chemical castration via estrogen injections over prison. The hormonal treatment caused gynecomastia and disrupted his physical and emotional life. On June 7 1954, his housekeeper found him dead in bed at age 41. What was the immediate cause of his death?
answer: Cyanide poisoning — a half-eaten apple beside the bed appeared to have been the delivery method
choices: Cyanide poisoning — a half-eaten apple beside the bed appeared to have been the delivery method
Heart attack secondary to estrogen treatment — natural causes attested by the coroner
Tuberculosis — caught at Manchester University and untreated due to his social isolation
Carbon monoxide poisoning — a gas-fire leak in his Cheshire home detected after his death
context: The coroner ruled suicide; the half-eaten apple beside the bed contained no measurable cyanide, but Turing's bedside lab contained cyanide for electroplating experiments. Some recent revisionist accounts have suggested possible accidental poisoning. Turing's WWII work at Bletchley Park breaking the German Enigma cipher had been instrumental in the Allied victory. Britain issued a formal posthumous apology in 2009 (Prime Minister Gordon Brown) and a royal pardon in 2013. The 2014 film The Imitation Game (Benedict Cumberbatch) dramatized the story. Turing was 41 at his death.

question: Hypatia of Alexandria (about 350-415 AD), Neoplatonist philosopher, mathematician, and astronomer, was the daughter of the mathematician Theon of Alexandria and the most prominent woman intellectual of the late antique Mediterranean. She had advised Roman officials, taught philosophy publicly, and corresponded extensively with the Christian bishop Synesius of Cyrene (her former student). In March 415 AD, during a period of political conflict between the Roman prefect Orestes and the patriarch Cyril of Alexandria, she was attacked by a Christian mob in the streets of the city. What happened to Hypatia in March 415?
answer: Dragged from her carriage to a church, stripped, killed by being torn to pieces with broken ceramic tiles, body burned outside the city
choices: Dragged from her carriage to a church, stripped, killed by being torn to pieces with broken ceramic tiles, body burned outside the city
Beheaded in the public marketplace under the order of Bishop Cyril for the crime of heresy
Drowned in the Mediterranean from a boat off Pharos under a sentence pronounced in absentia by the Patriarchate
Buried alive in her own house under masonry collapsed during a Christian riot against her teaching
context: The account is from Socrates Scholasticus's Historia Ecclesiastica written about a generation later. The murder is widely treated as a symbolic close of the antique Greek philosophical tradition in Alexandria, though the philosophical schools continued elsewhere (Athens until Justinian closed them in 529; the Eastern Christian intellectual tradition continued at the Patriarchal Academy of Constantinople). Hypatia's mathematical commentaries (on Apollonius, Diophantus, Ptolemy's Almagest) are lost. The story has been politicized in various ways since Edward Gibbon's Decline and Fall (1776). Charles Kingsley's novel Hypatia (1853), Carl Sagan's Cosmos (1980), and Alejandro Amenabar's film Agora (2009) are influential modern treatments.

question: Georg Cantor (1845-1918), German mathematician, founder of modern set theory, proved during the 1870s-80s that there are different sizes of infinity — the natural and rational numbers are countable, but the real numbers form a strictly larger infinite set, and an infinite hierarchy of larger infinities (the transfinite cardinals) exists. Cantor's senior contemporary Leopold Kronecker — the dominant figure at Berlin — denounced his transfinite numbers as 'mathematical insanity' and blocked his career for years. What happened to Cantor in later life?
answer: Suffered a major nervous breakdown in 1884, spent the last years of his life in and out of psychiatric clinics, died of malnutrition at Halle in 1918 during WWI
choices: Suffered a major nervous breakdown in 1884, spent the last years of his life in and out of psychiatric clinics, died of malnutrition at Halle in 1918 during WWI
Won the Fields Medal at its founding in 1936 in posthumous recognition of his foundational work
Emigrated to England to escape Kronecker's persecution, settled at Oxford where he founded modern English logic
Recanted his transfinite theories in 1910 under combined pressure from Kronecker and Henri Poincare
context: Cantor's depression and breakdowns are well documented in correspondence; he spent extended periods at the sanatorium at Halle. He died there January 6 1918 of heart failure exacerbated by malnutrition during the wartime German food shortages. By the time of his death the mathematical community had recognized his work as foundational; David Hilbert famously said 'from the paradise Cantor has opened to us no one shall be able to drive us out.' Modern set theory and the formal foundations of mathematics depend on Cantor's work; the continuum hypothesis he posed in 1878 was eventually shown to be independent of standard set theory axioms (Godel 1940, Cohen 1963).

question: Ludwig Boltzmann (1844-1906), Austrian physicist who developed statistical mechanics — the mathematical bridge between Newtonian mechanics at the microscopic scale and thermodynamics at the macroscopic scale — was attacked through much of his career by other physicists (Ernst Mach, Wilhelm Ostwald) who did not believe atoms physically existed. He suffered from cyclothymic mood disorder. On September 5 1906, on holiday at Duino near Trieste with his family, he hanged himself. His tombstone in Vienna's Zentralfriedhof carries one specific equation that summarizes his greatest work. What equation is on Boltzmann's tombstone?
answer: S = k log W — entropy equals Boltzmann's constant times the logarithm of microstates
choices: S = k log W — entropy equals Boltzmann's constant times the logarithm of microstates
PV = nRT — the ideal gas law in Boltzmann's complete derivation form
F = ma — Newton's second law as Boltzmann had refined it through statistical foundations
E = h-nu — the Planck quantum-energy relation that Boltzmann had anticipated
context: S = k log W is Boltzmann's entropy formula — the statistical interpretation of the second law of thermodynamics — connecting entropy (S) to the number of microscopic configurations (W) producing a given macroscopic state, with k (Boltzmann's constant) the conversion factor. The formula is one of the founding equations of statistical physics. The atomic hypothesis Boltzmann had defended was conclusively confirmed by Einstein's 1905 paper on Brownian motion and Jean Perrin's experimental confirmation 1908 — but only after Boltzmann's death. Boltzmann's grave in Vienna with the engraved equation is a destination for physicists; Stephen Hawking visited and reportedly said it was 'the most beautiful equation in physics.'

question: At 5:29:45 AM on July 16 1945, in the New Mexico desert north of Alamogordo, the United States detonated the world's first nuclear weapon — the plutonium implosion device codenamed Trinity. The fireball rose an estimated 40,000 feet; the heat at zero exceeded the surface temperature of the Sun. Watching from a base camp 10 miles away, the scientific director of the Los Alamos laboratory — already a student of Sanskrit literature — later said that a verse from the Bhagavad Gita ran through his mind as he watched the cloud rise. What was the verse?
answer: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds'
choices: 'Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds'
'I have seen the fire that consumes the gods'
'In the heart of the desert, the dawn before dawn'
'We have lit a fire we cannot extinguish'
context: J. Robert Oppenheimer's quote is from Bhagavad Gita Chapter 11, verse 32 — Vishnu's self-revelation to Arjuna in his world-destroying form. Oppenheimer had been studying Sanskrit for years with Arthur Ryder at Berkeley and translated the verse himself from the original. His pacifist brother Frank Oppenheimer, also present at Trinity, recalled Robert's first reported words as the simpler 'It worked.' Trinity confirmed the plutonium implosion design; the uranium-gun Little Boy bomb dropped on Hiroshima August 6 1945 had not been tested. Oppenheimer's security clearance was revoked in 1954 in a closed AEC hearing widely regarded as politically motivated; the AEC formally vacated the decision in December 2022.

question: On the second voyage of HMS Beagle (1831-36), the young naturalist Charles Darwin spent several weeks in the Galapagos Islands in September-October 1835. He observed that the islands' finch species had specialized beaks suited to different food sources — but did not understand the significance until the ornithologist John Gould examined his specimens in London in 1837 and explained that what Darwin had taken as different finch species from a single island were in fact varieties from different islands, each adapted to its specific ecological niche. How long after the Galapagos visit did Darwin publish On the Origin of Species?
answer: About 24 years — the Beagle returned 1836; Origin was published November 24 1859
choices: About 24 years — the Beagle returned 1836; Origin was published November 24 1859
About 5 years — Darwin published the theory immediately after Gould's 1837 identification
About 50 years — Darwin's mature theory required half a century of correspondence and refinement
About 100 years — Origin was published in 1859 but the theory only fully developed posthumously
context: Darwin had the essentials of natural selection worked out by 1838 — Thomas Malthus's Essay on Population had been the catalyst — but delayed publication for over two decades while gathering further evidence and corresponding with naturalists worldwide. In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace's letter from the Malay archipelago, describing essentially the same mechanism, forced Darwin's hand. Their joint paper was presented at the Linnean Society in July 1858 with neither author present (Darwin's young son had died of scarlet fever). Origin was published November 24 1859 by John Murray; the first print run of 1,250 sold out the first day. The book has been continuously in print since.

question: Marie Sklodowska Curie (1867-1934), Polish-born French physicist and chemist, isolated two new radioactive elements — polonium (named for her native Poland) and radium — from tons of pitchblende ore processed in a converted shed in Paris with her husband Pierre Curie. She made one specific Nobel Prize history that has been matched only twice since. What did Marie Curie achieve in Nobel terms?
answer: First person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics 1903 (with Pierre and Becquerel) and Chemistry 1911 (solo)
choices: First person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics 1903 (with Pierre and Becquerel) and Chemistry 1911 (solo)
First person to win three Nobel Prizes — Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911, and Peace 1925
First person to share a Nobel Prize with a spouse — establishing the precedent later followed by the Joliot-Curies
First woman to win the Nobel Prize in any field — Physics 1903 with Pierre and Henri Becquerel
context: Marie Curie was first to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (Physics 1903, Chemistry 1911). She was also the first woman to win a Nobel of any kind (1903). Only Linus Pauling (Chemistry 1954, Peace 1962) has since matched the achievement of multiple Nobels by one person in different fields. Her daughter Irene Joliot-Curie won Chemistry 1935 with her husband Frederic Joliot-Curie — making the Curies the only family with five Nobel laureates in two generations. Marie Curie died of aplastic anemia in 1934 from cumulative radiation exposure. Her notebooks remain so radioactive they are stored in lead-lined boxes and handled in protective clothing; they will not be safe to read directly without protection for approximately another 1,500 years.

question: In March 1989 a 33-year-old British software engineer at CERN — the European Organization for Nuclear Research outside Geneva — submitted a paper to his supervisor titled 'Information Management: A Proposal' outlining a hypertext system to allow physicists to share documents across CERN's heterogeneous computer network. His supervisor's only marginalia were 'vague, but exciting.' Over the following two years he wrote the underlying protocols (HTTP, HTML, URL) and the first browser. He released the project to the public in 1991 — and chose, against the counsel of senior CERN staff, not to patent it. Who built the World Wide Web?
answer: Tim Berners-Lee — released the WWW to the public domain in 1991 without patent royalties or licensing
choices: Tim Berners-Lee — released the WWW to the public domain in 1991 without patent royalties or licensing
Vinton Cerf — designer of TCP/IP, who scaled the Web up to global commercial application from his Stanford lab
Robert Cailliau — Berners-Lee's CERN collaborator who actually wrote the first published browser
Marc Andreessen — University of Illinois undergraduate whose Mosaic browser opened the public Web in 1993
context: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989-91. Robert Cailliau co-developed the first publicly released browser. The decision to release the protocols royalty-free in 1991-93 — Berners-Lee resisting CERN management pressure to patent the technology — is one of the most consequential intellectual-property decisions in modern technological history. The Mosaic browser of Marc Andreessen's NCSA team (1993) opened the Web to non-expert users; Netscape Navigator (1994) launched the dot-com era. Berners-Lee was knighted in 2004 and received the inaugural ACM Turing Award in 2016. The Web is now used by about 5 billion people worldwide.

question: On January 28 1986, the Space Shuttle Challenger broke up 73 seconds after liftoff from the Kennedy Space Center, killing all seven crew members including the schoolteacher Christa McAuliffe. President Reagan appointed a presidential commission chaired by former Secretary of State William Rogers to investigate. The most famous moment of the commission's televised hearings came when one of the commissioners — Caltech physicist Richard Feynman — demonstrated the cause of the disaster live on national television with a piece of O-ring rubber and a glass of ice water. What did Feynman show?
answer: He dropped a clamped piece of O-ring rubber into the ice water — showing it lost its flexibility at near-freezing temperatures and confirming the cold-launch failure
choices: He dropped a clamped piece of O-ring rubber into the ice water — showing it lost its flexibility at near-freezing temperatures and confirming the cold-launch failure
He heated the O-ring with a Bunsen burner — showing it became sticky and friction-bound above operating temperatures
He compressed the O-ring in a vise — showing it failed to seal at the specific psi of solid-rocket-booster joints
He froze the O-ring overnight — showing it became brittle and cracked under load at the next launch
context: Feynman had been investigating O-ring temperature data on his own initiative; the launch had occurred in unusually cold Florida weather (overnight low 24 F, well below the O-ring's certified operating range). His ice-water demonstration in the February 11 1986 commission hearing made the technical issue concrete for a non-engineering audience. Feynman's individual appendix to the commission report — sharply critical of NASA management failures — was published over Chairman Rogers's objection. Feynman: 'For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for Nature cannot be fooled.' He died of cancer in February 1988, two years after Challenger.

question: On December 17 1903 at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first sustained powered controlled flights of a heavier-than-air machine. They had flipped a coin; Orville won. Orville's first flight covered 120 feet in 12 seconds; the fourth flight by Wilbur covered 852 feet in 59 seconds. Almost no American newspaper reported the event correctly for years; aeronautical journals worldwide were skeptical. What had the brothers done that previous experimenters had failed at?
answer: Combined three-axis controlled flight (pitch, roll, yaw) with a sufficient internal-combustion power-to-weight ratio for sustained level flight
choices: Combined three-axis controlled flight (pitch, roll, yaw) with a sufficient internal-combustion power-to-weight ratio for sustained level flight
Built the first internal-combustion engine light enough to lift its own weight off the ground
Used the first pure-fabric wing instead of the heavier wood-and-canvas wings that had failed
Used the first compass-and-altitude instrument cluster permitting controlled flight in cloud
context: The Wrights' key contribution was three-axis control through wing-warping (for roll), forward elevator (for pitch), and rudder (for yaw, coordinated with the wing-warp). Other experimenters (Langley, Lilienthal, Ader) had powered platforms or gliders, but no one had solved control. The Wrights had refined their understanding through extensive wind-tunnel testing in Dayton 1901-02 and through unpowered glider trials at Kitty Hawk in 1900-02. Their 1903 Wright Flyer is at the National Air and Space Museum in Washington DC. The brothers received credit only slowly — Wilbur died of typhoid in 1912; Orville lived until 1948 and helped establish the modern understanding of their priority.

question: On June 26 1963, ten months before his assassination, President John F. Kennedy stood on the steps of Schoneberg City Hall in West Berlin and addressed a crowd of about 450,000 people — roughly two-thirds the population of West Berlin. The address was a moral declaration of American commitment to a city encircled by the Soviet bloc and divided by the Berlin Wall built less than two years earlier. The peroration ended with a German phrase that became iconic across the Cold War. What did Kennedy say?
answer: 'Ich bin ein Berliner' — 'I am a Berliner'
choices: 'Ich bin ein Berliner' — 'I am a Berliner'
'Heute Berlin, morgen die Welt' — 'Today Berlin, tomorrow the world'
'Berlin gehort euch nicht' — 'Berlin does not belong to you' — directed at the Soviet ambassadors
'Wir sind alle Berliner' — 'We are all Berliners'
context: Kennedy quote: 'All free men, wherever they may live, are citizens of Berlin, and therefore, as a free man, I take pride in the words: Ich bin ein Berliner!' An urban legend that the article 'ein' made it 'I am a jelly doughnut' is false — 'Ich bin ein Berliner' is correct German that a native speaker would also use in the metaphorical sense Kennedy intended (the citizen-of-Berlin reading dominates context). The speech is now widely regarded as one of the great Cold War American speeches alongside Reagan's Brandenburg address 24 years later. Kennedy was assassinated November 22 1963 — five months after the Berlin trip.

question: On December 2 1942, on a squash court under the disused west stands of the University of Chicago's Stagg Field, the Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi supervised the world's first controlled self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. The pile (Chicago Pile-1) used about 360 tons of graphite as moderator, with 45 tons of uranium oxide and uranium metal embedded in the graphite. The cadmium control rods were pulled out fractionally over six hours; at 3:25 PM Fermi calculated they had achieved criticality. The senior present, Arthur Compton, telephoned James Conant in Washington with a coded message. What was Conant told?
answer: 'The Italian navigator has just landed in the new world' — 'How were the natives?' Compton: 'Very friendly'
choices: 'The Italian navigator has just landed in the new world' — 'How were the natives?' Compton: 'Very friendly'
'The egg has cracked' — 'And the chick?' Compton: 'It is breathing healthily'
'Columbus has arrived' — 'And the natives?' Compton: 'Welcoming and peaceful'
'The dam holds' — 'And the river?' Compton: 'Flowing through cleanly'
context: The 'Italian navigator' was Fermi himself; the 'natives' were the neutrons. The Chicago Pile demonstration confirmed the Manhattan Project's central physical premise; the plutonium production reactors at Hanford, Washington and the uranium-enrichment plants at Oak Ridge, Tennessee followed at industrial scale. Fermi was 41. He had emigrated to the United States with his Jewish wife Laura in January 1939 to escape Mussolini's racial laws (using his 1938 trip to Stockholm for the Nobel as the family's exit). Fermi died of stomach cancer in 1954, age 53. The Chicago site is now marked by Henry Moore's bronze sculpture Nuclear Energy (installed 1967).

question: On February 28 1953, James Watson (24, American) and Francis Crick (36, English) walked into the Eagle pub on Bene't Street in Cambridge for lunch. Crick announced to the patrons that they had 'discovered the secret of life.' That morning they had finally fitted together a physical model — six feet tall, of metal plates, rods, and clamps — of the structure of DNA. They had benefited critically from one specific X-ray image obtained by another researcher at King's College London — shown to them without her permission. Whose work made it possible?
answer: Rosalind Franklin — her crystallographic Photo 51 shown to Watson by Maurice Wilkins without Franklin's permission
choices: Rosalind Franklin — her crystallographic Photo 51 shown to Watson by Maurice Wilkins without Franklin's permission
Linus Pauling — his preliminary triple-helix paper that Watson and Crick obtained in draft from Caltech
Erwin Chargaff — his published 1948 base-pairing ratios that established the A-T and G-C equivalences
Maurice Wilkins — his independent crystallographic series at King's College that confirmed the helix without further controversy
context: Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51 (May 1952) showed the unambiguous diffraction pattern of a helical structure. Maurice Wilkins showed it to Watson without Franklin's knowledge in January 1953. Watson and Crick's April 25 1953 Nature paper credited Wilkins and Franklin in passing; the 1962 Nobel Prize was awarded to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins — Franklin had died of ovarian cancer in 1958 at age 37 and Nobels are not awarded posthumously. Modern accounts (especially Brenda Maddox's 2002 biography) have substantially restored Franklin's recognition. Watson's 1968 memoir The Double Helix presented a candid (and to many readers ungenerous) account of the discovery race.

question: In 1931, at age 25, the Austrian mathematician Kurt Godel published a paper in the Monatshefte fur Mathematik und Physik demonstrating that any sufficiently powerful consistent formal axiomatic system of arithmetic must contain statements that are true but cannot be proved within the system itself. The result destroyed David Hilbert's program to derive all of mathematics from a complete and consistent axiomatic foundation. Godel emigrated to the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1940. He developed paranoid delusions in his later years. What was the cause of his death in January 1978?
answer: Starvation — Godel refused to eat any food not prepared by his wife Adele, who was herself hospitalized; he weighed 65 pounds at his death
choices: Starvation — Godel refused to eat any food not prepared by his wife Adele, who was herself hospitalized; he weighed 65 pounds at his death
Heart attack — natural causes despite years of mental decline and increasing isolation from colleagues
Suicide — he hanged himself in his hospital room days after Adele's death in a Vienna nursing facility
Murder — he was killed by a mugger near the Princeton train station on a winter evening walk
context: Adele Godel had managed his food paranoia for decades; in her final hospitalization in winter 1977-78 Godel could not eat, weighing about 65 lb at his death on January 14 1978. Godel's 1931 incompleteness theorems are among the most consequential results in 20th-century mathematics. He was a close friend of Einstein at the Institute for Advanced Study; the two reportedly walked together to and from the Institute almost daily. Godel also discovered a solution to Einstein's field equations of general relativity (1949) describing a rotating universe permitting closed timelike curves (time travel into the past). The 'Godel universe' is mathematically valid but does not appear to describe our actual cosmos.

question: On December 14 1911, the Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and four companions reached the geographic South Pole with their dog sleds. They planted the Norwegian flag and stayed three days taking observations to confirm they were within a mile of the actual pole. They returned safely. About a month later, on January 17 1912, a competing British expedition under Robert Falcon Scott reached the same point. What did Scott find at the South Pole?
answer: Amundsen's tent and Norwegian flag — with a letter from Amundsen asking Scott to deliver one enclosed if Amundsen did not return alive
choices: Amundsen's tent and Norwegian flag — with a letter from Amundsen asking Scott to deliver one enclosed if Amundsen did not return alive
Open ice with no marker — Amundsen had broken camp without leaving any sign of his prior arrival
A small commemorative cairn — built by Amundsen's men but no further documentation
Amundsen's broken sled — abandoned when he had been forced to retreat before reaching the pole
context: Amundsen had left the Polheim tent, the flag, and supplies, plus a written record of his arrival and a polite letter asking Scott to deliver an enclosed letter to King Haakon VII of Norway if Amundsen did not return safely. Scott wrote in his journal: 'Great God! this is an awful place and terrible enough for us to have laboured to it without the reward of priority.' Scott and his four companions all died on the return journey from the Pole. The bodies of Scott, Bowers, and Wilson were found 8 months later in their tent, 11 miles from the next supply depot. Amundsen later said he had succeeded mainly by using dogs (Scott had used ponies and motor sleds, both unsuited to the conditions). Amundsen disappeared in 1928 on a flight to rescue Italian explorer Umberto Nobile.

question: On January 28 1986, in cold conditions at the Kennedy Space Center (overnight low about 24 F), the Space Shuttle Challenger lifted off carrying STS-51-L. At 73 seconds into the flight a leak from the right solid rocket booster's lower field joint ignited propellant; the external tank ruptured; the shuttle broke apart at about 46,000 feet. All seven crew members were killed. The catastrophe was watched live by millions of American school children because of one specific crew member. Who had drawn the public attention?
answer: Christa McAuliffe — the New Hampshire high school teacher selected for the 'Teacher in Space' program
choices: Christa McAuliffe — the New Hampshire high school teacher selected for the 'Teacher in Space' program
Sally Ride — NASA's first American female astronaut, returning for a third flight
Dick Scobee — a veteran shuttle commander whose father had been a Tuskegee airman
Ronald McNair — a respected astrophysicist who would have become the second African-American in space
context: Christa McAuliffe (1948-1986) was a social studies teacher at Concord High School in New Hampshire selected from over 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space Project. The other crew members included Commander Dick Scobee, Pilot Michael Smith, Mission Specialists Judith Resnik, Ellison Onizuka, and Ronald McNair, and Payload Specialist Gregory Jarvis. President Reagan's January 28 1986 televised address (delayed from a scheduled State of the Union) ended with the John Gillespie Magee Jr. lines about slipping the surly bonds of earth to touch the face of God. The Rogers Commission's investigation identified the O-ring failure and broader NASA management issues.
